The Śaktisaṅgama Tantra. First Part.
The Kālī Section.
Salutations to the venerable gurus.
The Śrī Śaktisaṅgama Tantra. The Kālī Section.
The First Chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
O Lord of Beings, whose form is without beginning, O Moon-crested Śaṅkara!
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, one to be worshipped by all, Sovereign of the gods!
O stainless one, formless one, eternal bliss, mine of virtues;
O Supreme Lord who transcends qualities, who is beyond all, and higher than the highest! 1-2.
The entire world, including all things stationary and moving, has arisen from you;
likewise, all the tantras—numbering in the hundreds of thousands, tens of millions, and billions—have been heard by us.
O God, O Lord, Sovereign of the Kings of Kings, I have heard the *Tantrārṇava* and other [tantras], and the King of Tantras has been heard, O God, as well as its various divisions. (1–4)
O Lord, I have heard of the elixirs (rasāyana) and various spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) have been heard;
now [I wish to hear] the supreme among the best of tantras, named Śaktisaṅgama. 1-5.
O Lord of the gods of gods, it was indicated in the scripture titled *Mantrasiddhi*, yet it was not told to me, O Deva; O Lord, cut through my doubt. (1-6)
"O Lord of Gods, please relate the Tantra which consists of four sections, which is the most supreme among all essences, and which has come down through the lineage of the oral tradition. (1.7)
O Lord, this sovereign king of tantras is complete, both with and without its dependencies;
it serves as a guide for those who have strayed from the traditional lineage.
"O Lord, tell me the Tantra that bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*) in the Kali age.
Śrī Śiva said:
"The King of Tantras, radiant with eight sections (*khaṇḍa*), was previously taught."
The first half and the second half consist of two and a half [syllables] each;
the first half is designated as beginning with *ka*, while the second is designated as beginning with *ha*.
O Maheśānī, in the sections beginning with *ka* there are four Vedic portions (*vedakhaṇḍas*), and likewise four in those beginning with *ha*;
in each section, O Great Goddess, there are three thousand and six hundred [verses].
"One hundred verses and thirty-six chapters per chapter—thus one section (khaṇḍa) is described; in this manner, they know there are eight sections. (1–12)
This work composed by Divyaugha shall be the gateway to the Guru;
it is the venerable Bṛhattantrarāja known by the name Śaktisaṅgama.
This auspicious tantra, consisting of sixty thousand [verses] and joined with the Veda-sections, was composed by Divyaugha; it is the most excellent among all tantras. (1-14)
The second form fashioned since beginningless time is Tārā;
the third is Sundarī, and the fourth is Chinnamastakā.
In each age, there are as many [Purāṇas] as the moon (one), but in the Kali age, there are four parts;
O Śivā, at the end of six hundred years, there are one hundred and seventy-two [verses].

O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, [the teaching] manifests through the gateway of the Divine Current (divyaugha) for the purpose of destroying the Buddhists and heretics, and indeed for the sake of the tradition. (1-17)
O Goddess, for the sake of destroying those who cause the confusion of traditions, for the purpose of establishing the true tradition, and for the protection of Brahmanahood; 1-18.
O Pārvatī, for the sake of accomplishing the science of mantras, Kālikā and Tārā manifest within the tantras; O Pārvatī, they abide there forever. 1-19.
Then, O Śrī Mahādakṣiṇeśvarī, having thus performed the *uddaṇḍa* rite,
[one should know] the supreme, beginningless *vidyā*, Śrī Kālī, who is designated as Mahātārā.
O Sovereign of the Six Śāmbhavas, you are the Vidyā beyond all that can be expressed, the supreme power (parā kalā);
having reached the great dissolution, you are the Mistress of ten million cosmic eggs.
Having unified the body composed of Śiva and Śakti, she remains eternally present;
while Bhava and the other Brahmās, possessing ten million faces, exist in the form of spirits (pretas).
O Pārvatī, having assumed the nature of guardians of the funeral pyre, they dance and sing in that cremation ground, crowded with predatory beasts. 1–23.
The infinity of the devotees of Maheśvara and the infinitude even in the form of Viṣṇu are well known;
but as for the counting of Śakra and the others, O sweet-spoken lady, there is none at all. (1.24)
As many grains of sand as there are in a river, so many Indras have passed away in the past;
likewise, everything stationary and moving, extending to the limits of ten million universes, [is subject to this].
The state of Indra has been attained by him countless times; indeed, as many atoms as there are within infinite millions of universes, so many times has he reached that position.
There exist upon that ground, in the form of the dust of the funeral pyres,
as many tens of millions of billions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) as there are [grains of dust] for those who have attained union with Māheśvarī.
There, O Goddess of the gods, the four Vedas are known as corpses; and the ages (yugas), having assumed the form of corpses, are the supreme ones situated within the seven pretas. (1–28)
Having reached the ocean, O Pārvatī, she indeed assumes every form,
herself bearing the supreme state through her all-pervasive nature of consciousness.
At that very moment, Śivā beholds her own reflection;
that reflection is indeed Māyā, and within it resides the mental Śiva.
For the purpose of producing creation,
one should mentally conceive the form of the Lord, the Primordial Master (Ādinātha), whose nature transcends all kalpas.
Beholding him, O Maheśānī, for the sake of producing creation,
one should conceive the Primordial Lord (Ādinātha) as one's own mental husband.
Having performed the inverted union (viparītarati) and having established the great void (mahāśūnya),
there are thirty arbudas, six vṛndas, and fifty padma koṭis.
O Supreme Goddess, during the ages she engaged in inverted sexual union;
O Goddess, in that inverted union, in ancient times, a single *bindu* was produced. (1.34)
There, one beautiful woman was born, possessing the splendor of great loveliness;
she was the supreme art (kalā), bearing the form of the illustrious Mahāsundarī.
And from her, a mental power (mānasī śakti) was born there, higher than the highest;
her name is conceived as Mahākālī Sundarī.
Upon seeing her, Mahākāla became overcome by great delusion;
addressing Kālī with words full of supreme pride, Kāla spoke as follows. (1.37)
From the Bindu and the Dhvani, however, each class of phonemes emerged;
at that time, the letters of the Mātṛkā were born, and thus it became known as "Akṣara" (the Imperishable).
(5) This entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is pervaded by resonance (dhvani).
Even today, O Goddess of the gods, the hearing of the resonance of Kādambarī [remains]. 1.39.

Kāla spoke to Sundarī, the supreme beloved of Mahāprāṇa, the beauty of the three worlds, the consort of Śrī, and the ocean of the nectar of compassion: uvāca sundarīṃ kālo mahāprāṇapriye pare | trailokyasundari śrīśe kāruṇyāmṛtasāgare || 1-40 ||
In the second sentence, O Goddess of the Gods, Śaṅkara spoke to Kālī: "O you of most terrible shrieks, O you with cruel fangs, O formidable one! (1.41)
Speaking these words, "O you with the lolling tongue and terrifying roar," Paracaṇḍikā, who is beyond all attributes, heard such speech.
The primordial Śrī Kālī is intent upon producing Māyā;
O Śivā, by the Māyā of Śrī Kālī, Time has fallen under the sway of delusion.
O Maheśvarī, the origin of the beginningless creation for the sake of its cause, as well as the infinity of the cosmic eggs, has been described by me in an instant. (1.44)
Having bestowed her illusory power upon Time, she herself became active; but Time became bewildered, wondering, "Where indeed has that beloved gone? (1.45)
"Alas, alas! Where has that Kālī, dear as my very life, gone?
Thus, fallen under the power of delusion, he became intent on wandering through the cremation ground. (1.46)
"Alas, alas! Where has Kālī, my beloved who is dearer than life itself, gone?
Thus he fell under the sway of delusion, and his mind thereafter became bewildered. (1.47)
For the sake of seeing her, he performed penance for fifty crores of padmas;
yet, O Śivā, ages passed there without a vision of Kālī.
"O Goddess of gods, he was born at a time when his devotion had strayed from the path.
Having realized this, O Maheśvarī, Mahākālī bestowed knowledge upon him. (1.49)
O Pārvatī, the intellect known as Ākarṣaṇā was bestowed upon Kāla;
she is Mahākālī, who delights in her devotees, and possesses the glorious, great southern face. (1.50)
She is known as Dakṣiṇā because she is skillful in granting boons;
by her, the attraction was accomplished in that very instant. (1.51)
O Maheśānī, at dawn there arose knowledge for one who was intent on straying from the path;
O Maheśānī, the supreme beloved of great devotees, Kālī was born. (1.52)
"O Maheśānī, knowing that this rite brings about the attraction of Śiva and bestows the state of union, she approached the presence of Śiva. (1.53)
Then, O Maheśvarī, having empowered the Samarasas,
she brought them and gave them to Kāla solely for the purpose of practicing the path.
O Great Goddess, without the path, how can there be progress here?
In that regard, time should be devoted to practice and intent upon the meditation on Kuṇḍalinī. (1.55)
The earring of human beings is traditionally said to have three and a half coils;
O Goddess, the auspicious earring of the Illustrious Goddess, however, is multiplied according to her own will.
When Śrī, who possesses the three qualities (guṇas) and the three powers (śaktis), becomes possessed of the qualities of the Vedas,
she is Ekajaṭā of four castes, the supreme mistress of the four Vedas.
O Goddess, when she possesses five qualities, she becomes Mahogrā;
when the Śakti is multiplied by six, she is proclaimed as Siddhikālī. (1.58)
When the power is sevenfold, it consists of seven syllables and is Kālasundarī;
when the power is eightfold, it consists of eight syllables and is Bhuvanāmbikā.
When the Śakti possesses nine qualities, she is the nine-syllabled Caṇḍikeśvarī;
when the Śakti possesses ten qualities, she is the embodiment of the Ten Vidyās.
When the qualities of Rudra have arisen, she becomes Kālikā of the cremation ground;
when, O Goddess, she possesses the qualities of the Sun, she is Dvādaśī Caṇḍabhairavī. (1.61)
O Goddess, when the qualities of desire and the various forms of desire become the savior Tāriṇī,
she arises as the fourteenth quality during the time of subjugation.
When the qualities of the lunar fortnight have arisen, she is known as the Great Fifteenth (Mahāpañcadaśī);
when the energy possesses the qualities of the sixteenth digit, she is then the Illustrious Great Sixteenth (Śrīmahāṣoḍaśī).
O Goddess, when she transcends the qualities (guṇas) of time, she becomes Chinnamastā;
O Goddess, when she possesses eighteen qualities, she becomes Mahāmadhumatī.
O Goddess, when Mahāpadmāvatī, who possesses nineteen qualities, is then multiplied by twenty, she becomes Ramā, possessing twenty steps and twenty syllables. (1.65)
O Goddess, Śrī Kāmasundarī is said to possess twenty-one qualities;
then, O Goddess, Dakṣiṇākālikā possesses twenty-two qualities.
O Goddess, when multiplied by twenty-three qualities, it then becomes the Vidyeśī;
when multiplied by the number of the principles (tattvas), O Śivā, it then becomes the Gāyatrī. (1.67)
O Goddess, when multiplied by twenty-five, the fifth [Vidyā] is then Sundarī;
when the Śakti is multiplied by twenty-six, it is proclaimed as the sixth Vidyā.
O Goddess, the supreme Mahāratneśvarī possesses twenty-seven qualities;
when that supreme digit (kalā) is multiplied twenty-eightfold, she indeed becomes so. (1.69)
The supreme knowledge of twenty-eight syllables is the reviver of the dead;
O Goddess, Mahānīlasarasvatī possesses twenty-nine qualities.
When the knowledge possesses thirty-fold qualities, it is then known as Vasordhārā;
when it possesses thirty-one-fold qualities, O Goddess, it becomes Trailokyamohinī. (1.71)
If it is multiplied by thirty-two, it is known as Trailokyavijayā;
if it is multiplied by thirty-three, it is the illustrious Kāmākhyatāriṇī.
O Goddess, when it possesses thirty-four qualities, that power is called Aghorā; when it possesses thirty-five qualities, it becomes Saṅgītamohinī. (1.73)
When multiplied by thirty-six, it becomes the Vidyā known as Bagalā;
when multiplied by thirty-seven, Śakti is declared to be the Vidyā Svarundhatī.
If she possesses thirty-eight qualities, she is considered Annapūrṇeśvarī; if multiplied by forty-nine, she is proclaimed as Nākulī. (1.75)
The power (śakti) is said to possess forty qualities, and the Vidyā is the "three-thorned" (trikaṇṭakī);
when multiplied by forty-one, it then becomes the digit (kalā) Rājeśvarī.
Multiplied by forty-two, she is then the Attractor of the Three Worlds;
multiplied by forty-three, she is known as Rājarājeśvarī.
The *kukkuṭī* is proclaimed to be multiplied by forty-four;
the *siddhavidyā* is proclaimed to be forty times nine. (1.78)
The venerable Mṛtyuhāriṇī is said to possess forty qualities of taste,
while Mahābhogavatī is considered to possess forty qualities of a sage.
Vāsavī is proclaimed to possess forty excellent qualities;
Phetkārī is proclaimed to possess forty qualities of apertures.
The Goddess Mahāśrīmātṛsundarī is multiplied by fifty;
Mātṛkotpattisundarī is multiplied by fifty moons. (1.81)
O Supreme Goddess, each individual letter of the Mātṛkā has arisen from the manifestation of its respective Vidyā, being the ultimate resort within its own origins. (1.82)
Whatever state is proclaimed for whichever [deity], the Supreme (Parā) is established in that very state;
having formed a coil by her own will, she abides like Kuṇḍalinī.
(9) Likewise, O Goddess, when knowledge has been well-generated, it takes the form of the unshakable Sage;
it is proclaimed for a human being as having three and a half coils. (1.84)
Thus, O Maheśvarī, the Vidyā arose from Kuṇḍalī;
from her was born Bālāmbā, solely for the sake of her former practice.
By the power of former practice, Sundarī may fall [into his state];
he, moreover, attains the state of time (kālatva) through union with Sundarī. (1.86)
Having assumed a fifth form through her power of knowledge (*vidyā*), she met with Kāla;
O Goddess, dear as life to her devotees, she was intent on union with him. (1.87)
Having attained the form of the fifth [vowel], the supreme digit (kalā) remained;
through the yoga of practicing union with her, he attained the state of Mahākāla.
He by whom she was previously seen is declared to be her *ṛṣi*;
others would then be her *upāsakas*. This is the opinion in brief. (1.89)
Now, therefore, O Goddess of the Gods, I shall explain Brahman in its proper sequence;
that Brahman is proclaimed to be born from the seed, the sprout, and the crystal. (1.90)
That very Brahman is declared to be the supreme, consisting of Kāla and Kālī;
for as long as it can be described, it remains possessed of attributes (saguṇa). || 1.91 ||
That very Brahman with attributes (saguṇa) is within the scope of description;
for when, O Maheśvarī, one becomes incapable of further description, [it is that Brahman]. (1.92)
That very [reality] is declared to be without attributes (nirguṇa), while that which possesses attributes (saguṇa) falls within the range of verbal expression.
It is called the "mouth" of Vāgbhava, and it is uttered from the mouth.
How could Brahman, which is inexpressible, come within the range of the mouth?
Since it is constrained by the power of speech, the primacy belongs to that power. (1.94)
Kālī is indeed that power (śakti), the original image (bimba) from which no reflection arises;
Mahākāla is proclaimed as the true shadow that pervades Kālī. (1.95)
From Mahākāla arises Māyā; she is called Bhuvaneśvarī.
O Goddess Maheśvarī, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others were born there. (1.96)
From that, the world-protectors were born; they are remembered as the Mātṛkās arising from Vāgbhava.
Then, O Goddess, [the mantra] was multiplied by one, originating from the first syllable.
Through that non-perishing nature, there is the state of being the Imperishable (akṣara);
for in the subtle Śiva, without Śakti, neither name nor abode exists. (1.98)
But the primordial Śakti is the sphere of the mass of bliss;
she is the very nature of Brahman, consisting of consciousness and bliss, and is nothing other than the supreme Brahman alone. (1.99)
When the primordial nature (prakṛti) exists, the transformation (vikṛti) is not more powerful;
the primordial nature is the supreme power, while transformation is its reflection. 1-100.
The first is Mahākālī, who is black; the second is remembered as Sundarī;
the third, O Maheśānī, is Bālabhairavī, who is red in color.
The fourth and fifth are the Vidyā; by practicing them, one transcends the state of time.
That Śakti, which is the root of the phenomenal world (prapañca), is proclaimed as the Mistress of the Phenomenal World (Prapañceśī).
By assuming that form of Māyā, Śiva becomes the self of phenomenal expansion (prapañca);
thus the three-eyed one is born as the possessor of the three qualities (triguṇa), and likewise the Lord is the self of the three qualities.
Then, O Śivā, by a mere fragment of His grace, Sadāśiva was born;
and there, O Supreme Goddess, she remained endowed with the quality of beauty.
The expansion belongs to Sundarī, yet she is manifested by the Nirguṇa;
the primordial Śrī is Nirguṇā, Kālī, beyond the expressible, and higher than the highest.
But through the supreme conjunction of the five [elements], they arise simultaneously;
therefore, this Vidyā is proclaimed as Sundarī, the Mistress of the Manifest World. (1.106)
O Supreme Goddess, from the moment that beautiful and most enchanting form was assumed, this phenomenal world came into being.
O Maheśānī, within the corner of Śakti, this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings—the infinite multitude of cosmic eggs—abides, O Queen of the Gods. (1.108)
O Goddess, her Kuṇḍalinī energy, whose form is the unshakeable serpent, is multiplied by her own will; she is the embodiment of the phonemes according to her own will.
O Goddess of the gods, Kālī showed her the Egg of Brahmā;
it consists of the sphere of Brahmā, the sphere of Viṣṇu, and the third, the sphere of Rudra.
O Goddess of the gods, O Śivā, first is the *golaka* of Lokeśa, then the *golaka* of the gods;
thereafter is indeed the *golaka* of the sages, and from these, there are *golakas* by the millions in succession.
From the Supreme Brahman, Prakṛti arises in the form of a reflection;
from that, the principle of Mahat is born, and after that, Ahaṅkāra.
From that, space was born; from that, wind is proclaimed to have arisen.
From that, fire was produced here; from fire, water is proclaimed to have arisen. (1.113)
From water the earth was born, and from that the auspicious medicinal herbs;
from the herbs food comes into being, and from food, it is proclaimed, life-breath (prāṇa) arises. || 1.114 ||
For from the vital breath (prāṇa) the individual soul (jīva) is born; from the individual soul come both the embodied self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman).
From the reflection of Brahman (brahmabimba), this entire world of moving and non-moving beings arises. (1.115)
Therefore, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is indeed Brahman;
having come under the sway of creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*), the eternal one exists in the form of Brahman. (1.116)
The living being is a worm, and from that it becomes a bee; yet for Śivā, the bee is not truly different from the worm.
The living being is Brahman, and again Brahman; from that, he is once more Brahman.
(12) Just as water becomes hot in fire due to the power of merit and the nature of the vessel,
O Goddess, if water alone were poured into the fire— (1-118)
The fire is destroyed, O Goddess; there is no need for deliberation here.
Through the union with the vessel of the body, the Supreme Self becomes the deity. (1.119)
Happiness, suffering, victory, gain, egoism, and even hypocrisy;
delusion, desire, hunger, yawning, thirst, touch, and movement. (1-120)
All this has arisen in that same way, O Maheśvarī, O Great Goddess;
when that knowledge has arisen, there is neither happiness nor suffering.
When the identification with the body has dissolved and the Supreme Self is known, there is neither happiness nor indeed suffering; there is only the absolute Supreme Brahman.
Just as burning, which is the power of fire, resides within fire, O Pārvatī, so too does Brahman always reside within every living being, O Pārvatī. (1-123)
Just as sparks from a fire, having reached various places, may reach extinction in water or find growth in grass; || 1.124 ||
Just as sparks emerge from wood, so too does Brahman manifest within Jīva and Śiva;
through the union with the worthy vessel, all these things, such as victory and attainment, arise in Śiva.
There is neither pleasure nor pain; it is only the supreme Brahman.
O Pārvatī, that knowledge becomes manifest through the yoga of mantra. 1-126.

O Maheśānī, when the supreme self in the form of the individual soul (jīva) is joined with desire, anger, and the like through association with another [condition], suffering arises; it is not otherwise.
If the mind is in one place and Śiva is in another, how can there be union with Śiva?
If, while the practice of union has been commenced, there should be contact with a woman, [the practice is ruined]. (1.128)

(13) "O Supreme Goddess, the destruction of the body and so forth occurs through the obstruction of the vital breath (*vāyu*) by means of [ordinary] destruction; however, it is not so in the practice of mantra or in meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). (1.129)
For as long as meditation has arisen, so long is one the god Maheśvara;
if meditation should dissolve, then the person is the Lord of the individual soul (jīveśvara). (1-130)
In this very case, there is no fixed rule; rather, a limit is proclaimed therein:
either the Supreme Brahman or the individual soul (jīva)—one or the other—[is the object], O Śivā. (1.131)
Thus has been briefly explained the reality of the syllable A.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Commencement of the Text," in the first section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 1 ||
The second chapter. Ugratārā said:
"O Akṣobhya, I wish to hear that which was previously indicated by you."
Tell that to me, O Lord of Gods, if I am dear to you.
Akṣobhya said:
O Mahogrā, listen now to this most secret of secrets;
it is declared, O Śivā, to be the end of the Brahma-world and the cosmic egg of the earth.
O Goddess, during the withdrawal, the universe becomes dissolved therein;
O Goddess, having placed the eternal Four-faced Brahmā at its forefront. (2–3)
Within the sphere, there are Brahmās extending as far as the limit of ten million faces;
and the earth-sphere with four faces is called the Brahmāṇḍa, consisting of ten million [such spheres].
Thus, O Pārvatī, the infinity of the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) remains;
Nīlaśāradā is the sovereign of infinite millions of cosmic eggs.
And beneath that is the Brahma-golaka, which is the domain of Sundarī; O Supreme Goddess, the Bhū-golaka is the domain of Bhuvanā.
O Pārvatī, authority has indeed been granted solely to Sundarī;
among those [goddesses] numbering ten million Mahāvidyās, she alone resides within the sphere of the *golaka*.
Then indeed, O Goddess, the Queen of the Queens of Kings, the most supremely beautiful one,
at one time became intent upon the origin of the *goloka*.
O Maheśānī, O Pārvatī, at her gateway everything stands—O Goddess, the multitude of nyāsas and so forth, as well as the various five-limbed [protections]. (2.9)
(15) In that very manner, O Goddess, according to the command of Kālikā, whatever is performed daily is all offered before Kālikā. (2.10)
And having gone there, O Goddess, Śiva, it is always said by Sundarī that before him [the Lord] is Brahman consisting of Kālī and Tārā.
O Maheśānī, the terrestrial globe has indeed been indicated by me in its three divisions;
the sages, beginning with Śaṅkara, have arisen from but a fraction of my own essence.
O Maheśānī, within the aggregate of consciousness (cittaskandha), that which is called the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is proclaimed;
and O Maheśvarī, the number of terrestrial globes is fifty crores.
Within the sphere of the Brahmāṇḍa, there may be a deficiency of five thousand [yojanas];
the terrestrial globe is proclaimed to have an extent of fifteen hundred [yojanas]. (2.14)
But the terrestrial globe, O Maheśānī, has the luster of a kadamba flower;
it constantly revolves, O Deveśī, endowed with the fivefold activity.
O Maheśānī, it has the form of a jar and is endowed with two fixed points;
O Devī, the mouth is at the right fixed point, while on the left is the shape of the base and the mouth.
The "conch-necked" is declared to be the jar, and it is remembered as the jar of the Śrīcakra;
words such as "twenty" and so forth are established in eternal oneness. (2.17)
The number ending in "hundred" (śata) is declared for the thousands and lakhs;
the number "ten" (daśa) should be employed for the crores and so forth, while for the [higher] units, it is simply "hundred" (śata).
In Arbuda there would be a thousand; in Kharva it becomes what is called a lakh.
In this sequence, O Mistress of the Gods, O Ishvari, it continues until the end of Parārdha.
When conjoined with the syllables and so forth, O Goddess, there may be a deficiency in the right [hand] and an excess in the left; one should apply them according to the appropriate method. (2-20)
O Goddess, there is a kadamba flower located within the Śrī-cakravāṭikā, and for the purpose of sprinkling that garden, there is a jar with a conch-like neck. (2-21)
O Goddess of gods, surrounding the Brahma-golaka in the shape of an umbrella;
O Maheśānī, she is the sovereign of the Great Śrīcakra within each of those images.
It always exists, O Goddess of Gods; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
It exists as the atom (paramāṇu), the minute particle (aṇu), and likewise as the dyad (dvyaṇuka) and the triad (tryaṇuka).
A lava, a truṭi, a kalā, a kāṣṭhā, and a nimeṣa, as well as a śvāsa;
from that, O Maheśānī, comes a kṣaṇa, and from that, a pala shall arise. (2.24)
It is the concise view that there are sixty such units (nāḍīs) [in a day];
likewise, there are the ghaṭikā, the muhūrta, the prahara, and the day. (2.25)
From that [day] come day and night, then a fortnight, a month, and likewise a season;
then a solstice, a year, a yuga, and the fourfold dissolution. (2.26)
Indeed, one set of four yugas is declared to be a great yuga (mahāyuga);
seventy-one of these are proclaimed to constitute a single Manu-period (manvantara).
O Śivā, fourteen Manus, seventy-one yugas, and likewise fourteen Indras are proclaimed. (2.28)
Four thousand yugas are proclaimed to be one day of Brahmā;
his night is of the same duration, during which fourteen Indras pass away.
Insects in trees, stones, grasses, and likewise worms—whatever has been born or is being born within the sphere of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍagola). || 2-30 ||
It is proclaimed that each of them shall hold the position of Indra once; this will serve the purpose of the phenomenal world, from a mere insect up to the entire universe. (2-31)
O Maheśānī, the human [life-span] is likewise stated, and the fortnight (pakṣa) is likewise; then the month, the season (ṛtu), the solstice (ayana), and the year (hāyana). (2-32)
Thus, a lifespan of one hundred years is proclaimed as the life-span of Brahmā; ten thousand such days of Brahmā are said to constitute a single day of Viṣṇu.
O Supreme Goddess, the periods of fortnights, months, years, and so forth must be understood;
the lifespan of Viṣṇu is proclaimed to be ten thousand years.

The lifespan of Śiva is one hundred thousand (lakṣa) years; that of Īśvara is double that amount. The lifespan of Sadāśiva is one hundred thousand years, but for the Parātpara, there is no calculation at all.
Beyond that, O Maheśānī, will be the Svarāṭcakra;
the Virāṭcakra is twice that, and the Sarvarāṭ is twice that again.
O Goddess, after the end of all Rāhus, there will then be emptiness;
thereafter, the supreme form of emptiness is the digit (kalā) Śrī Mahāsundarī.
Sundarī is the sovereign of the kings of kings, the mistress of the great universe;
then there is Mahāśūnyā, and Tārā follows in the sequence of doubling that [measurement]. (2–38)
Having united everything with liberation through the infinite Mahāsundarī,
she indeed remains thus for a hundred years, bringing about the great dissolution.
That which is called the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), however, occurs only once;
when the great dissolution has occurred, thereafter everything will become empty. (2.40)
She is the form of Brahman, supreme bliss, absolute, the supreme savior;
everything is indeed dissolved within her, for everything is of that very nature.
Thus, O Goddess, the Great Void, the Great Dakṣiṇakālikā, remains pervading all, O Queen of the Gods; the Void is of the nature of Kṛṣṇa.

Thus it has been briefly stated. Now hear concerning the arrangement within the spheres (golaka): namely, the individual (āṇava), the karmic (kārmaṇa), and that which consists of Māyā and Prakṛti. (2.43)

The ego (ahaṅkāra) shall be the fifth; likewise, it presides over creation, maintenance, and dissolution, as well as the favoring of primordial matter (pradhāna), O Goddess. Listen attentively to the established order.
The *āṇava* [impurity] pertains to the individual soul (*jīva*) alone; the *kārmika* [impurity] belongs to Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
that rooted in *māyā* belongs to Rudra; and likewise, the *prākṛta* [impurity] belongs to Īśvara. (2.45)
The ego-sense belongs to Sadāśiva; for Paraśambhu there is nothing [of his own].
Creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace [are his functions]. (2.46)
Gradually, through the Māyā of the Supreme Śambhu, the group of five arose:
first the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), then the path of measures (mātrādhvan), and immediately after that, the path of principles (tattvādhvan).

The path of mantra, the path of worlds, the path of kalās, and that known as the path of seasons—this path is said to be threefold, according to the sequence of the individual self, the body, and the subtle essence. (2.48)

The wheel of the body within the egg is likewise threefold—pertaining to the elements (ādhibhautika), pertaining to the divine (ādhidaivika), and pertaining to the self (ādhyātmika)—O Goddess; listen now with diligence to its arrangement. (2.49)
Situated in the midst of the six cities according to the Laṅkā and Cīna traditions,
O Goddess, the one named Laṅkāpuri is established in the central portion.
Because it is equally divided on all sides, it is employed for the purpose of Mount Meru;
indeed, seven oceans are recorded as being to the southern side of Laṅkā.
In that regard, O Maheśānī, the number of continents is indeed eighteen;
O Deveśī, there are seven oceans, which are proclaimed as the seas. (2.52)
O Goddess of the gods, those regions have sweet water, and there indeed is the submarine fire (vaḍavānala).
At its edge the hells are said to be located, while in the middle lies the city of Bhogavatī.
(19) Laṅkā, however, is situated in the middle of the earth and is entirely level, O Auspicious One; on the side of Gandhamādana, Himavat-Meru is proclaimed to be located. (2-54)
Beyond that is the heavenly realm, where the worlds are established;
the worlds above and below are provided with a hundred enclosures.
In the Dakṣottara [region] is the pair of Dhruvas, and there indeed the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is situated;
below it are the seven netherworlds (pātālas), and above it are the seven worlds (lokas).
Thus the three worlds were born, and that egg revolved;
[therein were] the planets, the lunar mansions, the sun, the moon, Indra, and the guardians of the directions. (2.57)
These are declared to be the abodes; in their midst are the Kinnaras and others.
Beyond those, the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the rest are proclaimed. (2.58)
Then, O Goddess, the one called Īśvara, and then indeed Sadāśiva; after that, the world of the Lord of Daṇḍinīs is proclaimed. (2.59)
The minister’s mother’s house was there, adorned with seven enclosures;
beyond that is said to be the Parāpara, and beyond that, the Parātpara.
Beyond that, Parātītā is proclaimed, and immediately after that, Citparā;
O Goddess, the seventh is Śrīpura, ten million yojanas above that.
The city of Tāriṇī is four-cornered, measuring one hundred thousand koṭis of yojanas,
endowed with nine ramparts, and infinite in its length and breadth.
O Goddess, the Kālacakra is there, and Kālanityā in due order;
O Goddess, the Śrīcakra is established within the city of Kālanityā.
Therein, O Maheśānī, within that bindu, there is the city called Nirvāṇa; and within that bindu, O Parameśānī, there is the city called Śāmbhava. (2.64)
O Goddess, within that drop (bindu) is the Rājasa [tattva], along with the Śāntyatīta-kalā;
there, one should always contemplate Sadāśiva, joined with the four Śavas upon a couch.
Therein, O Maheśānī, is the supreme Mahākāmeśvara, who transcends the *kāmakalā*; upon his lap is the supreme *kalā* known as Śāntyatītā. (2.66)
O Supreme Goddess, the Mother who is the Mistress of the ninefold [principles] and the Sovereign of millions of cosmic eggs—this entire universe is proclaimed to be enriched by her. (2.67)
O Pārvatī, there is a cremation ground (śmaśāna) there, enclosed by a wall of artistic divisions (kalā),
and therein lies the city of Śrītāriṇī, known as Pratyālīḍhapada.
The sixty-four spikes are white and extend infinitely in length and breadth;
that is the Śrī Dakṣiṇā cremation ground, which constitutes the eight cremation grounds themselves.
O Goddess of the gods, it is surrounded by a hundred gates,
adorned with millions of Brahmāṇḍa-pretas, and joined by Bhairava.
O Śivā, it consists of thirty *nikharvas* and six *padmas*, joined with *śarabhas*;
it is blazing with great flaming fires and adorned with *muṇḍas* and *bindus*.
The dark goddess Kālī, who has passed through the seven states of existence as a preta, stands there;
by her command, the masters of archery stand at the door of Sundarī.
O Goddess of the gods, at the door of Sundarī are the four Vedas with their six limbs:
the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda.
Grammar, ritual, prosody, astronomy, and etymology—these are proclaimed as the six auxiliary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), as well as the six philosophical systems (ṣaḍdarśana). || 2.74 ||
O Maheśānī, there are six Āmnāyas; likewise, O Śivā, there are six Śāmbhavas.
These are proclaimed to be of two kinds, according to the sequence beginning with 'Ka' and 'Ha'. (2.75)
O Dear One, there are eighteen kinds beginning with *kā* and eighteen beginning with *hā*;
and there is a group of four Upavedas known by those same names—listen to this, O Pārvatī. (2.76)
The Dhanurveda is adorned with branches of the Ṛgveda;
the Āyurveda is crowded with a hundred branches from the Yajurveda. (2.77)
O Maheśvarī, the Gāndharvaveda is declared to be [the essence] of the Sāmaveda;
O Goddess, it is adorned with branches and is the supreme bringer of delight to Kāla.
The scripture of Atharvaṇa is adorned with its branches;
O highly fortunate lady, that scripture is proclaimed to consist of fifty [parts]. (2.79)
It exists at the door of all time throughout the three worlds by way of the triple sequence:
four steps for the Brāhmaṇas and three steps for those born as Kṣatriyas.
O Goddess, Kṣatriyas never have the authority over the Atharvaveda;
the performance of its rites should be carried out through the mediation of Brāhmaṇas. (2.81)
The *saṃskāras* alone [distinguish] the fourth [order]; among the Kṣatriyas, the lord of the twice-born [is established].
The Brāhmaṇas are said to have four feet; the Kṣatriyas are remembered as having three feet. (2.82)
The fourteen great burdens are in heaven, in the house of Śrīsundarī;
and the number of the ten great burdens is in Pātāla, in the house of Padminī.
The great burden of the enumeration of the principles is established in the world of mortals, in the presence of the flood of the gods—the nine Siddha Lords. (2.84)
O Goddess Pārvatī, in the abode of Sarasvatī, he dwells in succession through the Śākta,
Śaiva, Gāṇapatya, Saura, and Vaiṣṇava systems.
But the Buddhist, O Goddess of the lords of gods, as well as the six systems of philosophy, the Vedic, the Saura, and likewise the Gāṇapatya; || 2.86 ||
O Goddess of the lords of gods, the Buddhist, the six systems of philosophy beginning with Tripura,
the Cāndra, the Svāyaṃbhuva, the Jaina, the Cīna, and the Nīla— these, O Maheśvarī,
are proclaimed as the six systems of philosophy, O Śivā, which are further categorized in three ways.
O Goddess, the triad of visions is the domain of the Kālī-vidyā.
The eighteen Purāṇas as well as the Upapurāṇa,
O Goddess Pārvatī, are said to belong to the Veda and its secondary branches (Upaveda).
The eighteen Purāṇas, as well as the Upaśamas;
Ekavīrā, Tvaritā, Kālikā, and likewise Sundarī.
Chinnā and Mātaṅginī are proclaimed as Gaṇeśa and Arka;
likewise Bagalā, Mālinī, Tārā, Trijaṭā, Akṣobhya, and Kālakī. (2.91)
Baṭuka, Sundara, Śambhu, and Śāmbhava are the ninefold [forms].
O Pārvatī, the eighteen Purāṇas are to be counted as supplementary [to these]. (2.92)
O Goddess of gods, the Śruti and the Veda, as well as the Upaveda and the Smṛti; O Goddess, the sixty-four arts and indeed the sixty-four supernatural powers (siddhis). (2.93)
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, fifty-two Upaniṣads are taught elsewhere;
O Queen of the Gods, they become sixty-four in total.
O Śivā, there are three thousand Sūktas and one hundred Tāṇḍavas;
three hundred Kauśalas are proclaimed, and the Kaumudī is called Kalā.
O Śivā, there are sixty-four Dīpikās, seventy Prakāśas,
fifty Sāṃkhyāyanas, and five Sūras.
O Goddess Śivā, there are two Vārtikas and two Tantrarājas,
known as the Nityāṣoḍaśikātantra, which is endowed with eight sections.
Through the system of the *hādikādi* and by means of the sequence of the *hādikādi*, the first half and the second half, when combined together, constitute the Virāj doctrine. (2.98)
The King of Tantras named Śaktisaṃgamatantra, which consists of the Kaha [scripture], is endowed with four sections; it is the most excellent among the best of the kings of tantras. (2.99)
O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, the Tantras are thus traditionally handed down in this sequence, consisting of fifty chapters and joined with five hexads.
O Queen of the Gods, the subtle Brahmāṇḍa here is the foundational support;
moreover, O Queen of the Gods, many Brahmāṇḍas are situated within its center.
Above that, O Maheśānī, is the form of the bud of the cosmic egg;
when its radiance appears in Jambudvīpa, one becomes the Lord of the Island (Dvīpeśvara). || 2-102 ||
O Maheśānī, by the very sequence of the universal form, day and night for human beings consist of sixty nāḍīs, having as their sole sphere of perception the body alone. (2.103)
O Great Goddess, for the ancestors it is two months;
for the Siddhas, day and night are proclaimed to be equal to a single season (ṛtu). (2.104)
O Great Goddess, for the gods, however, two human years constitute one [divine] year;
that which is called the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is their night, and the other is their day. (2.105)
O Maheśānī, sixty *kālikās* constitute one *nāḍikā*, and by sixty *nāḍīs* here, a day is proclaimed. (2.106)
Thus, O Goddess of the Gods, she who always dwells in the midst of the void shall remain eternally indestructible, even while devouring millions of cosmic eggs.
O Goddess, within the two royal teeth, the infinite multitude of cosmic eggs is proclaimed to be of two kinds, distinguished by their gross and subtle natures. (2.108)
O Maheśānī, eternal in time, she remains pervading everything at all times;
the *Saptaśatī* is said to consist of thirty-six [thousand verses] and twenty thousand. (2.109)
O Maheśānī, Kālanityā exists in the form of atoms and other such minute entities;
she is proclaimed as Kālanityā within a pala and within a ghaṭī. (2.110)
O Goddess of the Gods, seven days are indeed said to consist of the form of a quarter-ghaṭikā; and here, a fortnight is proclaimed to be of the form of a muhūrta.
Two of those constitute a month, and two of those are indeed a season (ṛtu).
Three of those, O Goddess, are a solstice (ayana), and two of those become a year (hāyana). || 2-112 ||
O Mistress of the Gods, pervading each [unit] individually, she is proclaimed as Kālanityā;
O Maheśvarī, beginning from a single atom up to the end of a year.
O Supreme Goddess, she remains pervading all time eternally;
O Goddess, it is said that two nāḍīs constitute the state known as a muhūrta.
O Goddess of gods, by the primary measure, it shall be two and a half nāḍīs;
O Goddess of gods, within the cycle of seven days, these are known as the days.
O Śivā, [this applies] up to the end of the day, and likewise up to the end of the month;
O Maheśvarī, up to the end of the season, the end of the solstice, and the end of the year.
This has been declared as the gross measurement; now hear the sequence of the complete recitation (pārāyaṇa): by day, by weekday, by fortnight, by month, or in thirty-six days. (2.117)
Through the distinction between gross and subtle, there arise the zodiacal signs, the ascendant, and so forth;
likewise, O Goddess, all this, including the planets and other factors, proceeds from it. (2.118)
That transition which exists is the zodiacal sign (rāśi) at dawn;
this is declared to be the subtle sign, while the sign of the departed spirits (pretas) is the Anu-rāśi.
The *palalagna* consists of a single *pala*, whereas the *sthūlalagna* consists of sixty *nāḍīs*.
O Śivā, the *ghaṭīlagna* is a *muhūrta* and the *praharalagna* is a watch (*prahara*). (2.120)
By means of the sequence of thirty nāḍīs and by the sequence of day and night, this ascendant (lagna) is declared to be threefold, based on the transition from one zodiacal sign to another. (2.121)
O Śivā, the lagna at that specific time is said here to be fourfold according to the planets,
by means of the divisions of coarse and subtle, [calculated] by the sages (7), the joys (9), the sounds (6), and the moons (1).
Whichever day of the week it is at sunrise, from that [day] and from that planet, the transition among the planets occurs according to the sequence of *pala* and *nāḍī*. (2-123)
O Goddess, the day is known to be the same weekday as the one at sunrise; a full day and night consists of ghaṭīs, palas, yāmas, and muhūrtas. (2.124)
O Śivā, that enjoyment which lasts for only one year for the classes of deities beginning with Brahmā, indeed becomes a single *vāra* (weekday) for human beings there.
O Goddess of gods, that enjoyment revolves by means of subtle measurement;
having attained subtle knowledge, one should then practice gross knowledge. (2.126)
O Śivā, in the ritual of Kālanityā, one should perform the conjunction with the phoneme that arises at that specific time; she is called Udayākṣarī.
O Śivā, in the rite of Kālanityā, one should practice the conjunction of the letters of arising through multiplication; O Goddess, she thus becomes Kāleśvarī. (2.128)
When there is a conjunction of ten syllables in the rule for Kālanityā, she is then called Digīśvarī, who bestows fruit swiftly. (2.129)
When, according to the rule for the eternal time resulting from the combination of colors from the interrogator, Jīveśvarī is then proclaimed as the witness of all living beings. (2-130)
Likewise, by means of the sequence of months, the month itself becomes fivefold, according to the order of the lunar, solar, sidereal, heliacal, and bārhaspatya [months]. (2.131)

The lunar month is proclaimed to end with the full moon (*paurṇimānta*). Furthermore, O Goddess of Gods, when it begins from the new moon (*amā*) and ends again with that same [new moon], the lunar month is proclaimed to be of two kinds, according to the visibility of the moon. (2)
O Maheśānī, this month is proclaimed as the one known as Sāvana. || 2-133 ||
O Śivā, that which begins from one constellation and ends at another is proclaimed as *nākṣatra* (lunar);
and that which ends at the conclusion of a transit (*saṃkrānti*), O Goddess of Gods, is designated as *saura* (solar). (2-134)
The month called Bārhaspatya consists of thirty-six days;
O Goddess, by means of the sixteen Nityās, there shall be sixteen months. (2-135)
O Goddess, eighteen days are proclaimed here as a fortnight;
two of those are said to be a month. Listen now to that sequence, O Pārvatī. (2.136)
O Maheśānī, in the sequence of worship, there is the Nityāṣoḍaśamaṇḍala;
O Devī, O Śivā, the group of sixteen Nityās is followed by Śānti as the seventeenth.
Śāntyatītā occurs at its end; thus, O Dear One, there are eighteen [kalās] in the circle of the eternal days and so forth, wherein there is neither waning nor waxing. (2.138)
In this very sequence of rising and setting, a full day occurs;
O Maheśānī, the fourth month consists of fifty days.
That which is called the *varṇamāsa* is said to consist of one syllable per day;
it comprises either forty-eight or forty-nine [syllables]. (2.140)
The maṇḍala is said to be threefold, consisting of the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā.
In the first [type], there is the consent of Baṭuka; in the second, the consent of Kāla. (2-141)
And its threefold nature has been proclaimed in the second [chapter], O Supreme Goddess.
Thus it has been briefly explained; what else do you wish to hear? (2.142)

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Ritual of Kālanityā," in the first section of the northern portion of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Tārā. || 2 ||
The Third Chapter.
The Holy Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the determination of the Yugas beginning with the Bhūta.
Śrī Śiva said:
This most secret of secrets is told in brief; listen.
The knowledge of the sum of days (ahargaṇa), beginning from the creation by Brahmā up to the present day, is proclaimed as the Siddhānta. (3-2)
The calculation of the total number of days (ahargaṇa) from the first day of the Kali age up to the present day is designated as the "Tantra. (3-3)
O Maheśvarī, beginning from the first day of the Yuga up to the end of the Śaka era,
I have proclaimed this *karaṇa* (astronomical manual) for the calculation of the *ahargaṇa* (the accumulated number of days).
In each day of the Yugas beginning with Kṛta, respectively, the Dinanityā occurs there;
that [deity] is the Dinanityā for every single day.
In the beginning, after eleven years had passed beyond the *kalā*,
then in the twelfth year, in the month called Caitra, on the ninth lunar day (tithi).
When the Lord born of Viśveśa had passed away on Wednesday, from that time until the end of the day, there were thirty-six syllables consisting of the phonemes. (3-7)
O Supreme Goddess, they exist according to the distinction of the ages and days;
one should count those vowels as sixteen for each syllable.
A minor yuga is known to consist of a syllable joined with each individual vowel;
the days are to be understood by the number of syllables within those minor yugas. (3-9)
In this manner, thirty-six syllables shall be [uttered] individually every day;
thus, sixteen yugas constitute one syllable, and a yuga is so considered. (3.10)
By these pairs of castes, numbering five hundred and seventy-six days,
thirty-six such periods are declared to constitute a Mahāyuga.
The number of days in a Mahāyuga is said to be twenty thousand and three hundred and sixty-six. (3.12)
In this [verse] beginning with "ā ī pallavita," the established phonemes (varṇas) are indicated here:
fifty-seven years, seven months, and six days. (3.13)
In the Kali age alone, a single cycle is considered to last for one thousand years; and beyond that, there are seven thousand such cycles in the Kali age.
And with eleven added, there are indeed six hundred;
this has been declared in brief—what else do you wish to hear? (3.15)
The Goddess said: O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the definitive determination of the sacred seats (pīṭhas),
by the mere knowledge of which a practitioner may attain perfection.
The illustrious Śiva said: The sacred seat (pīṭha) is declared to be fivefold according to the path of the five abodes (pañcāyatana);
it is joined with its steps according to the path of Meru and Kailāsa.
In the Śaiva [tradition], it is indeed the bull-form treading upon the Goddess;
in the Vaiṣṇava, it is Garuḍa treading [upon Viṣṇu]; and in the Gāṇapa, it is the elephant treading [upon Gaṇeśa]. (3-18)
(29) The seat of Sūrya is marked by a swan; that of Kālī is accompanied by a corpse; and that of Sundarī is said to be joined with nine steps. (3-19)
Equipped with a staircase and having a height of one finger-breadth—thus has the pedestal been described by me; now hear about the Ṛtuśāmbhavaka.
O Maheśvarī, beginning from the month of Caitra and ending with Phālguna;
O Maheśvarī, beginning from spring and ending with the winter season.
I have thus declared the six seasons; herein lies the sequence of Śambhu.
Through the conjunction of the dark and light fortnights, there are sixty days in two months. (3.22)
By the application of six groups of sixty, there are three hundred and sixty rays; the first lunar day (pratipad) is proclaimed as the spring season, characterized by sweetness and darkness.
Madhukṛṣṇā is called Vasantā; this second [name] is proclaimed.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should apply them in this same sequence during the bright fortnight as well. (3-24)
O Śivā, the first and second days of the dark fortnight of Mādhava (Vaiśākha) follow;
thus, the application [of the lunar days] is everywhere according to the sequence of the bright fortnight.
Alternatively, listen now to the Śāmbhava [system] according to another sequence.
Fifty-six great cities are proclaimed to exist within the earthly realm.
O Maheśānī, the sixty-two Jalagrāmas are proclaimed; O Goddess, the sixty-two Āgneyaraśmis are likewise celebrated. (3.27)
O Goddess of the gods, the Vāyavya villages are said to be fifty-four;
now, the number of the Nābhasa villages shall be seventy-two.
Now, O Maheśvarī, hear the number of the mental villages (*mānasagrāma*);
they are said to be sixty-four, which in sequence become sixty-six in the *Ṣaṭśāmbhava*.
The great cities beginning with Śrīpura are proclaimed in the section known as the Pārthiva; the number of the villages beginning with the six Śāmbhava locations will be stated hereafter.
(30) Each of the names is indeed told in the *Siddhikerala*;
listen as that which was previously indicated to you is now being explained. (3-31)
O Great Goddess, it must be kept secret like one's own womb or another woman;
those who worship Śrī Kālī constitute what is celebrated as that *kula*. (3.32)
O Goddess of the gods, their assembly is proclaimed by me as the Kula;
O Śivā, it is for those who worship the Kālī-vidyā during the ritual of Kula-worship.
O Goddess, one must proceed with effort; one should not go elsewhere to wander.
O Śivā, if one were indeed to go elsewhere, that would become defiled by impurity.
Whichever deity is proclaimed for someone, that deity is declared to be his favorite;
the honey-wine (mādhvīka) situated within the vessel is indeed the remnant of the libation (tarpaṇa).
By performing the libation with leftover food (ucchiṣṭa), one incurs the curse of the deities;
for this very reason, O Maheśānī, fetters arise. (3-26)
Having thus understood everything and abandoned all attachment, one shall become happy;
O Great Goddess, within this wheel, one should proceed to the Kula and Akula.
O Maheśānī, listen with reverence to the secret [teaching] at the conclusion of the worship,
beginning from the third and ending with the fifth, together with the purification of the jar (ghaṭa).
O Goddess, after offering to the Goddess, the meal for the heroes (vīrabhojana) follows at the end;
in that meal for the heroes, O Goddess, there occurs the gratification of one's own deity.
O Maheśānī, how can there be a libation with what has been left over?
O Goddess, through ignorance of this, one may incur the curse of the deities. (3-40)
But when the curse of the deity has taken effect, bondage certainly arises.
This has been declared as *kulākula*; now hear about *akula*, O Pārvatī. (3-41)
Sundarī, Bhairavī, and Dhūmrā are proclaimed as belonging to Akula; O Maheśānī, one should always proceed with their worship within Akula. (3.42)
"In brief, it is our view that they must not go elsewhere;
if they should go out of negligence, a curse will certainly fall upon them. (3.43)
O Śivā, the absence of the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is considered the Vīra-pakṣa;
O Maheśānī, in the Full Wheel (pūrṇacakra), one certainly becomes a possessor of the Full Wheel (pūrṇacakrī).
O Great Goddess, in the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya), one who belongs to the Upper Tradition should always proceed;
O Goddess, one initiated into Nirvāṇa should proceed to the worship of Nirvāṇa. (3–45)
O Goddess, in the sequence of the six Śāmbhava [initiations] and in the ritual procedure for the worship of Śambhu, one should proceed;
O Goddess, this measure declared by me does not apply to the ritual procedure of the initiation of intelligence (medhādīkṣā).
O Great Goddess, once the [mantra] has attained its perfected form, one may perform ritual action according to one's own will;
this occurs through the sequence of the Gauḍa, Dakṣiṇa, and Kāśmīra traditions.
O Maheśānī, I have described to you everywhere the journey in Gauḍa; however, in the sixfold tradition (Ṣaḍāmnāya), the journey takes place in Kāśmīra.
Travel to Kerala may occur through the distinction between the *kula* and *akula* paths;
for those who are endowed with the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*, travel everywhere is auspicious. (3-49)
O Goddess of the gods, the region in which one who has received the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) shines becomes blessed for a hundred thousand yojanas in every direction. (3.50)

The descent of power (*śaktipāta*) arises for those endowed with the full initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), and even for one who is otherwise unfit, provided he is devoted to the *Kālī* mantra over time. (3.51)
O Goddess, the descent of power (śaktipāta) occurs certainly in sixty-four ways;
in the Nīlasārasvata Tantra, it is proclaimed to be fivefold.
O Maheśānī, the descent of power (śaktipāta) for Śrīsundarī is eightfold;
O Goddess, in the rite for severing ignorance (chinnāvidyā), the descent of power is fourfold. (3.53)
O Goddess, in the Vidyās such as Bagalā and others, the descent of power (śaktipāta) is twofold;
however, in the Vaiṣṇava and other Āgamas, O Goddess, the descent of power is fivefold.
Thus has the secret been briefly declared; listen with reverence!
O Great Goddess, he who performs worship without Śakti— || 3.55 ||
That poor man was my enemy; his destruction shall come to pass.
Having attained the nature of Śakti and Śiva, he shall perform worship. (3-56)
The mortal who acts in this manner becomes Śiva; there is no doubt about this.
The worship of Śakti must be performed for the attainment of the fruit of divine state. (3.57)
Thus has the classification of vessels been briefly explained; listen, O beloved, to how the total number becomes most excellent when measured by vessels numbering sixty-four. (3.58)
The middle count is said to be measured by vessels numbering the *kalās*;
the lowest count is said to be measured by vessels numbering the *nāthas*. (3.59)
In the common ritual, the number [of vessels] is measured by the count of arrows;
these are the Kerala, the Kāśmīra, and the Gauḍa as the third.
O Goddess, in the doctrine known as Kerala, the water vessel is indeed on the right;
in Kashmir, there is a difference regarding the libation (tarpaṇa), while in the Gauḍa tradition, it occurs in the left hand.
The Devī-praṇava, the Nirguṇa-praṇava,
Bagalā, Kamalā, Vāṇī, Parā, and others— more than a hundred [mantras] in total.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the definitive exposition of the Praṇava;
listen, O Pārvatī, to its sequence as it is joined with the five kalās.
The letter *a* and the letter *u*, and the letter *m* as the third;
*nāda* is declared the fourth, and *bindu* is said to be the fifth.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these five great pretas are fully supported by the Praṇava. (3.65)
Listen with care, O Goddess of gods, to that which has the form of the seven kalās;
the nature of the seven kalās and their fivefold division have been declared.
The letter A, the letter U, and the letter M as the third;
then the Nāda and Bindu, O Goddess, and beyond that, one becomes the Transcendent Nāda (Nādātīta).
The seventh, which transcends the knots (bindu), is proclaimed as the Śāmbhavī.
Listen, O Maheśānī, to the [powers] of Śakti; what secret is there even beyond this? (3.68)
The letter A, the letter U, and the letter M as the third;
then the Nāda, that which transcends it, and the Bindu thereafter. (3-69)
The seventh [kalā] is Bindvātītā; thus, O Śiva, the Śaktikalā is established.
In this very sequence of the Śākta-śakti, the seven kalās have been described. (3.70)
In the beginning, Parā is pointed out; then indeed Parātparā;
that which transcends it shall be the third, Citparā, as the fourth.
The fifth is to be known as Tatparā; that which transcends it is called Rasā. That which transcends all is the seventh. Thus, there are sevenfold Kalās.
O Goddess of gods, listen now to the seven kalās of Satī in their sequence:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. (3.73)
Śānti, and that which transcends it (Tadātītā)—these are said to be the seven kalās.
The fourfold [principles] are Kaśipu, Mṛtaka, and Sadāśiva. (3.74)
Brahmā and the others are the four legs, while Sadāśiva is the mattress;
Kāmeśa is the covering cloth, and the beautiful Kalā resides therein. (3.75)
The *praṇava* has the form of Sundarī and is joined with seven *kalās*;
however, in the conjunction of five *praṇavas*, there are five groups of seven *kalās*. (3.76)
That which was previously described as the "Seven Tāras" is indeed the Kāmakalā in the form of a swan; its true nature is now being declared. (3.77)
By the letter *ha* one goes out; by the letter *sa*, one enters again.
Upon the elision of both *ha* and *sa*, the Kāmakalā arises. (3.78)
Devoid of both wings, the *haṃsa* becomes the *kāmakalā*;
O Goddess of Gods, that "I" (so'ham) is the form of this [reality] known as *kāmakalā*. (3.79)
O Goddess of gods, in this expression "so 'ham" (I am that), the Praṇava is firmly established;
because it abandons both sides, the individual soul (jīva) is proclaimed as the Praṇava.
In the *Parāprāsādavidyā*, it is proclaimed in this very way:
there are two syllables in the letter *sa* and likewise two in the sky (*gagana*). (3.81)
When there is a conjunction of two *rakāras*, the arising of the letter *sakāra* is taught;
when there is a conjunction of *īkāra* and *ekāra*, the letter *hakāra* has been proclaimed by me. (3.82)
Therefore, O Great Goddess, she is the embodiment of the four quarters,
the form of the four feet, and the supreme deity of the temple.
Having abandoned the first [syllable] in the first case, but including it at the end in the latter case,
the Praṇava is proclaimed as being relinquished through both sides.
The letter *ra* is the first part, while the letter *e* is the second;
O Goddess, [this applies] both to that which begins with the seed-syllable of Māyā and to that which begins with the seed-syllable of Rati.
O lady of pleasant speech, the origin of the *praṇava* exists;
O Goddess, the letter *ha* is proclaimed as Ardhanārīśvara. (3.86)
Thus the seed-syllable of Śakti has been declared; now listen to the Kāmakalā, O Śivā.
It is considered to be half of the letter *ī*, with a dot (*bindu*) at its mouth, and the sun (*bhānu*) situated below. (3.87)
The two breasts are Fire and the Cool-rayed One (Moon); the womb is the half of *ha*, which becomes the *kalā*.
O Goddess, in the half-syllable of *ha*, the letters *ī* and *ai* are said to be present.
O Maheśānī, the face is the bindu, and below that are the two breasts;
O Dear One, they know the yoni-cakra to be the form of the half-kalā of the letter Ha.
O Maheśānī, the lower bindu is proclaimed to be the form of Parā; O Maheśānī, the yoni-bindu possesses that form of Parā. (3.90)
O Maheśānī, the Kucabindu is proclaimed as that which transcends it;
Citparā is the second, while that which transcends it resides in the mouth. (3.91)
Transcending all and possessing a fierce form, she is established above the seed-syllable.
O Śivā, know her to be the digit beyond the denotable, the digit situated above the letter *ī*.
Thus, the form of Kāmakalā has been described by me to you;
furthermore, the letter Śa is likewise enclosed within two Śaktis.
The letter *ra*, O Maheśānī, is Kālī, the mantra of the Kāmakalā;
O Goddess, Kālī as the Kāmakalā is the primary one, situated within the Haṃsa.
Thus has it been briefly declared; what else do you wish to hear?
Śrī Śiva said:
I shall explain the architecture of the house (gṛhavāstu) by which one may become divine.
The Vāstu-serpent is proclaimed to extend from Īśāna to Nirṛti;
its two hands would extend from Vāyu to Agni. (3.96)
O Goddess, the pair of feet is in the western direction (paitryā) and the head is in the northeastern direction (aiśānī);
this is declared to be the serpent-bodied [form], and having understood it, one should perform the rites. (3.97)
From striking the head, death occurs; at the tail, there is the destruction of all goals. (p.
36) At the pedestal (piṇḍikā), there will be suffering; at the chest, there is the accomplishment of all goals. (3-98)
The site (vāstu) is proclaimed to be of two kinds, according to the distinction between mobile and stationary;
O Goddess, one should worship the Lord of the House, Vāstusarpa, in the southwest.
Having performed the worship of the site (vāstupūjā) and having diligently ascertained the location of the tortoise (kūrma),
and having purified the place, one who observes the vow should himself become established there.
One should avoid, even in thought, the property of others, as well as receiving gifts from others, the wives of others, and the censure of others. (3.101)

The tongue is scorched by the food of others, the hands are scorched by accepting gifts, and the mind is scorched by the wives of others; O fair-faced one, how then can there be spiritual success? (3.102)
O Maheśānī, one should avoid accepting gifts in every way;
O Śāmbhavī, listen with care to the sin arising from the acceptance of gifts. (3.103)
Upon death, however, they go to hell according to their respective karmas;
thereafter, O Maheśānī, they proceed to the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka).
Then, O Goddess, those who have accepted [the gift] go to the world of the Sun;
from there they go to the city of the Moon, and thence they attain the state of the Moon. (3.105)
O Goddess of gods, having attained the state of a *bhārata* through yoga, he rains down upon the earth;
for that food previously given is indeed now within the range of direct perception here. (3-106)
O Great Goddess, without giving, fulfillment is never seen anywhere;
that food shall go to the state of being burnt in fire by the keeper of the vessel. (3.107)
In the state of digestion, however, it is consumed by all living beings for the sake of filling the belly, provided that it was given or caused to be given in a previous birth. (3.108)
O Goddess, that very [karma] which has been given is what is obtained; what has not been given does not accrue. Neither more nor less than that is ever obtained by living beings anywhere. (3.109)
O Goddess of the gods, that food shall become his excrement;
there, O Goddess, having become a worm, he shall thereafter take on another womb. (3.110)
Having renounced the acceptance of gifts, one should practice the perfection of the mantra;
at its beginning there is birth-impurity, and at its end there is death-impurity.

O Goddess Śivā, that mantra joined with the two types of birth-impurity (sūtaka) does not succeed at all; for there is a tenfold series of purificatory rites (saṃskāra) arising from the birth-impurity, O Auspicious One.
O Śivā, the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras), beginning with birth and ending with the rite of seclusion,
are proclaimed as the period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) lasting for ten days, O Goddess.
By means of the application of the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras), the obstacle of birth-impurity (jātasūtaka) is removed;
indeed, the preliminary service (puraskriyā) consists of ten parts, beginning with recitation (japa) and ending with the meal offering (bhojana).
This impurity of death and birth is indeed considered to last for ten days;
for just as a body deprived of life is incapable of all actions, so too is one [impure]. (3.115)
Indeed, a mantra devoid of *puraścaraṇa* is proclaimed to be such;
this second [topic] has been declared by me. What else do you wish to hear? (3.116)
The Goddess said:
O Lord of the Universe, I desire to hear about the wheel known as the Eight-Eights;
tell me, O ocean of compassion, that which is the secret beyond secrets.
The Lord said:
This is indeed a secret, even a most profound secret; keep it concealed.
It is of three kinds: superior, middling, and thirdly, inferior.
The Śiva-cakra is the highest; the Vaiṣṇava-cakra is the middle;
the Kāma-cakra is the lowest; and it is remembered as the Jīva-cakra.
(38) Thus has the *jīvacakra* been described, as well as this *jīvameru*.
O Goddess of Gods, one should recite [the mantra] either in the form of a line or in the form of a wheel. (3-120)
Abiding oneself in the station of the Bindu, free from conceptual construction and with senses subdued,
one should, having attained the immutable state, perform worship with diligence.
But the practitioner who undergoes transformation while being born certainly perishes.
O Goddess of the gods, there are three hundred and sixty powers in the enclosure of the Goddess.
O Queen of the Gods, there are twenty-five powers of the pentads in sequence;
they are declared as six in the Ṣaḍdarśana, while in the Ṣaḍāmnāya, there are six.
O Maheśānī, seventy-two powers of Nirvāṇa are recorded;
O Deveśī, three hundred and sixty are the rays of the Śāmbhava-krama. (3.124)
O Maheśvarī, sixty-four crores of Yoginīs have been declared;
they are those who are proclaimed as the entirety of the powers (śaktis) arising from the sixteen-fold installation (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
O Maheśānī, when there is equal power, it is proclaimed to be ten million in number;
one should multiply that by eight, which is what I have described as the "group of eight" (aṣṭaka).
One should perform [the rite] with eightfold qualities everywhere; thus, in due order, there shall be eight groups of eight.
This is declared to be the Śaiva-aṣṭaka, which is to be accomplished through Śambhu and not otherwise.
O Dear One, for each [of the mantras], there may be eight crores or one crore of kalās;
in the case of Śrīvidyā, this would be the lowest [grade], while in the case of Nirvāṇa it would be the middling.
O Supreme Goddess, in the initiation beginning with the Ṣaṭśāmbhava and ending with Medhā,
O Goddess, the excellent sequence known as the Aṣṭāṣṭaka has been described.
Now listen as the group of eight eights known as Vaiṣṇava is described: O Goddess, the powers of the cycles are proclaimed to be three hundred and sixty.
O Śivā, if one lacks the capacity for [all] the powers, one should worship with effort eight powers.
It is held that there are two thousand, eight hundred, and eighty powers. (3-131)
Each wheel is said to possess eight qualities; thus, this [entirety] is called "eight times eight.
When each of these eight [wheels] is previously described as having eight qualities, it is called "eight times eight. (3.132)
O Śivā, that which is called Ānandabhairava has been declared as the eight groups of eight;
O Maheśānī, it consists of two hundred and forty thousand [verses].
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, this doubled is four hundred thousand;
O Goddess, sixty thousand [verses] are considered to be eighty Śaktis.
Two hundred and twenty is said to be the group of eight Ānandas;
twenty-four thousand is the group of forty Śaktis.
But upon completion, O Great Goddess, there are three hundred and sixty rays;
thus, one complete worship is joined with eight enclosures.
This Ekāṣṭaka has been declared; thus, there would be an Aṣṭāṣṭaka consisting of two thousand eight hundred and eighty Śaktis.
This is declared to be the eight-times-eight [set], according to the sequence of five fives;
one who is joined with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is duly initiated into the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya).
O Goddess, one should perform the eight groups of eight in sequence according to the sixfold Śāmbhava method;
he who possesses the realization of these eight groups of eight is Śiva himself, without a doubt. (3.139)
O Śivā, one’s head should be given, wealth should be given, and a wife should be given with effort;
a house filled with riches should also be given—this is the supreme means. (3.140)
O Maheśvarī, this is indeed a supreme secret, more hidden than the most hidden; it has been told by me, O Goddess. What else do you wish to hear? 3-141.
The abundance of its fruit cannot be described by me:
women are the gods, women are creation, and women are the bringers of prosperity. (3-142)
O Maheśānī, whatever female form exists upon the surface of the earth, if even one young woman is worshipped, the entire surface of the earth is worshipped. (3.143)
O Goddess of gods, by the mere sight of women, the worship of the entire surface of the earth has been performed; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (3.144)
Having seen a form that produces bliss, one should bow to that form;
once the bliss of form has arrived, what further purpose is there elsewhere? (3.145)
Form after form is the supreme abode; form after form is the supreme austerity;
form after form is the supreme reality—such has never been, nor will it ever be.
Thus the summary has been declared; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the first section of the northern part of the *Śrī-Śaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā, in Uttarakerala.
The third chapter, titled "The Description of the Eight Octads. || 3 ||
The Fourth Chapter.
The Holy Goddess said:
"The 'Eight-Eights' (Aṣṭāṣṭaka), which bestows all accomplishments upon the earth, has been taught by you."
What is proclaimed as the knowledge of a worthy recipient according to the path of the tradition? || 4-1 ||
"Tell that to me, O Mahādeva, if I am dear to you.
Śrī Śiva said:
"I shall proclaim a secret; listen as this knowledge is being told."
The Kerala, the Kāśmīra, and the Gauḍa path as the third—pervading everywhere through the distinctions of fifty-six regions, it remains established throughout. (4.3)
The Gauḍa style is proclaimed to prevail across eighteen regions,
extending from the land of Nepal as far as Kaliṅga.
Beginning from Āryāvarta and extending to the oceans, the system known as Kerala has been proclaimed in twenty-one regions. (4–5)
O Goddess of the gods, in a land other than that, there is the auspicious Krama known as Kāśmīra;
yet Śaṅkara would be external, like a twice-born who stands outside the Veda.
Listen now to the determination of the vessels according to the sequence beginning with Kerala:
the skull of Viśvāmitra is proclaimed for Kerala. (4.7)
In the tradition known as Kāśmīra, the vessel is a gourd-shell (tumbīkapāla);
and in the Gauḍa path, the vessel is proclaimed to be a great skull-cup (mahākapālapātra).
The skull is said to be of three kinds according to the tradition of transmission:
the great skull (mahākapāla) is of three types—conch, shell, and cowrie.
The vessel called *kaparddikā* is the most excellent of all vessels;
according to the sequence of the oral tradition, it is declared to be the *mahākapāla*. (4.10)
O Maheśānī, for the general *arghya* there should be crystal, and for the special one, *viśvāmitra* (amber);
silver is used for the *arghya*, while the vessel for the Guru should be golden.
In the Bhairava [tradition], the vessel is made of mother-of-pearl; in the Vīra [tradition], it is called a conch shell;
in the Śakti [tradition], it is made of glass; but in the Yoginī [tradition], it is a skull-cup.

O Maheśānī, the vessel for the bali offering should be made of copper, and the vessels for the water for the feet (pādya) and so forth should be made of jewels in their proper order; however, in the absence of those, they should be as previously described.
The Krama known as Kerala has been proclaimed; now hear about Kashmir, O Pārvatī.
O Maheśānī, one should prepare the general *arghya* offering with copper.
Regarding the special arghya vessel, it may be made of gourd, or of crystal, or of mother-of-pearl;
the vessel for the Guru may be a jar made of silver.
In the Bhairava [tradition], the skull should be that of a hero; in the Vīra [tradition], it should be born from the skull of a sage.
The vessel for the Śakti should be made of crystal, and that of the Yoginī should be made of copper. (4.16)
A vessel for the *bali* offering should be made of glass, copper, or mother-of-pearl for the rite of washing the feet (*pādya*);
for the rites of the *arghya* and *ācamana*, one made of conch shell is prescribed.
Other vessels may be made of copper, while those for enjoyment (bhogaka) should be made of sugar;
or a shell-vessel may be used according to the Gauḍa tradition, or it may serve as the ordinary vessel for the arghya offering.
For the special *arghya*, that which is called a skull is prescribed; in its absence, it may be made of crystal.
A vessel made of gold is declared [for the deity], while the vessel for the Guru should be made of silver.
O Maheśānī, that which is called Bhairava is known as Nārikela;
the vessel of glass is the Vīrapātra, while for the Śakti, it is one made of sugar.
The jewel vessel belongs to the Yoginī, while the offering vessel is made from tortoise shell;
O Maheśānī, one should hold the water for the feet and other items at their proper times.
The vessel for enjoyments (bhogapātra) is in Kāśmīra, while the vessel for the self (ātmapātra) is in Gauḍa;
the divine vessel (divyapātra) is in Kerala—such is the determination regarding the vessels. (4.22)
O Goddess, listen to the determination regarding the vessels for one who possesses only consciousness:
a conch shell vessel is for general purposes, while one made of coconut is for special occasions. (4.23)
A crystal vessel is for the Guru, while a jar made of glass is for [other] purposes;
the gourd is the vessel of Bhairava, whereas the vessel of sugar is for the heroes (vīra).

The vessel for the Śakti should be made of skull-bone; that for the Yoginī should be made of copper; the hero’s vessel (vīrapātra) should be made of conch-shell, and the vessel for water for the feet (pādyapātra) should be made of copper.
Silver is prescribed for the act of sipping water (ācamana), while gold is for rites such as the offering of arghya;
likewise, O Śivā, it is the same for the arghya, the madhuparka, and the ācamana.
The bathing vessel for Śiva, the Lord of Knowledge, should be made of jewels;
in Kerala, one should accomplish all rites using a coconut.
One should fashion all vessels using only a hero-vessel;
one should fashion all vessels using only a golden vessel. || 4-28 ||
One should have all the vessels made solely from silver;
however, among the vessels mentioned, the performance of all rites may be accomplished with just one.
O Śivā, O Queen of the Gods, one should diligently prepare all the vessels using a single type of material, according to the sequence of the oral tradition.
Bell-metal, iron, silver, gold, O Supreme Goddess;
crystal, that which arises from mercury, and likewise emerald, O Śivā. (4.31)
Whether made of gems and lapis lazuli, or produced from the nine precious substances,
or from coconut and the great conch shell— each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.
O Goddess of the gods, among trees, that which is increasingly superior and bestows all accomplishments is the giver of all siddhis. (4.33)
O Goddess of the lords of gods, O Śivā, whatever [liṅga] is made from wood among trees, one should have it fashioned from bilva wood or from sword-iron according to the appropriate rule. (4.34)
A vessel that has the shape of an aśvattha leaf or indeed the shape of a kutapa, or one that is triangular in form, is proclaimed to be a kutapa. (4.35)
The form of the womb, resembling the face of a young girl, is most enchanting;
a vessel made of jewels belonging to Sundarī is prescribed for the rite of severing the severed head (Tārācchinnā). (4.36)
O Maheśānī, the form of the petals is proclaimed as being merely the mantra;
however, the form of the Aśvattha leaf pertains to the fivefold Vidyā.
O Goddess of the gods, that which is joined with action is proclaimed as the triple-triple power (tritriśakti).
O Goddess, the triple power is threefold; there is a triad within each of the three.
O Goddess of gods, the triangular vessel is proclaimed for the Mantramātra;
the circular one is prescribed for the Vaiṣṇava, while the one with a handle pertains to Śiva.
In the absence of a skull-bowl, however, one made from the skull of Viśvāmitra [is used];
in its absence, O Great Goddess, that which has the appearance of bone [is used]. (4.40)
O Goddess, one must diligently apply glass [beads] to Bagalā;
they should be arranged in the left-to-right sequence, and likewise in the reverse order.
Alternatively, O Goddess of the gods, the skull is the sphere of all;
therein, the gourd-skull is proclaimed in the Kāpālika doctrine.
O Goddess of gods, according to the Nīlacīna-krama tradition, the skull-bowl is the vessel;
or else, O Sovereign of the God of gods, the great vessel is the kaparddika.
O Pārvatī, Kapardīśa resides within the center of the vessel;
because he bestows success swiftly, he is remembered as such in the ritual of the five vidyās.
The skull of Viśvāmitra is proclaimed as belonging to a Brāhmaṇa;
in its absence, O Maheśānī, the supreme [skull] is equal to a vessel of the Kula. (4.45)
O Śivā, know that the auspicious *arghyapātra* bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
When the *arghya* is made of copper, the deities reside there for sixty-four years.
O Goddess, the deity resides for a hundred years in silver, for a thousand years in a golden vessel,
and for ten thousand years in crystal.
Likewise, O Goddess, a pair of jewels produced from emerald and born of gems [is obtained];
but in the skull of Viśvāmitra, O Pārvatī, [the result lasts] for a hundred thousand years.
O Goddess of gods, O Pārvatī, [the merit] is ten lakhs when offered in a skull-bowl;
O Beloved, it is ten thousand when on a sword, and twenty when on a pearl.
O Maheśvarī, whether in the skull of Viśvāmitra or in a [human] skull, all the deities are granters of boons; he alone is the Supreme Lord.
He is blessed, he is wise, and he alone is considered truly discerning;
he is the performer of all sacrifices and the knower of the secret of all sciences.
