He is indeed the knower of Brahman, the very essence of all secret mantras;
he is the self of bliss, the supreme self, [manifesting] through the various divisions beginning with Sakala.
Or one should have all the vessels made from the skull of Viśvāmitra;
or, O Maheśānī, one should have all the vessels made from a skull.
O Goddess of the gods, one should contemplate all vessels within a single skull;
O Pārvatī, this applies even to the skull of Viśvāmitra.
Just as no one truly understands the knowledge of Śiva and Śakti, so too no one truly understands the realization of the skull (kapāla). 4-55.
O Supreme Goddess, whatever [form] Kapardin may take, that very same [form] should be fashioned from coconut, whether it be a garland of vessels or a mechanical device.
The third is crystalline, O Goddess; it is considered both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala).
That which produces fire from the sun, O Goddess, is proclaimed as "with parts" (sakala). || 4.57 ||
Furthermore, hear about all the others according to their eastern and northern divisions:
by the mere sight of the moon on the full moon day in the month of Āśvina.
O Goddess, this entire [mantra] is proclaimed as the most excellent, causing the flow of water;
with that nectar-water, one should indeed satiate Kālī and Tārā.
In the tradition known as Kerala, there is worship with the coconut offering;
in the tradition known as Kashmir, there is the worship with the crystal offering.
O Maheśānī, in the Gauḍa tradition, worship is performed with the skull as the vessel for the arghya offering;
O Devī, there is indeed some difference in the substances used between the Kāśmīra and Gauḍa traditions.
Taking a coconut that is well-ripened, beautiful, and firm,
one should cause it to burst open in the middle, possessing the auspicious marks of eyes and a nose.
Having established the two eyes, which possess a beautiful form and excellent qualities,
one should fashion them from nine colors or from five colors.
O Maheśānī, having obtained eyes made of silver, eyes made of gold, or eyes made of sapphire and other gems, one should perform the rite of the nose [nasikā] there.
O Maheśvarī, the face should be made between the two eyes;
such is the subtle form proclaimed for the purpose of the garland.
That form made of crystal is considered in the doctrine known as Kāśmīra;
or, a crystal in the shape of a triangle or a yoni bestows auspiciousness. (4-66)
In Gauḍa, the skull is proclaimed; one should perform the rite of the mouth at the nose.
The Keralan tradition belongs to the Upper Transmission (ūrdhvāmnāya), while the Kāśmīrian would be the Western.
The one named Vilāsa, the one named Vaiṣṇava, and the Dakṣiṇāmnāya;
Caitanya is proclaimed in the east, and Gauḍa indeed in the north.
(47) Through the distinctions of knowledge (vidyā) and convention (saṅketa), the skull [is used for] the three Tāriṇīs;
if one is unattached even to the great conch, one should perform the recitation with a crystal rosary. 4-69.
O Goddess, if a skull is not obtained, one should certainly have a crystal [vessel] made.
I shall now declare the determination of the vessels according to the sequence of their different numbers.

O Śivā, one should contemplate the placement of the vessels according to the sequence of the tradition; they should be understood as being composed of the letters [of the alphabet] within the apertures of the Great Kalās and Kalārands. (4.71)
The general arghya should come first; the general arghya is remembered as being of two kinds:
with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala). That which is with parts arises from the worship of the door.
O Goddess, that which is partless and absolute, and that which is partless yet the range of all; these are the two general *arghya* vessels, and the jar is the third.
The fourth is the special *arghya*, while the fifth is the vessel of the Guru.
That which is called the Divine Current (*divyaugha*) is proclaimed, as is that called the Siddha Current (*siddhaugha*), known as the Essence (*rasa*).
O Goddess, the seventh is celebrated as the one named the Human Current (*mānavaugha*).
Then the vessel of the Guru is proclaimed, as well as the one called Bhairava, which is the cavity (randhraka). || 4.75 ||
The tenth is the vessel for the Śakti, and the vessel for the Vīra is named after Śiva;
thereafter, the vessel for the Śrīyoginī shall be known by the number of the sun (twelve).
There are indeed nine vessels for the bali offering, distinguished by categories such as the Sakala;
the vessel designated for the presentation of the bali is proclaimed to be the Sakala.
O Maheśānī, Vaṭuka and the others, as well as the Siddhis, are partless.
O Parameśvarī, [these are] Vaṭuka, the Yoginīs, the Kṣetras, and the Gaṇapas.
O Goddess of the gods, all the bhūtas as well as Tārā and Akṣobhya [are worshipped];
likewise, O Goddess, the three-fold water for the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) are prescribed.
O Goddess, there should be three *arghya* vessels; in the *madhuparka*, there should be three;
in the *pañcāmṛta*, five; and for the purpose of bathing, [there should be] those numbering nine (*guṇa*).
Then, the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, and thereafter that produced for washing the hands.
Then the vessel for incense, the vessel for flowers, and the vessel for food offerings. || 4.81 ||
Then there is the vessel called pure water, then the vessel for enjoyments,
then the cooking vessel, and then the items for the lustration ceremony and so forth.
The local pedestal-vessel and four lamp-vessels;
ghee and oil on the right and left, as well as fragrance and the intoxicant.
The number of vessels is said to be sixty-four in Kerala;
in Kashmir, there is likewise a sacred seat (pīṭha). Now hear indeed the number of kalās.
These two are declared to be the most supreme among the divine, bringing immediate accomplishment and being unsurpassed.
Now, O Supreme Goddess, listen to the description of the sixteen vessels.
The general arghya, the special arghya, the śrīpīṭha, the vessel of the Guru, the fifth called Bhairava, and the hero’s vessel known as rasa. (4.86)
The vessel for the *śakti*, the *yoginī* vessel, and likewise the vessels for the *bali* and the *pādya*;
the vessel known as the *ācamanīya*, and likewise the *arghya* vessel. || 4.87 ||
The vessel called madhuparka, followed by the vessel for the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
the bathing vessel, the vessel for hand-cleansing, and likewise the prokṣaṇī vessel.
The vessel is said to be sixteen-fold, both in Kerala and in the West; O Goddess, it is called "Śaṅkhā" after the offering of Madhuparka, even in the Kaulika tradition. (4.89)
O Pārvatī, hear now about the vessels in the tradition of Consciousness and Bliss:
the general vessel, the special vessel, the pitcher, and the vessel of the Guru.

The vessel for enjoyments, the vessel for power, the vessels for the Yoginīs and the heroes, as well as the vessels for the offering, the water for the feet, the water for sipping, and that called the water for honor and bathing, O beloved. (4.91)
(49) O Queen of the Gods, these sixteen vessels are known as the "Devī-śaṅkha" [the Conch of the Goddess].
Alternatively, there may be a jar, a conch, and three vessels for the Śaktis. (4.92)
The vessels for the enjoyment of the Śrīguru are contained within three vessels; O Goddess, this is the procedure according to the doctrine known as Ānanda, and thus the vessels have been proclaimed.
The general arghya, the special arghya, the jar, the vessel for the Śrī-guru’s meal, the vessel for the Śakti, the Yoginī, the vessel for the Vīra, and likewise the bali offering. (4.94)
The water for the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamanīya) should be in the vessel named Bhogacāra;
likewise, the vessel of the Goddess, the venerable Guru, the vessel of enjoyment (bhoga), and the Yoginī [should each have their respective vessels]. (4.95)

The vessel for the offering (bali), the vessel for the power-drink (śakti), the vessel for the hero (vīra), and likewise the vessel for sipping water (ācamana)—this is the procedure regarding the blisses of consciousness (cidānanda). || 4.96 ||

O Supreme Goddess, the vessels for the enjoyment of the goddess and the guru, those born of the power of the Yoginīs and Brahman, and the vessels of the path of perfected consciousness—these are the vessels. 4.97

O Maheśvarī, according to the system of the Five Wheels (Pañcacakra), there is the offering of water for the feet and other honors to the Yoginīs and Vīras; this sequence of the divine Lord Ānandavīra has been proclaimed.
The general arghya, the specific arghya, the jar, and the Guru-Bhairava—
these are all declared at the outset according to the general terminology.

O Pārvatī, I have described to you the path of Pañcamānandanātha, consisting of the nine [offerings]: bali, water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the respectful offering (arghya). 4-100.

The pentad consists of the power of enjoyment (*bhogaśakti*) and that which is called Viśvarūpa; [it includes] the goddess, the guru, the power of enjoyment, the yoginī, and the vessel of the hero (*vīrapātra*). (4.101)
The offerings of water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the respectful oblation (arghya) arise from the combination [of syllables];
they are performed according to the sequence of emanation and withdrawal, and by means of the process of rotation.

Oḍḍiyāna is square, and Kāmarūpa is circular; Jālandhara is a half-moon, while Pūrṇagiri is triangular. (4-103) There are five [vessels]: the conch, the mantra-vessel, the vessel for enjoyment, the vessel for worship, and the vessel for the bali offering.
Having established [the goddess] from her own right up to her left, one should worship Śivā.
The doctrine of Kulanātha has been proclaimed; now hear the doctrine of Bhairava.
O Goddess of the gods, [perform] the rite of establishing the arghya and other offerings on your own left side. (4.105)

The water for the feet, the respectful offering, and the water for sipping, as well as the general and the special arghya; O Goddess, the vessel for the general arghya and the Śrīpātra should be placed before the deity.
O Maheśvarī, to the left of oneself, in the place of the water-pot, is the madhuparka;
to its right, one should carefully arrange the water for sipping (ācamanīya) and the water for washing the feet (pādya).
O Maheśvarī, the doctrine known as Nivāpa has thus been declared in brief.
Now, O Deveśī, I shall speak of the doctrine of Śambhunātha; listen.

First, there is the water-pot (kumbha), as well as the conch, the vessel of Śrī (śrīpātra), the vessel of Śakti (śaktipātraka), the vessel of the Guru (gurupātra), the vessel of enjoyment (bhogapātra), and the vessels for the offering (bali), the foot-washing water (pādya), and so forth.
The vessel for the yoginīs and the heroes, following the counter-clockwise sequence,
as well as the general arghya jar, and immediately after that, the śrīpātra.
One should place all the vessels between the Śrīpātra and the jar;
the Guru’s vessel at the end of the jar, and the Bhogapātra at the end of that.
At its end is the vessel for the Śaktis, and the vessel for the Yoginīs;
at its end is the vessel for the Vīras, and at its end is the vessel for the Bali offering. || 4.112 ||
The water for washing the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamanīya), followed by the vessel for the respectful offering (arghyapātra),
then again the water for sipping, and likewise the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
The [five] kalās are designated as follows in the [tantra] called Kāśmīra: snānīya, prokṣaṇī, that which arises from washing the hands, and likewise pañcāmṛta. (4.114)
Then, O Śivā, according to the doctrine known as Kāśmīra, there are eighteen vessels:
the general *arghya*, the special *arghya*, and the *śrīghaṭa* (glorious jar), O Supreme Goddess. (4.115)
Within the jar is the vessel for the Guru, and within that, the one named Bhairava;
then, O Śivā, the vessel for the Śakti is prescribed, and after that, the vessel for the Vīra.
The vessel for the offering (bali), the drinking vessel for the yogins, and likewise the vessel for enjoyment—these, O Goddess of gods, O Pārvatī, are the nine vessels. (4.117)
O Maheśānī, the water for the feet and the other offerings are placed generally in the western direction;
to the south of that are the vessel for the water for the feet, the arghya vessel, and the vessel for the water for sipping.
O Maheśānī, one should establish the *prokṣaṇī* vessel as before, O Śiva;
then the *guru-pātra*, with [offerings] at its two feet, along with Bhairava and the *baṭuka*. (4.119)

The vessel for Śakti belongs to Bhuvaneśī, the vessel for the Vīra belongs to Śiva, and the vessel for the bali offering belongs to Gaṇeśa and the others; for the Yoginī, it should be her own mantra. (4.120)
In this manner, for all other vessels, this procedure is performed with the *praṇava* alone;
however, one should worship the gurus of the divine lineage (*divyaugha*) in the guru-vessel with the special *arghya*.
O Amṛteśvarī, by means of the Bhairava-vessel and the Śrīpātra, the Goddess is thus declared to be the Root-Śāradā at the station of the Root-Goddess. (4.122)
O Śivā, one should satisfy the god Ānandabhairava with [the offering of] Bhairava;
Gaṇeśa and the others with the bali-offering; and the Yoginī with the Yoginī.
One should especially worship the Goddess in the heart with the *śrīpātra* along with its enclosure;
the ritual of emission (*protsarga*) is specifically taught to be performed with the heart-mantra and the *śrījala*.
And for others, O Supreme Goddess, [one should offer] with a common vessel;
the lords of the worlds with the hero’s vessel, and the Mothers, Brāhmī and the rest, with the Śakti vessel.
Worship beginning with the special vessel and so forth—that worship is the most excellent of all.
O Maheśānī, upon returning, one should offer [the remains] to the deities. (4.126)
Then, following the six-limbed meditation, the measure of breath control (prāṇāyāma) is performed;
furthermore, the enclosure is to be worshipped with fifteen, sixteen, or ten [offerings]. (4-127)

Having performed the recitation (japa) and offered it up, preceded by breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other rites, the surrounding deities (āvaraṇa) are to be worshipped again; thus is the sequence of the surrounding deities described.
In this manner, O Queen of the Gods, one should worship all the enclosures in sequence;
having returned from each enclosure, one should display the prescribed mudrās according to the ritual rules.
That which was not mentioned regarding the enclosure of mudrās shall consist of their respective weapons; the *saṃghaṭṭanā* is the *yonimudrā*, and the *khecarī* is their weapon.
When there is a contraction of the veil, O Maheśānī, it consists of that very veil; if there is expansion, then [the goddesses] beginning with Saṃghaṭṭā are at its end.
Again, having offered a handful of flowers, one should recite [the mantra] together with the weapons, the vehicles, the powers (śaktis), the mudrās, and the siddhis.
In all three traditions, O Goddess, there is indeed the performance of the ritual acts in sequence (kāṇḍānusamaya); the general arghya vessel is first, and the special arghya is the third.
O Śivā, worship may indeed be performed according to the sequence of the three vessels:
the general vessel, the special vessel, and the third, the Śrīghaṭa.
However, O Maheśvarī, there is a special worship specifically for this;
O Maheśānī, hear now the determination regarding the vessels according to the Gauḍa tradition.
O Goddess, there are two types of general [offerings]: from the doorway up to the end of the path;
however, before the deity is the special arghya, and at the end of the jar is the vessel for the Guru.
O Queen of the Gods, the vessel known as the *śrīpātra* is proclaimed for the special *arghya*;
then, O Goddess, the *bhogapātra*, and after that, O Śivā, the *śaktipātra*.
O Śivā, the vessel for the *bali* offering is the vessel of the Yoginīs and Vīras;
O Maheśānī, the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) is said to be another, specifically distinguished [vessel]. (4.138)
O Śivā, [there are] three vessels for the *arghya* offering for the Guru, then the vessel for Bhairavī,
the vessel for the Śakti, the Yoginī, and then the vessel for the *bali* offering.
There should be three vessels for the *arghya*, and likewise three for the *pādya*;
there should be three for the *ācamana*, O Goddess, and then the *madhuparka*, O Śivā. (4.140)
The ritual for bathing and hand-cleansing is recorded as the Yajur-Gauda procedure.
Having taken the *prokṣaṇī* vessel to his right, he should fill it with water. (4.141)
Having taken a little of the arghya water, he should add it to the prokṣaṇī water;
then the wise man should place the vessel together with its support in front of him.
To its side is the offering of water for the feet (pādya), and to its side is the offering of the respectful oblation (arghya);
the water for sipping (ācamanīya) is also to its side, while the honey-mixture (madhuparka) is on the left.
Furthermore, one should place the water for sipping (ācamanīya) and the water for bathing (snānīya) in sequence;
likewise, the fragrant flowers on the right and the hand-washing water at the back. (4-144)
One should place the water-pot to one's left and hold it with the left hand;
having grasped that water at the side while reciting the mantra "Oṃ Āḥ," [one should proceed]. (4-145)
Now, with the mantra "nu kṣaura," one should touch oneself, the sacrificial materials, and the perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the *devatīrtha* [finger-position]. (4.146)
One should sprinkle [the area] with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel using the *gāyatrī* mantra and the root mantra.
Between the person to be initiated (*sādhya*) and the practitioner (*sādhaka*), there should be a distance of thirty-six finger-breadths.
The wise man should place [the vessel] there such that it is twelve finger-breadths high, one finger-breadth at the bottom,
and twelve finger-breadths in its middle.

O Goddess, one should draw a triangle on the ground to the left of oneself; O Beloved, there should be twelve and a half for the purpose of the arghya offering, and twelve [triangles] for the sake of the beloved.
Propitiation, installation, worship, and likewise fulfillment;
the arrangement of scents and flowers for the maṇḍala, and the placement of the flowers. (4-150)
The consecration as nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), the vessel, and this ninefold realization—this procedure for the Sāmaga-Gauda tradition has been revealed in brief. (4.151)
In the auspicious Sāmagauḍa tradition, O Śivā, there are twenty vessels; this is the rule in the auspicious [tradition].
The first triad consists of the Guru, Bhoga, and Śakti, and the Yoginī, O Śivā. (4.152)

The vessel for the hero, the vessel for the oblation, the vessels for water for the feet, the guest-offering, and for sipping, as well as the vessel for washing the hands and the one that initiates the root-mantras. || 4-153 ||

The general *arghya*, the *arghya* ending with the sipping of water (*ācamana*) produced by the purification of the hands, the vessel for the remnants of the offering (*ucchiṣṭa-bali*), and the seven vessels for the offerings (*bali*). (4.154)
Now, regarding the vessel for cooking and the ritual procedure in the Krūragauḍa tradition of Śiva,
there are twenty-one vessels here in the Gauḍa tradition as well.
O Goddess, O Śaṅkarī, this has been declared for the Śākta and the Vīraśākta;
however, O Mistress of the Gods, the conch is not primary in the Śaiva and Śākta [traditions], and one should not employ it.
One should perform the placement of the conch for the purpose of manifesting to the world;
in the Śaiva tradition, one should perform the placement of the vessels precisely in a linear sequence.

The general offering (sāmānyārghya), the special offering (viśeṣārghya), the water-pot (ghaṭa), the vessel for water for the feet (pādyapātra), as well as the water for rinsing the mouth (ācamanīya), the offering (arghya), and again the water for rinsing the mouth (punarācamanīyaka).

O Goddess, when Śambhu is joined with Śakti, there is the offering of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), the nectar (amṛta), the bath-water (snānīya), and likewise the sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī); then follows the worship of the jar (kalaśa). (4.159)
If water is not available, he should be established [as an image] and worshipped with Vedic rites;
if he has been initiated with the full initiation (pūrṇadīkṣā), he should perform the rites concerning the vessel for the Śakti and so forth.
O Goddess of gods, one should perform [the rite] with a *bilva* leaf-vessel, as Viśvāmitra has prescribed;
but for a Vaiṣṇava, O Great Goddess, there should first be a common vessel. (4-161)
O Pārvatī, the conch-vessel for one's own deity should be on the left side,
the materials for worship on the right side, and the Supreme Lord in the middle of them.
O Pārvatī, in the Vaiṣṇava and Devadakṣa [mandalas], the conch should be placed in those directions;
and water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) should be arranged in their proper sequence.
And that water-vessel with six compartments is for the purpose of holding the water;
having established the directions according to the prescribed method, the jar should be placed to the left and right.
O Maheśānī, I have explained this to you for the Vaiṣṇava who is endowed with spiritual power; for one who lacks such power, it would not be like an ordinary pot.
If he has received a special initiation, he should have the Śaktis, Vīras, and so forth perform [the rites];
even in the Śaiva tradition, however, from his own right side, there is the general *prokṣaṇī* water.
At the end of that, O Goddess, one should establish [the deity] in the solar [tradition]; listen, O Maheśvarī!
In the solar and Gauḍa traditions, two lineages are common, both belonging to the domain of the Sun.
O Supreme Goddess, one should establish [the ritual] ending with the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) according to the specific [tradition];
however, in the Jaina and Buddhist traditions it is like the Tārā [rite], while in the Bhairava [tradition] the procedure is that of Kālikā.

O Goddess, having brought together the special arghya-pitcher and other implements at the site of vision (darśanāyatana), ending with the sprinkling water (prokṣaṇī) according to the sequence beginning with Kerala; 4-169.
O Goddess, in the case of Gaṇeśa, both are required; however, for the ritual rinsing (ācamana), there should be a conch shell.
In the general water offering (sāmānyārghya), there should be water that is both general and specific.

O Goddess of the gods, the *śrīpātra* should be prepared for the *arghya*, as well as for the self-manifested (*svāyaṃbhūva*) [liṅga], just as it is for Gaṇeśa; otherwise, it is not the word of Śaṅkara.
O Supreme Goddess, in all cases, through the application of power (*śakti*), one should act like a Śākta;
however, in the Gauḍa and Kaula traditions, the vessel (*pātraka*) follows the counter-clockwise sequence alone. (4.172)
In Kashmir, it is through the Dakṣavadana [tradition], and in Kerala, through the Maṇḍalakrama;
in Kerala alone, the goal is accomplished by the mere sound of the conch.
The articles for worship are on the right [hand], and the food offering (naivedya) is behind;
however, the vessel for washing the hands is prescribed to be behind oneself.
A ghee lamp should be on the right and an oil lamp on the left;
or they may be arranged in the shape of a triangle, following the sequence of the fire-wheel.
O Goddess, in the ritual procedure for the initiation of wisdom (medhādīkṣā), the installation is proclaimed;
having placed all the vessels to one's left, above the water-pot (ghaṭa).
O Goddess, the mouth of the jar is proclaimed to be on all sides;
O Goddess, the mouth of the conch, however, is in front of the deity.
"I worship and satisfy [the deity], ending with 'namaḥ'—this is the doctrine in Kerala.
'I satisfy and worship, namaḥ'—this is the practice of Kashmir. (4-178)
When this heart-mantra is joined with the word *sāmrāj*, it is called the Keralī;
[one says] "I worship, obeisance, O Goddess," and likewise "I satiate, obeisance. (4.179)

O Supreme Goddess, in the ancient kingdom of Kerala, the prefix "mahat" (great) is prescribed for [words such as] *kīrti* (fame); furthermore, in Kerala, the word *namaḥ* (salutation) is used for both worship (*pūjā*) and libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Pūrṇānanda, Citānanda, and Bodhānanda are proclaimed;
O Maheśānī, these are the eight divisions resulting from the application [of the mantra] beginning with and ending at the heart. (4.181)
Even in the Madhyayoga, O Śivā, various divisions have been proclaimed;
furthermore, in the Gauḍaka tradition, the offering of the bali-oblation occurs at the beginning, the middle, and likewise at the end.
In Kāśmīra, the offering of the *bali* is prescribed at the beginning; however, in Kerala, the *bali* is performed at the end, or even if there is only the libation (*tarpaṇa*). (4.183)
O Goddess, at that time, when the worship of Viśvarūpa is performed according to the Kerala tradition, there is a rite called Vilāsa, consisting of both worship and libation. (4.184)
O Dear One, it may be the word *śrī* preceding the *pādukā*, or the *pādukā* alone, or the propitiation of that deity; it may be either short or long. (4.185)
O Maheśānī, one should practice either with the bindu or in its entirety;
this applies even in the Cīna tradition for Tāriṇī and Mañjughoṣa as well, O Pārvatī. (4.186)
"Accept the vajra-flower, svāhā"— with these words ending in *svāhā*,
one performs the worship in a counter-clockwise sequence and by the order of right and left.
O Śivā, O Supreme Goddess, thirty-eight varieties have been proclaimed for you, consisting solely of the clockwise rotation and solely of the left hand.
By means of the yoga of Kevalānanda, from the yoga of Kevalānanda, by means of the yoga of Ānandanātha, and through the lineage of Nāthānanda. || 4-189 ||

Through the awakening of the consciousness of wisdom, such as that of the Siddhas, Mānavas, and Divyas, by means of the yoga of the sequence of manifestations, and likewise through the sequence of Sarasvatī; 4-190.

The multiplicity of divisions has been described precisely according to the sequence that will be explained; thus it has been stated in brief, O Dear One, and now the specific details are being told. 4-191.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Determination of Vessels," in the first section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Tārā. || 4 ||
The Fifth Chapter.
The Holy Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear that which is the most secret of secrets."
Śrī Śiva said:
O Pārvatī, listen as I speak that which is the most secret of secrets. 5-1.

Having first formed the latent impression (vāsanā) of the true Brahman and abiding as the Supreme Śiva, she became the object of meditation; that [meditation] arose through the hearing of the sacred tradition, having entered into the latent impression of Brahman.
O Great Goddess, from the moment that the supreme form, most captivating to the consciousness, was assumed, from that moment on there was manifestation (prapañcatā).
O most beautiful one, if the Kādimata alone were to exist, then all men would be of the nature of Mahākāla. (5.4)
O Maheśānī, all women are considered to be composed of Kālī and Tārā; when such an understanding arises, there is indeed no longer any conception of saṃsāra. (5-5)
For the purpose of producing the effects of saṃsāra, this phenomenal world (prapañca) has been fashioned;
[it consists of] the Śākta, the Śaiva, the Gāṇapatya, the Vaiṣṇava, the Saura, and the Bauddha systems.
Thus, O Queen of the Gods, this doctrine was composed in due order;
from that time forth, O Maheśvarī, there have been doctrines of great number.
O Maheśānī, these have certainly arisen for the sake of phenomenal manifestation, just as the terms ambhodhi, jaladhi, samudra, and sāgara [all refer to the ocean]. (5.8)
Just as these are synonyms, so too are these doctrines:
(p. 59) censure of Śakti in the Vedic tradition, and censure of Vaiṣṇavas in the Śaiva tradition. (5.9)
In the Vaiṣṇava [sect], there is the disparagement of the Gaṇas; in the Gāṇapa [sect], the disparagement of the Sauras;
in the Saura [sect], the disparagement of the Cāndras; and in the Cāndra [sect], the disparagement of the Bauddhas. (5–10)
O Maheśvarī, there is the censure of Svāyambhuva in the Buddhist path;
the censure of Saubhari in China; and the censure of the Jaina in China. (5-11)
In the Paurāṇika [tradition] there is censure of the Jainas, and in the Jaina [tradition] there is censure of the Paurāṇikas;
O Supreme Goddess, in the Paurāṇika [tradition] there is also censure of the science of mantras (mantraśāstra). (5.12)
O Maheśānī, in the Dharmaśāstra there is likewise censure of the Kaulikas;
thus, O Maheśvarī, these various divergent views have arisen. (5-13)
O Maheśvarī, the abundance of scriptures among the Vedas is for the sake of elaboration;
thus, O Maheśvarī, when this censure was concluded, a division arose.
But the mind of no one is fixed upon a single point, O Supreme Goddess;
there is mutual disparagement everywhere, and thus unity does not arise. (5.15)
For the sake of perfectly establishing their identity and for the purpose of worldly manifestation, they praise what is distinct as being distinct and revile one another. (5.16)
If there is mutual disparagement, one does not attain the accomplishment of knowledge; they become agitated like piśācas, and thus unity is not produced. (5-17)
Then, for the sake of perfectly accomplishing their unity, one should worship Kālikā and Tāriṇī;
furthermore, for the destruction of the Daityas and for the bestowal of grace upon devotees.
Bearing a form that is beautiful, yet cruel and most fierce, Śivā has manifested this appearance for the sake of the phenomenal world; indeed, it has been described by me to you.
O Goddess, the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Sāṃkhya, Pātañjala, Vedānta, Vyākaraṇa, and the Dharmaśāstras along with their auxiliary sciences; || 5.20 ||
(60) Prosody, astronomy, medicine, and so forth—these are the fourteen sciences.
I have taught them for the sake of worldly manifestation; their unity arises from transformation. (5.21)
The subject at hand is now being told, O Goddess; listen and be attentive.
She is proclaimed as Caturvedeśvarī, the illustrious Mahābhavatāriṇī. (5.22)
The supreme Śrī Mahākālikā is the presiding deity of the Atharvaveda;
without Kālī and without Tārā, there is no ritual procedure of the Atharvaveda anywhere. (5.23)
In Kerala she is called Kālikā; in Kashmir she is considered to be Tripurā;
in Gauḍa she is proclaimed as Tārā—she alone is the transcendent one. (5.24)
Indeed, this triad beginning with *ha* has been proclaimed in brief;
now, in Kerala, that Tripurā beginning with *ka* is proclaimed. (5.25)
Tāriṇī is proclaimed as Bālā in Kaśmīra, and Kālī is celebrated in Gauḍa;
Śivadevī becomes Parā through the distinction of the Dakṣiṇāmūrtti lineage.
Now, O Pārvatī, according to the different traditions known as Ānanda and Bhairava, this [teaching] was received from the presence of the Goddess by means of her power, down to one's own guru. (5.27)
O Maheśvarī, that lineage of power which is never interrupted is to be known as the lineage of the Goddess (Devī-paramparā) precisely through the sequence of names and commands.
O Maheśvarī, that lineage which was received from Śambhu down to one's own guru,
by the very sequence of their names and commands, is the supreme transmission of Śiva.
O Goddess, from Dakṣiṇāmūrtti down to one's own guru in due order, and by the sequence of their names and commands— that indeed is his lineage.
O Maheśvarī, when that [lineage] indeed becomes uninterrupted through the union with the four Śaṅkaras, then another tradition (sampradāya) shall arise.
Kerala, Kāśmīra, and Gauḍa as the third—O Mistress of the Gods, O Beloved, this triad exists within all four [regions]. (5.32)

"I take" (gṛhṇāmi) and "may he accept" (pragṛhṇīyāt) are used for the act of drinking during the *vilāsa* [rite]; "I offer" (juhomi) and "may you enjoy" (juṣasva) are used for the act of drinking during the *kerala* [rite]. || 5-33 ||
"I shall offer; please enjoy," thus is the drink prescribed for Kaśmīra.
By drinking from the Vidyā-siddha and others, the Lord shall be perpetually intoxicated. (5.34)
When a man, through the sequence of the triad, becomes one who delights in worship, he is proclaimed as Nandanāthī; indeed, such a person is of that very nature.
He who is called Mahānanda is proclaimed [as the authority] in Gauḍa; now hear the sequence of drinking (pānakrama).
The worship of the drink from the left hand is proclaimed as the Vāmī-krama.
One is called a Kaula because of drinking from the right hand, because of satiating with the left hand, and indeed because of worshipping with the right hand. (5.37)
Because worship is performed with the right hand alone, it is called Dakṣiṇa;
that very same [tradition] is declared to be Kerala, and is celebrated as the Pure Path (śuddhamārga).
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrttibheda, however, there are the three [streams] beginning with Divyaugha;
through that division, there is a threefold classification, and each of these possesses nine subdivisions.
In the tradition of Ānandabhairava, the lineage of eighty-five gurus is proclaimed;
it is celebrated as consisting of eighty-five [teachers] beginning with the divine, the perfected, and the human. (5.40)
Each being threefold, according to the sequence of seven sevens, the fifty-fifth is proclaimed; and by that sequence, it is called the Command of Names (nāmājñā).
And there are nine divisions according to the sequence of the nine lords (navanātha),
due to the specific distinctions of the sequential initiation (kramadīkṣā) for the eighty-four Siddhas.
There are eighty-four divisions according to the sequence of their names;
having ascertained both debt and wealth, the Guru should cause the Name-command to be bestowed.

(62) O Pārvatī, I shall now explain the wheel of debt (*ṛṇacakra*) according to its sixfold division, based on the distinction between the letters of the goal (*sādhya*), the letters of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and so forth, as well as the distinction between consonants and vowels. (5.44)
First, the numerical values (aṅka) should be grasped according to the sequence of the Mātṛkā alphabet;
[the total] is tripled by the name of the object to be accomplished and joined with that of the practitioner. (5.45)
One should divide by seven; the other [result] is the reverse.
By reversing the previous figures, there is the subtraction of debt from wealth.
O Goddess of the gods, he whose numerical value is greater is indeed considered a debtor;
O Goddess of the gods, he whose numerical value is less is proclaimed to be a creditor. (5.47)
The practitioner possesses wealth while the vidyā possesses debt;
their multiplication may be by three or by seven, even if it results in a negative value.
The rule is proclaimed by way of three reversals of the seven [positions]:
where there is an increase by two, there is a piercing by elephants.
Having seen it as empty, there is no further portion; this has been stated in brief. Where there is an increase by three, from that follows a division by seven.
Where there is division by eight, there is increase by two, according to the rule for counting the syllables of the mantra and the practitioner. (5.51)

Or else, O Goddess, having divided [the mantra] according to the distinction between vowels and consonants, the name of the one to be accomplished (sādhya) is doubled and joined with the name of the practitioner (sādhaka). || 5.52 ||
One should take the share with the fires; the rest is otherwise.
[This applies] to the letters of the mantra-practitioner according to the sequence of the fifty mother-letters (mātṛkā).
One should collect the numerical values of the letters up to that point;
this may be done according to the distinction between vowels and consonants, or simply by the number of syllables.
In that case, the numerical markers for the syllables of both [the mantra and the name] should be made;
having tripled the mantra-syllables, they are to be combined by the practitioner. (5.55)
One should divide that other [number] by seven; the reverse applies to the remainder.
However, in another context, there may be multiplication instead of division. (5.56)
Multiplication by means of the desired digits and division are proclaimed here;
indeed, I have explained them to you according to the sequence of the digits. (5.57)

Starting from the first syllable of the name up to the first syllable of the mantra, one should divide it into three parts and differentiate them by means of the vowels; the other [method] is the reverse of that.
O Śivā, beginning from the first syllable of the mantra up to the syllable of the name, one should divide it into three parts seven times; the other [method] is the reverse of that.

By reversing the order of the *mātṛkā* and dividing the mantra consisting of the letters of the name into three parts, and then multiplying by three, this becomes the aggregate of the mantra (*mantrarāśi*). || 5-60 ||
Other cycles of debt have been described by me to you;
O Goddess, now understand properly the debt that takes the form of devotion.
That which was hidden in the Koṭitantras has been revealed today;
therein, through the practice of preliminary service (pūrvasevā), devotion becomes firm. || 5.62 ||
That mantra, O beloved, should be known as a debt; the debt takes the form of devotion.
Otherwise, O Goddess, how could there be devotion? O beloved, the debt is of the nature of devotion.
Thus has the purification of debts and wealth been explained in due order;
having understood both the debt and the wealth, O Maheśvarī, one should bestow the name.
Otherwise, O Supreme Goddess, if the name is bestowed [without due care], the fruit will not correspond to that name; the practitioner becomes fallen. (5–65)
"You are a fool; in this Kali age, you do not understand that [the Lord] is intent on destroying the wicked.
Having understood all this, the Guru should cause the name-injunction to be granted. (5-66)
p. 64) But the fruit is progressively greater for the divine, the perfected, and the human [levels].
The Śrī Devī said:
How should the bestowing of names be performed even within all six systems of philosophy? (5–67)
O Lord of Gods, likewise in the six traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya) and in the pair of Śāmbhava;
O Supreme Lord, likewise in the five traditions and in the Vedic tradition.
O Maheśvara, O Śaṅkara, tell me how the bestowing of names should be performed by means of the divine internal sovereignty of wisdom.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Śivā, you inquire about that which is the most profound secret;
I know it, as does Kālī and Tārā, but no others.
Even those who possess some knowledge and even those with divine forms there know only a little;
therefore, O Goddess, it must be kept secret in every way and must not be spoken of to just anyone.
Therein, the six cakras are fully described as establishing four designations:
in the first is the piercing of the consonants (varṇa), and in the second is the piercing of the vowels (svara).
In the third [cakra] there is the piercing by emptiness (śūnyavedha); in the fourth, the piercing by the peak (kūṭavedha);
in the fifth, there is the piercing by the group (gaṇavedha); and in the sixth, something by means of the wheel (cakreṇa).
O Great Goddess, O Beloved, there are six wheels, as well as other wheels;
there are five other wheels, and likewise those of the nature of Rudra. (5.74)
There, in the midst of the six wheels, are the Sādhya, Siddha, Susiddhaka, Daivata, the one called Parā, and that named Devatādarśana. (5.75)
O Maheśvarī, one should give a name called "Vision of the Deity," as well as the name belonging to the three lineages (oghatrika) of the practitioner.
One should take the well-known name by which, when one has fallen asleep, one may wake;
beginning from the first syllable of that name up to the first syllable of the mantra. (5.77)
O Goddess of the gods, having tripled [the sequence] according to the distinction between vowels and consonants, O Śivā, it becomes a numerical figure through the enumeration of the Mātṛkā.
Having unified [the letters] in the practitioner's [name], one should extract [the sum] mixed seven times;
this is called the "name-pile," while the "mantra-pile" is otherwise.
And that which is not to be given even by debtors—beautiful and most enchanting—the name of the divine stream is bestowed only through great fortune. (5.80)
O Goddess of the gods, that which is named Siddhaugha brings about accomplishment through good fortune;
that which is named Mānavaugha is obtained by one who is indebted through good fortune.

The disciple is gazed upon by the Guru, and the Guru is gazed upon by the disciple; through this mutual regard, the defects of the mantra are removed, just as the debts of those who fail to repay are cleared by non-payment [of interest]. (5.82)
In the initiation of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), one should cause the name to be bestowed,
pertaining to the realms of the initiation of wisdom (medhādīkṣā) and so forth, up to the sovereignty and the divine sovereignty.
O Maheśānī, a name should be given that is either beautiful or contrived;
initially it should be a well-known name, or if that is not obtained, a contrived one.
O Maheśvarī, the name may be mounted upon a mantra or enriched with a vidyā;
otherwise, it is joined with the asterism of that day according to the sequence of the rising syllables.

Then that which is taught as the daily [rite] of Udayārṇa is proclaimed according to the sequence of the daily [rites] of Kāla, and that which is taught as the daily [rite] of Yuga is proclaimed according to the sequence of the annual [rites]. || 5.86 ||
That which is called the "eternal obscuration" has been explained according to the sequence of the tradition;
in the tradition known as Kāśmīra, it is fashioned by means of that vidyā-mantra. (5.87)
In Gauḍa it is named Kālāntaka, and in Kerala it is Sarvagocara; having purified them from one another, O Maheśvarī, one should then bestow the name.

(66) That which is spoken by the Nātha and that which is spoken by the Siddha, through the application of the five preceding [categories], is indeed the excellent leader for one who has become a debtor. (5.89)
O Maheśānī, the three currents bestow success in an ever-increasing degree;
if one enters the divine current (divyaugha), he becomes possessed of a divine form.
If he comes within the stream of the Siddhas, he bestows the perfect accomplishment of the form of a Siddha;
in the stream of humans, he is the Lord of the Kinnaras—this is how it occurs in the Śākta scripture. (5.91)
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, why indeed is it called 'Śākta'?
Śrī Śiva replied:
In the Vaiṣṇava, the Gāṇapatya, the Śaiva, and likewise in the Svāyaṃbhuva [Purāṇas].
O Maheśānī, [the worship] may be performed in the Cāndra, Pāśupata, Cīna, Jaina, Kālamukha, or even Vaidika systems, or it may belong to its specific enclosure (āvaraṇa).
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, one should give a name derived from its synonym; one should assign the name ending with the root and ending with that [synonym] to the north of the door.
O Śivā, O Goddess, in the rite of Sparśatārā during the [age of] Bālā and Sparśakālī,
and in the rite of Sparśacchinnā, [it is performed] according to the sequence of six and sixteen moons.

O Maheśānī, in the sequence of the arts (kalākrama), [the mantra] belongs to Raktacaṇḍī; in that same sequence, [it belongs to] Durvāsas, Manu, Agastya, and so forth, as well as in the ritual of Svapnāvatī.
And in Madhumatī, the divine streams are proclaimed to be of diverse forms;
likewise in Ṣoḍaśī, in Parā, and also in Parāprāsādaka.
In the Ṣaḍvidyā and the Śāmbhava [traditions], the gurus possess distinct forms;
they are situated within the garland, within the ritual placement (nyāsa), and likewise within the primary rays.
(67) O Maheśvarī, this procedure for the bestowing of names has been proclaimed by me;
it was previously declared in the Śāmbhava [tradition] according to the sequence of the oral lineage. 5.99.
O Goddess of Gods, that which was not stated there, nor even in the Siddhamatam,
is what is to be known here, O Goddess of Gods, according to the sequence of the four sections.
This should not be considered a redundancy, for there is a distinction due to the difference in the types of knowledge.
The Śrī-cūlikā and the Ūrmilā-cakra are within the scope of those beginning with the Rāja and ending with the Paśu.
O Goddess of the gods, the nine wheels are now being described; listen attentively.
The tenth, called Kerala, shall likewise be of three kinds for each.
O Goddess, listen as this analysis is told in brief;
O Maheśvarī, hear also of the threefold nature and the sequence within the Śrīcakra.
One hundred and eight powers (śaktis) are traditionally taught to reside in the Śrīcakra;
however, in this context, there are fifty-four [powers] in the central cakra, according to the sequence.
The youngest is proclaimed to have nine powers;
O Maheśānī, that which is called Cūlikā is likewise proclaimed to be of three kinds.

Or [they are worshipped] by means of the names of the fifty seats (pīṭha), or from among the thirty-six castes (jāti), according to the sequence of the divisions of the ten Vidyās, their forms, castes, and scents. || 5.106 ||
By means of the lineage-transmission (krama) of both the Kulākulika and the Kashmiri-Gauda traditions,
through the application of the eightfold nyāsa, it is proclaimed as the "Youngest" (kaniṣṭha).
O Maheśānī, understand this sequence exactly as it is:
O Pārvatī, O Queen of the Gods, having summoned the Śakti and taken her garment, [proceed]. (5.108)
The Goddess should cause each individual bodice to be placed in the hand of Śiva;
having tied a knot in the garment, she should then unite him in a state of aesthetic identity (sāmarasya).
O Goddess, O beloved, hear now about this cūḍācakra called Ūrmilā;
having summoned Śakti with effort and having carefully grasped the crest-lock (cūlikā).

Having placed [the image] in a jar and worshipped it, and having respectfully invoked Śiva, she—residing in the center of the wheel—belongs to whichever person she has approached in whatever manner. (5.111)
O Goddess, the sequence known as the Cūlikā has been told; now hear the Śrīkrama, which is the placement within the Śrīcakra through the union of mutual affection. 5-112.
O Goddess, in the tradition known as Kerala, each dwelling place is distinct.
Thus it has been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (5.113)

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Wheel of Debtors and Creditors," in the first section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Tārā. || 5 ||
The Sixth Chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
O Lord, tell me now the fruit of these [practices].
Śrī Śiva said:
O Maheśānī, this knower is indeed Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt.
The arresting of youth, the attraction [of beings], as well as the subjugation of the three worlds; likewise, collyrium, forehead-mark, concealment, sandals, and the pill.
The accomplishment of the Vetāla and Yakṣiṇī, the threefold discourse, and that which follows it;
the great accomplishments beginning with Khecarī, and the entry into another's body. || 6-3 ||
The power to curse and to bestow grace, speech, the ability to assume any form at will, elixirs, and the mastery of the three worlds like Mahendra and others— these are the arts of a magician.
O Goddess, the eightfold [powers] beginning with *aṇiman*, as well as the sword [power] and invisibility;
likewise, the muting, blinding, and paralyzing [powers], as well as the destructive sword [power].
The dual-banner battle yields victory and the destruction of barrenness;
it bestows manliness, mental stability, and is the delighter, the Golden Bhairava. (6-6)
And likewise Dhanadā, Śāstā, Padmā, and Madhumatī;
[the teachings on] the Secret, the Extremely Secret, and the Most Extremely Secret.
"It must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret again and again!
Thus it has been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear?"
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the most excellent, supreme secret.
The Śrī Śiva said:
Everything has been explained in detail; now hear the sequence beginning with the letter Ka.
And by the lineage of the Great Kāla of the Divine, Siddha, and Mānava; and by the lineage of the Heroic Lord whose face is exceedingly black and terrifying.
There are five in Atikāla and nine in Karāla; ten in Pārvatī, O Mahākāla, and nine divisions in the three times according to the lineage of the gurus.
O Goddess, a hundred varieties of gurus are proclaimed in the Vīranātha [tradition];
through the distinction of the pair of nine nāthas, equality with the Siddhas occurs in the Kahe [tradition].
O Goddess of gods, initiation according to this sequence is approved by the Kādi tradition;
O Great Mistress, it is precisely in this [tradition] that Śambhu holds primacy.
O Goddess, the state of Śāmbhava arises from the thought "I am Śiva, devoid of qualities";
and because of the preeminence of Śakti, there is the state of Śākta, for she is that very one who has the form of the Goddess. (6.14)
I am Kālikā, and I am always in the form of Mahātārā; from that non-duality, Śiva-Śakti arises—this is the view in brief. (6.15)
O Supreme Goddess, having remained [there], the drinking from the divine stream is proclaimed; O Maheśvarī, having established oneself in the stream of the Siddhas, one should perform the drinking.
Having arisen within the flood of human beings, the triad is said to manifest in succession; O Kuleśvarī, consciousness then becomes unified with its source.
O Goddess, following the dismissal (visarjana), the tradition of Bhadranātha is proclaimed; O Goddess, following the satisfaction of the heroes (vīratṛpti), there is the sequence of the Atikālamata.

Having established the separate vessel for the *śakti* according to the tradition of Dakṣiṇāmūrtti, one should take up the vessel for the *śakti* according to the doctrine of Vīranātha, O Śivā. (6-19)
The *kulacakra* belongs to Kālī, the *akula* to the fire-mantra of Kālikā, and the *kulākula* to Tārā; these exist within the three lineages (*sampradāya*). (6.20)
And by means of the sequence of the divine path, the hero’s path, and the animal path,
one should bestow the names of the commands through the yoga of the full consecration.
O Goddess of the gods, the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is described according to the sequence beginning with *ha* and so forth;
O Mistress of the God of gods, listen and be attentive. (6.22)
In an auspicious month, under an auspicious constellation, at an auspicious lunar mansion, and during an auspicious rising;
when the day of Kālarātri had arrived, as well as the day of Vīrarātri.
And on the day of the Night of Delusion, likewise on the day of the Great Night,
O Goddess, on the day of the Night of Wrath, and likewise on the day of the Terrible Night.
Also on the night of Tārārātri, or on a night arising from the conjunction of Abalārātri, or during a terrible conjunction, or at the junction of Capricorn and Aquarius.

Having reached a secluded place—such as a mountain, a formidable forest, an empty house, or a cremation ground—and having first performed the purification of the site and other preliminary rites; (6.26)
In a solitary linga, in the abode of Śiva, in the eight cremation grounds, in the house of Cakrapāṇi, by a river, in a city, and in the eight sacred seats (pīṭhas), O Śivā; || 6-27 ||
Either in the midst of the fifty sacred seats (pīṭhas), or during the Flower Festival (puṣpiṇyutsava),
or within the Ganges, in a pond, in the house of a courtesan, or at a confluence of rivers.
Or in a grove of family trees, or in the midst of a grove of plantains;
or else, O Goddess, in a grove of betel-nut trees, or likewise in a grove of coconut trees.
In a divine plantain grove, in a variegated garden,
in the midst of a forest of Palāśa trees, and especially in a sacred field.
In the midst of the house of a wanton woman, within a circle of dancing procuresses,
having reached a distinguished location, one should have a pavilion constructed there.
O Maheśvarī, [the altars] may be one cubit, two cubits, nine cubits,
or five cubits in size, O Maheśānī, according to the sequence of the nine fire-pits (navakuṇḍī).
Alternatively, O Supreme Goddess, one should have the pavilion constructed according to the sequence known as the Single Pit (ekakuṇḍa), O Goddess, following the path of the practice of Meru.
O Goddess, the temple of Śrī Meru-maṇḍapa, according to the prescribed initiation,
is richly adorned with canopies and banners, and is surrounded by secure ramparts.
O Goddess, it should be provided with gate-towers and adorned with various arches;
O Supreme Sovereign, one should construct the worship pavilion in front of that.
O Pārvatī, the arrangement of these [energies] occurs indeed according to the sequence of eight times eight and three, and by way of five times five. (6.36)
Likewise, having entered the pavilion, one should then arrange lotuses;
O Goddess, one should perform the Sarvatobhadra design consisting of a thousand squares.
In that regard, O Goddess, one should fashion the wheel on a copper plate, or in gold, silver, or clay, or upon a cloth; now hear from me concerning that wheel.
The *sarvatobhadra* pedestal is proclaimed for the deity’s seat;
there is one lotus on the vessel of the Yoginī, and five lotuses on that of the Kṣetrapāla.
O Supreme Goddess, having fashioned the nine-petalled lotus for Gaṇeśa and the Liṅgabhadraka for Vaṭuka, one should perform the Meru-maṇḍapa.
O Goddess, the ritual practice for accomplishing Meru for a worshiper of Śrīvidyā is twofold: with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala). || 6.41 ||

For one who worships the threefold knowledge—Śrīvidyā, Kālikā, and Tārā—the Śiva [mantra] is with parts (sakala) as an ancillary to initiation, and without parts (niṣkala) as an ancillary to the fulfillment of desires. (6.42)
O Goddess, the accomplishment of Meru has been proclaimed as essential for initiation;
O Maheśānī, apart from this, there can never be an initiation anywhere. (6.43)
And hear now the sequence of the lineage for the worshippers of Śrīvidyā:
first Bālā is prescribed, and after that Pañcadaśī is considered [the next].
Likewise, the Śrīṣoḍaśī-vidyā is the supreme knowledge (parāvidyā) following that;
after that, there should be the initiation of the feet (caraṇadīkṣā), and from that, the initiation of liberation (nirvāṇadīkṣaṇa).
Then follows that which is called the sixfold Śāmbhava initiation; after that, the initiation beginning with the "cloud" (megha), joined in due order, shall be known by the name Meghādīkṣā.
Then, when one [of these] proceeds, from that comes the initiation into imperial sovereignty;
and immediately following that, there occurs the sacrifice of divine imperial sovereignty.
O Goddess, the one named Vidyārājñī exists for the purpose of severing ignorance;
she brings about the supreme sovereignty that is within the range of Bagalā. (6.48)
Bagalā has Śrīvidyā as her limb, and Chinnamastakā has Tārā as her limb;
O Goddess, after this initiation, there is no other initiation anywhere.
Then, for the child [initiate], there is purification of the body, followed by eligibility for the Vidyā;
once eligibility for the Vidyā has been attained, one should perform the worship of the venerable Ṣoḍaśī.
O Goddess of gods, the one authorized in the sixfold [system] should install the five-fold Ṣoḍhā upon his body;
having performed the installation of the five-fold Ṣoḍhā, he should always recite the Parā-vidyā.
Then, having performed the placement of the *parāṣṭaka*, one should contemplate the feet;
then, having placed *nirvāṇa*, one should practice the *śāmbhava* [state].
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of that triad of sixfold [mantras], one should practice the visualization of the rays;
then, one should place the pair consisting of the Śrī-raśmi and the Parā-raśmi.
Then, O Pārvatī, the initiation of intelligence (medhādīkṣā) becomes complete;
thereafter, O Maheśānī, one should install the initiation of imperial sovereignty (sāmrājyamedhikā) following the initiation of intelligence.
Then, having deposited the [mantra] named *divya*, the person becomes equal to Sadāśiva; [he attains] the knowledge of the piercing of Meru and so forth in the *Śrīmahāsiddhaśaivaka*. (6.55)
In the Kālikāmnāya-tantra, it is proclaimed in the Ūrdhvāmnāya;
here too, O Goddess of the gods, it is told in the final ritual procedure.
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, the arrangement of the sacrificial pits and so forth is exactly as it occurs there;
it has been indicated according to the traditional lineage. Now listen, O Pārvatī, to the subject at hand. (6.57)
Having constructed the previously described pavilion, adorned with various colorful paintings,
enriched with the resonance of ringing bells, and resembling the interior of a mirror.
O Maheśānī, having prepared the ground, one should perform what is about to be described;
having fashioned a wheel in its center, one should place that jar within the wheel.
Having filled [the vessel] with decoction water, I shall sprinkle [the disciple] while reciting the mantra,
for one who is devoted and intent upon the traditional practices passed down through the lineage.
Having fashioned a large wheel with sixteen sections according to their respective origins,
and having then constructed triangles, one should place a jar in the center.
Whether it be made of gold, silver, copper, glass,
or even clay, [the vessel] is filled with a decoction prepared by boiling medicinal herbs that do not decay.
Having deposited the nine gems, various maidens,
gold, and copper, one should also wrap them in fine cloth.
With two red [threads] joined with sandalwood, and with shoots of the *panasa* and *aśvattha* trees bound together with the *śatakratu* creeper and provided with *mātuluṅga* fruits.
One should place other covering jars, one by one, upon the others;
their number is stated in sequence as thirty-six hundred and sixty.
Having placed the elements beginning with water in the middle wheels and having performed the external worship,
one should recite the mantras of Kālātmanityā on the preceding day.
O Maheśvarī, the mantras whose nature is Time (Kālātmanityā) also begin with the letter *ka*;
O Maheśvarī, the Kālī-cakra is located within the Śrīcakra at the position beginning with *ka*. (6-67)
In the various divisions beginning with the triangle, equality is proclaimed;
O Maheśvarī, in the place of Kālikā within Tārā, there is the Tārā-cakra.

In the case of time, the self, and permanence, as well as in the absence of these, the goddess of speech and the deities of the letters of the limbs are said to be equal everywhere; indeed, everything should be understood as being like the letter *ka* and the others.

Having risen early in the morning on one's birth-star (janmarkṣa), one should worship one’s own Nityā there; O Goddess, in the ritual of Kālitārā, one should recite the mantra at the place of the Nityā.
Thereafter, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) on all sides;
prior to that, one should perform the expiation (prāyaścitta) for sixteen days.
The recitation sixty times of the Kālanityās, as well as the pārāyaṇa;
O Goddess, likewise the pārāyaṇa of the mantra and the pārāyaṇa of the cakra.
O Goddess, the thorough mastery of the Yantra may be achieved either by oneself or by one's own guru, in a day, a week, a fortnight, a month, or within thirty-six days. (6–73)
The four junctions (sandhyās) are at the beginning of the *ha*-group and the *ka*-group; in each pair, there are three [vowels].
Having performed the expiation, one should prepare the materials for the eightfold worship (*aṣṭakārcana*).

Having performed and established [the ritual] with diligence, one should apply the *tilaka* as prescribed in the *Vidyā*, accompanied by horns, *kāhala* drums, conchs, and other musical instruments, as well as songs and dances. (6–75)
The Guru himself should perform the consecration together with the joyful throngs of Yoginīs, who are each of the nature of a deity, surrounded [by them] and fully honored. (6.76)

O Goddess, one should consecrate [the disciple] with the mantras of the sixfold initiation (ṣoḍhābhiṣeka) as they arise in the sequence beginning with *ka-ha-hā*, or else with the thousand root-mantras (*mūlabheda*).
The Kālacakra should be made of silver, and the wheel therein should be made of gold;
having placed it upon a great vessel, one should consecrate the Vidyā therein. (6-78)

O Great Goddess, having been consecrated with the waters of knowledge and endowed with the grace of the Guru, one should diligently perform [the rites] beginning with Cakṣuṣmatī and ending with Sāntaka.
Having established the disciple within a svastika maṇḍala according to the three traditions and having sprinkled him with effort upon his limbs while preceded by recitation; 6.80.
The form of the Goddess within the body of the disciple, together with the syllables of the jar,
[is established] by means of the sequence of the supreme body and the sequence of the living insect.

O Goddess of gods, having placed that life-force into the body of the doll, one who is devoted to the bliss of Brahman should cause the disciple to attain the state of a *bhṛṅgin* and awaken him. (6.82)
Having previously been a worm, the living soul attains the state of a bhrṅgi;
then, having effected the piercing of the six cakras, it becomes a consumer of that essence.
O Maheśānī, having placed that pollen upon the pedestal of the yantra,
one should write the mantras there and perform their recitation.
By means of that, the row of bees proceeds through the union with the syllables of the mantra-cakra.
How many and what indeed are the mantra-syllables and the cakra-syllables? (6.85)
Having contemplated this, one should count until the state of fullness of the parts is reached;
then [one becomes] a living insect, then a bee, and then likewise all that is moving and unmoving.
Therefore, that which is called the *bhṛṅgāvalī* is difficult even for yogins to attain;
yet for those endowed with the sequential initiation (*kramadīkṣā*), the state of being a *bhṛṅgin* becomes easily accessible through the gradual process.
By that, one becomes the form of the mantra; therefore, wisdom (medhā) is proclaimed as the sovereign (samrāj).
Śakti herself and those two [mantra and wisdom] are Śakti through the application of her own sequence.

O Pārvatī, having understood the wheels (cakras) in this manner—whether as Śaiva-Śākta or Śākta-Śaiva through the application of those two sequences—according to the path described, [one attains success]. (6.89)
Having pierced through the wheels, that which has their very nature as its own nature—neither the state of a worm nor the state of a bee—is the deity by its very own nature. (6.90)
Through the manifestation of the deity's form, one becomes that very form in an instant;
first, however, having fashioned a doll, one should install the vital breath (*jīva*) therein. (6.91)
Having understood this condition, O Goddess, one should then exert self-restraint toward Śivā;
for in the Kali age, which is filled with sin, there is neither meditative absorption (samādhi) nor the state of yoga.
O Goddess, if there were yoga alone, there would be no fruit therein;
for that reason, O Goddess, one should practice the yoga of mantra.

From that time forward, he too should explain his own ritual sequence (*svakrama*), and he [the disciple] should perform it without interruption; in the event of his [the teacher's] passing away, he should follow the succession of that lineage.
Endowed with the consecration, one should recite the vidyā a thousand times for sixteen days, or even for nine nights, O beloved.
One should certainly accomplish [the rites] for five nights or three nights according to the rules;
first, one must certainly accomplish those beginning with Cakṣuṣmatī and ending with Medhā.
All mantras arising from the divisions of the six traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya) and others should be employed,
as well as the mantras of the eighteen traditions (aṣṭādaśāmnāya), according to the sequence beginning with 'ka' and 'ha'.
O Dear One, the mantras designated as the Six Darśanas, which arise from the various divisions of the Ten Vidyās—all of these are to be seen here, and some of them are to be heard. (6.98)
O Goddess of the gods, certain [mantras] are to be recited; here, the yoga of initiation is the cause.
Indeed, a man who has thus attained this yoga becomes one whose form is Śiva.
O Maheśvarī, [the goddesses] are Cakṣuṣmatī, Vāṅmatī, and Sparśanityā;
likewise Varṇadīkṣā, Kriyādīkṣā, and Kalāvatī.
O Śivā, there is also that which consists of the five seats (*pañcāyatanika*) and likewise that which consists of piercing (*vedhamayī*).
O Goddess, piercing is of five kinds, as has already been explained previously. (6.101)
O Maheśānī, there is the Pūrṇadīkṣā, which consists of the Ūrdhvāmnāya;
likewise, O Deveśī, there is the Nirvāṇadīkṣā, born from the division of Śāmbhava.
Indeed, by the application of the sequence of the Vedas, arrows, and Paśupati,
there are Medhā and Sāmrājyamedhā, who possess the form of divine sovereignty.
This Keralan [system] has been thus briefly elucidated;
however, that which begins with Cakṣuṣmatī and ends with Ūrdhvā is proclaimed in Kashmir. (6.104)

The Gaudī initiation is proclaimed to begin with Cakṣuṣmatī and end with Pūrṇā; the sixty principles (tattvas) and the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) are likewise proclaimed in their proper sequence.
It is joined with the vessels of Mahākāla, Kalā, Randhra, Bāṇa, Tattva, and so forth,
as well as the ten-fold and five-fold limbs previously described by me.
O Goddess of the Gods, all this has been proclaimed in the third section; through the rite for wisdom, there shall be the accomplishment of all one's desires. (6.107)
Alternatively, one should place ninety-six jars there;
having invoked the Śaktis into them and worshipped them, one should perform the consecration.
Having made the birth-day [of the disciple] exclusively fruitful, one should perform the consecration with the Nāthas,
the Tattvas, the Nityās, and the Kālī-nityānta-vidyā.
Meditating upon the all-pervading consonant and vowel at the base, the heart, the head, fire, the sun, and the moon, one should recite the mantra at the three junctions of the day.

And one should perform the placement (nyāsa) in the locus of the Mātṛkās for the sake of attaining that body, during the adverse transits of the planets, at the birth asterism, or during an eclipse of both [the sun and the moon]. (6.111)
When one has fallen into distress or when enemies cause affliction, one should perform an ablution;
by that, faults never touch him, nor can they do so by force.
Minor and cruel rites, as well as magical spells (*kṛtyā*) devised by enemies—[these are neutralized].
(p. 79) The Illustrious Goddess said:
"O Supreme Lord, how may there be power for this consecration (*seka*)? (6.113)
"Tell me that power by which the afflictions are destroyed without remainder.
Śrī Śiva said:
"By means of contact with water in the form of the moon, the sun, and fire... (6.114)
All defects without exception perish; therefore, there is nothing equal to the consecration (sekasama).
The nature of water is proclaimed to consist of the moon, the sun, and fire. (6.115)

Therefore, for the sake of pacifying the affliction of all suffering without exception, there should be an ablution with devotion during the seven hymns, at auspicious times, and on other meritorious occasions. (6.116)
One should perform worship accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) directly before the Guru;
or, upon the occurrences of the aforementioned arisings, one should worship with golden flowers.
Having been consecrated according to the prescribed rite, one should bestow a sacrificial fee upon the preceptor;
likewise, one should do so for the preceptor who has attained knowledge in his presence, as well as for his younger brother.
One should satisfy the teacher’s teacher and his teacher as well, along with those who have received the knowledge from them,
by means of worship consisting of prostrations, offerings, hymns of praise, service, and so forth,
before one's own eyes; otherwise, one's power will pass away to them.
Combined with abundant sandalwood, Kashmiri saffron, jewels, and musk.
O Śivā, one should draw the two feet of the Guru everywhere with colored powders;
O Maheśānī, one should perform the ritual consecration every year.

O Great Goddess, one who is endowed with the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka) should, having approached a Guru, always study the eightfold [tradition] beginning with the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya) for the sake of that initiation.
Thus, O Maheśvarī, the initiation of *medhā* has been briefly described.
O Great Goddess, listen now as it is told according to the sequence beginning with the letter *ka*. (6.123)
O Maheśvarī, O Goddess, [the power] is all-pervasive in form, consisting of both energy (śakti) and knowledge (jñāna).
O Goddess, that which is higher than the highest is considered by you, O Goddess, to be twofold.
O Maheśānī, *kā* is the beginning of the Kālī-mata and *hā* is its end; *ka* and *hā* together constitute the Tāriṇī-mata.
*Ka* is the beginning of the system known as Śrī Tripurā, and *ha* is its end. || 6.125 ||
Whoever recites the mantra there, Kālī grants him boons;
O Maheśvarī, the various dialects of the Śabaras are used for the mantra alone.
For the authority regarding the granting of boons belongs to Kālikā;
the detailed account of this, however, is found in the *Kādihādivinirṇaya*.
O Goddess, that was previously proclaimed by me in detail;
in both cases, there may occasionally be a difference in the arrangement of the *medhā* (mnemonic verses) during the recitation (*pārāyaṇa*).
O Goddess, first is the touchstone (sparśamaṇi), and likewise the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), O Beloved;
then Siddhakālī, the Queen of Great Vidyās, and the Kāmakalā.
Haṃsakālī and Guhyakālī, through the sequence of the five Vedas and the five flavors (rasa), O Supreme Goddess, are proclaimed as Śāmbhava; by this sequence, they are celebrated as Medhā.
O Goddess, through both methods, the sovereign Medhā is proclaimed;
it is known as the Pārāyaṇa of the channels (nāḍī) and likewise the Pārāyaṇa of the mantra.
O Goddess, the Cakrapārāyaṇa, as well as the Pūrṇordhvāmnāya,
the Caraṇa, the Turyacaraṇa, and likewise the Ṣaṭśāmbhava, O Śivā.
O Supreme Goddess, Medhā and Sāmrājyamedhā follow in sequence in the *jātaka* concerning the birth year, country, and so forth, which arises from the science of those questions. (6.133)
The eternal time and the wheel of time are equal in both;
that which is declared as the Śiva of those two is said to be the manifest Supreme Śiva. (6.134)
O Śivā, [the lineages] known as Śivadevī, Vaṭeśa, and likewise Ānandabhairava, as well as Kerala, Kāśmīra, and Gauḍacaitanyaga; (6.135).
Each of these four lineages has been described;
the Guru should, in due order, bestow the yogapaṭṭa known as the Ājñā.
The Avadhūta is all-pervading; this is indeed the conclusion previously stated.
There are five divisions within the Kāpālika, and there are two divisions within the Caṇḍa.
O Goddess, three are proclaimed in the Svāyambhuva, and eight in the Kaula;
five in the Vīra, O Maheśānī, and ten in the Vaiṣṇava, O Pārvatī. (6.138)

O Maheśānī, there are eight [sects] among the Gāṇapas; among the Jains, there would be two hundred; O Maheśānī, among the followers of Sūrya there are five, and among the Buddhists there are merely one hundred. (6.139)
O Maheśvarī, ten [traditions] are proclaimed in the Pāśupata, and thirty in the Muṇḍī;
and in Kerala, O Pārvatī, there are likewise divisions according to Kāśmīra and Gauḍa.
In Kerala, it is said to be Bhāvanā; in Kashmir, Anukalpana;
and in Gauḍa, Pratyakṣadāna—thus the triad of wheels is described.
O Goddess Śivā, in the Vaṭavāsinī doctrine, there are three Keralas:
Guptakerala, Ugrakerala, and likewise Śuddhakerala.
O Goddess, that meditation on the substance (taddravyabhāvanā) is proclaimed at the very end;
for this Keralam is threefold according to the Vaṭavāsin doctrine, O Śivā.
O Maheśānī, these divisions are revealed in the Tārāsūkta;
O Maheśānī, this [mantra] is proclaimed to have five [forms] by means of divine herbs.
Having propitiated Kalahaṭṭa and likewise Puṣpacakrī and Jīvacakrī,
O Maheśānī, hear now of another tradition.

The state of being preceded by the ten incarnations belongs to Caitanya; immediately after that is the state of being preceded by the word "Brahmā" and so forth, up to the fifty ending with Īśvara. (6.146)
O Maheśvarī, there are fifty [mantras] beginning with Īśvara and ending with Caitanya;
likewise, there are fifty beginning with Keśava and those beginning with Gaṇapa. (6.147)

O Maheśānī, [the mantra] beginning with Tripura; O Parameśvarī, [the mantra] beginning with Kāma; or, O Maheśānī, [the mantra] beginning with Rati—these are especially [prescribed] for Chinnā. (6.148)
O Goddess, it may be headed by the Ḍākinīs and so forth, or likewise headed by Bhairava;
it may be headed by Nṛsiṃha, or it may be Consciousness (Caitanya), or perhaps the lineage of the regions.
Kalahaṭṭa, Ātatāyin, Gomukhī, Vallabha, Vijñānin, Vāmavijñānin, and likewise Siddhadīkṣita. || 6-150 ||
The King of Knowledge, the Sovereign, the Master, the Universal Emperor, and the Mandala itself—these have reached the pinnacle of their lands through the application of great siddhis. (6.151)
Because he serves the purpose of the Kula scriptures for those who are devoid of the traditional lineage (sampradāya),
he is proclaimed as the one called Bhairava, who is said to be despised by all.
Just as one who is outside the Veda has been described, so too has this [region] been proclaimed.
Those who have gone beyond this country—listen indeed to others, O Pārvatī! (6.153)
Tārāvatī, Bhogavatī, and likewise Vimalāvatī;
Prajñāvatī, Madhumatī, and likewise she who is considered Prajñāvatī.
The goddess Udbhaṭāmbāvatī, these [others] born from the divisions of the Arhatas, and those known as Anugraha-caitanya and likewise Nigraha-abhidha. (6.155)
And [the forms] known as Nigraha and Anugraha, Rājacaitanya, Kalā-caitanya by name, and likewise Śrīcaitanya, O Śivā. (6.156)
O Goddess, divine consciousness (divyacaitanya) is likewise denoted by the term *prajñāna*;
it is called *śāmbhava-caitanya* as well as *vijñāna*. (6.157)
Furthermore, there is that which is called the consciousness of others, and indeed the consciousness of the Self;
likewise, there is the consciousness known as Vairāja, and similarly the consciousness of Śrī Caitanya. (6.158)
And [the one] named Prajñā-caitanya, as well as the one called Prāsāda; the Caitanya named Nirvāṇa, and Medhā-caitanya indeed. || 6-159 ||
Then there is Śāmbhavacaitanya, as well as Śrīcaitanya,
the one named Vidyācaitanya, and Siddhacaitanya himself.
These, established on the Kāśmīra path, are Tripurā according to the divisions beginning with *ka* and *ā*;
likewise, O Śivā, there are Raṅgavāra, Devavāra, and Māyādeva. (6.161)
Kālākhya, Kāñcīśa, and another, Brahmavāra; Rājavāra, Siddhavāra, and another, Viśvarūpa.
The one named Unmattabhairava possesses the power of speech and is endowed with the perfection of poetry;
the one named Bhūtabhairava is the manifestation of form and the embodiment of the sphoṭa. (6.163)
The one named Virāṭ-Bhairava is intent on the movement and speech of the forms;
the one named Svarāṭ-Bhairava is within the sphere of the perfection of speech and desires.
The one named Samrāṭ-Bhairava is endowed with the perfection of assuming all forms;
the one known as Śrīmad-Baṭuka bestows curses and favors in the Kali age.
In Ānandabhairava, there is the state of being all forms everywhere;
likewise, O Śivā, Asitāṅga, Vākpara, and Añjanayuk exist.
The accomplishment known as the conceptualization of the differentiation of form, as well as concealment, entry into another's body, and the Khecarī [mudrā], are found in Caṇḍabhairava. (6.167)
Otherwise, the creation of illusions such as sorcery and the great Indra-trick occurs within the Kāpālabhairava tradition known as Krodha.
O Pārvatī, listen now to these divisions within the Vīracakra in Kerala, which bestow the terrifying names such as "Drying up of Rivers and Oceans" (nadīsamudraśoṣa). (6.169)
Divyabodha, Ānandanātha, and Kalānātha are denotators of the end;
Nandanātha alone is the denotator of the name alone. (6.170)
O Goddess Śivā, within that one [syllable], a triad is joined in sequence:
namely, the one called *mānava* (the letter *ma*), ending with the third [letter *na*], conjoined with the fire of perfected consciousness (*siddhacaitanya*). (6.171)
Endowed with the quality of divine consciousness and possessing divine wisdom itself—O Supreme Goddess, endowed with these qualities through the lineage of Nāthānanda. (6.172)
O Maheśānī, Nandanātha, having joined with Bāṇasaṃkhyaka, [becomes] Vilāsākhya, ending in Caitanya, which expresses the number five (bāṇa). || 6-173 ||
And the one named Siddhacaitanya, O Dear One, is fivefold as before;
beginning with Siddha and ending with Vilāsa, it denotes the number five.
O Maheśānī, the one beginning with *satya* and ending with *vilāsa* denotes the number of arrows (five); likewise, *siddhaprajña* denotes the number of arrows (five). (6.175)
O Maheśvarī, that which is named Ṛddhicaitanya is the proclaimer of the number five; this concludes the group of eight beginning with Aṇimā. (6.176)
There are forty divisions according to the sequence of the Mātṛkā, and there are forty divisions in due order, O Supreme Goddess. (6.177)
The three currents are in the middle of duality; at their end is Sarasvatī.
O Śivā, that which begins with Śambhava, preceded by the middle, and ending with Sarasvatī—[is the sequence].
Bāṇamedhā is at the beginning of the middle [section], and Sarasvatī is at its end;
thus, O Goddess of the Gods, the ten divisions have been proclaimed in this sequence.
Cinmedhā, Citprajñā, and Śrīnātha— within that interval,
O Goddess, are the three lineages (sampradāya) which express the number five.
First the word *sārasvata*, then *sundarī*, O Śivā;
first the word called *nigraha*, then *sarasvatī*. (6.181)
Ending with Sundarī and beginning with Siddha, it bestows both curses and favors;
O Great Goddess, ending with Sundarī and beginning with Kāla, it is Sarasvatī.
O Great Goddess, at the beginning of Sāmrājya is Sarasvatī;
O Great Goddess, at the end of that is Saubhāgya, and at its end is Sarasvatī.
In the lineage of the Goddesses, however, it has been briefly revealed:
beginning with the Divine (divya) and ending with the Glory of Śrī (śrīvilāsa), it is expressed by the number of Bāṇas (nine).
And Mahāprajñā is Divyādya, which expresses the number of arrows;
[the others are] Samrāṭ, Vairāṭ, Svārājya, Adhirājya, and Rājyaka. (6.185)
