Great sovereignty, the supreme state, and likewise lordship;
being an emperor of the whole earth, a universal monarch, and likewise the joy of Śakra.
The bliss of Brahman, the bliss of consciousness, and likewise the full bliss;
the bliss of the great equilibrium of flavors, and likewise the great bliss. (6.187)
O Goddess of the gods, by means of the sequence of arrows, there are ninety divisions;
thus the doctrine of Baṭuka has been declared, and the names have been indicated. (6.188)
And its etymological explanation, O Maheśānī, O Śivā, is told after the various types of initiation, O Parameśānī; what else do you wish to hear? (6.189)

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Explanation of Names," in the first section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 6 ||
The Seventh Chapter.
The Holy Goddess said:
O Śiva, [explain] the three traditions according to the sequence beginning with 'Ha' and beginning with 'Ā'.
Speak, O Mahādeva, if I am dear to you.
Śrī Śiva said: The technical definition has been indicated; now listen as the detailed explanation is told.
O Goddess, one who is endowed with the initiation of *medhā* is proclaimed as a *Kerala*.
O Maheśānī, there is the Ṣaṭśāmbhava with its questions, as well as that which is endowed with the eight groups of eight; likewise, there is the Ṛkkerala and the Śrīyajuḥkerala.
The goddess Śrīsāmakeralī as well as Atharvakeralī;
in the Atharvaveda there are many divisions [known] by the divine Siddhas and others through their various honors.
Ānandabhairava and Śivā, Dakṣiṇāmūrti as well, the Goddess, and the Nine Lords (Navanātha), according to the sequence of the divisions of the Siddhas.
O Maheśānī, by means of the sequence of Śiva and Śakti within the three floods (oghatriya),
and by means of the sequence of the Supreme Sixfold Path (parāṣoḍhā), there is the "Lopa" [destruction] through the dissolution of this.
The Goddess [is attained] through the performance of those [practices], according to the sequence of the eighteen [deities] of Śambhu,
by means of the yoga of that current-sequence, and by the direct (anuloma) order.
And [it is established] through the sequence of Agasti, Durgā, Caṇḍīśa, and Svapnāvatī;
through the sequence beginning with Mahāvidyā; and according to the various divisions of their respective lineages (ogha).
The Atharva and Kerala are the divisions proclaimed as belonging to the Śākta;
however, those of the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and Saura traditions, as well as the Gāṇapatya and Bauddha, are distinct.

(87) Worship should be performed with the right hand, while libation (tarpaṇa) should be done with the left. Furthermore, both libation and drinking are proclaimed to be performed with the right hand. (7–10)
O Goddess, worship with the left hand is proclaimed in due order:
water, milk, "lost milk" (naṣṭadugdha), and likewise the pill of the essence of consciousness (saṃvidrasavaṭī).
O Goddess, eggplant, surana, and likewise the essence of milk;
O Goddess, the worship of Kumārī and the terminology used in Kerala.
Through the worship of the Supreme Lord and other such practices, one shall always become identical with His very form;
O Goddess of gods, he shall never again be inclined toward any other activity.
The water issuing from his hand becomes like pearls in an instant;
he enters the bodies of others and travels to the cities of both moving and stationary beings.

The stabilization of youth, the extraction [of power] from all things mobile and immobile, and whatever else exists within the cosmic egg or upon the surface of the earth—[all this is attained]. (7.15)
O Goddess, for the practitioner this will certainly become as clear as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand; O Goddess, this is the fruit taught in the Kādi-Hādimata system.
I shall fully explain Kāśmīra; listen with respect, O Pārvatī.
It is endowed with the Ūrdhvāmnāya and other [traditions], and it possesses the descent of power (śaktipāta) characteristic of the Kāśmīrīs.
Endowed with the eight groups of eight, the Kashmiri is possessed of the attainment of reality (tattvasiddhi);
he is the Kashmiri of the Ṛgveda, the Kashmiri of the Yajurveda, and indeed the Kashmiri of the Sāmaveda.
Then, by the Atharvaṇas, the Kashmiris, and the divine Siddhas and other humans,
[it was established] through the various forms of Dakṣiṇāmūrti as well as through the various forms of Bhairava.
The Lord Sadāśiva himself, according to the sequence of the nine masters (navanātha),
and the eighty-four Siddhas, beginning with the divine stream (divyaugha) and the stream of Śiva (oghaśiva).
Due to the omission of that [element] in the Śaiva and Śākta [traditions], the Ṣoḍaśī [Kalā] is supreme in sequence;
this occurs through the conjunction of the three divisions (caraṇas) and by means of the order of the Maṅgala-mantra.
Lopā, Durgā, Caṇḍeśī, and likewise Svapnāvatī, in due order;
through the union with the tenfold stream of the Vidyās, [these] are the vessels of division in Kāśmīra. (7.22)
There is indeed a distinction between the Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Gāṇapas, Bauddhas, and Sauras;
for them, worship with the left hand and libation with the right hand is prescribed.
O Goddess of the gods, the secondary rites (anukalpas) have been proclaimed by Dakṣa regarding the drinking [of wine];
now I shall explain the rite involving molasses (gauḍa), so listen attentively as it truly is.
Endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) and accompanied by the eight groups of eight,
there are the Gauḍa of the Ṛgveda, the Gauḍa of the Yajurveda, and the Gauḍa of the Sāmaveda as the third.
Now, O Goddess, O Pārvatī, hear from me the divisions of the Atharva-Gauḍa,
categorized according to the lineages of the Divine (divya), the Siddhas (siddha), the Human (mānava), the Current (ogha), and the Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Ānandabhairava, the lineage of Sadāśiva, the Goddess, the nine Nāthas, and the Siddhas as well, O Maheśvarī. (7.27)
In the triad [of letters], through the conjunction of Śiva and Śakti and by means of the process of their elision,
one should likewise perform the elision of the sixteenth vowel according to the sequence of Agasti.

Durgā, Caṇḍeśvarī Devī, and likewise Svapnāvatī, in sequence, according to the divisions of the tenfold stream of knowledge (daśavidyāugha) and the distinctions of their respective enclosures (āvaraṇa). || 7-29 ||

Furthermore, the distinction between the Atharva and the Gauḍa is proclaimed within the Śākta path; likewise, there are distinctions among the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and Saura traditions, as well as within the Buddhist and Gāṇapatya traditions, O Śivā.
O Maheśānī, the sequence is reversed: worship is performed with the left hand, while the libation and the offering of the drink are done directly with the right hand.
O Pārvatī, there is the Great Vidyā, the Accomplished Vidyā, and the various divisions of Vidyā;
[these arise] from the nature of the Vidyās, their respective conducts, and through the application of the sequence of those Vidyās. (7.32)

Due to the division of the *cakras*, the division of the traditions (*āmnāya*), and the difference in their practice, this sequence applies to both [traditions] in the Gauḍa path; thus, the Vidyā is to be worshipped. (7.33)
O Maheśānī, O beloved, within the body of Śakti—the lake of the universe—there is equality even in the triad, as well as in the recitation of the names. (7.34)
O Goddess, the recitation of mantras (maṃtrapārāyaṇa), O Śivā, the recitation of the channels (nāḍīpārāyaṇa),
and the recitation of the wheels (cakrapārāyaṇa), O Goddess, are declared in the Hādimata, O Śivā.
Now, O Maheśānī, listen to the sequence of the oral tradition (sampradāya) beginning with the letter *ka*;
one who is endowed with the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of *medha* and so forth shall become a venerable Keralī of the *kādi* [tradition]. (7.36)
The Ṛk-Keralī, the Yajus-Keralī, and likewise the Sāma-Keralī, joined with five groups of five and endowed with the descent of power (śaktipāta). || 7-37 ||
The scope of the knowledge of the three times is joined with the six questions concerning Śambhu;
O Goddess, now listen with diligence to the Atharva-Kerala. 7-38.
And by means of the sequence of the divine, the perfected, and the human [lineages] of Mahākāla;
and then by means of the sequence of Ānandabhairava and Sadāśiva.
O Goddess of the gods, by means of the sequence of the Goddess (devīkrama), through the divisions of the nine lords (navanātha),
and by the eighty-four Siddhas within the triad [of the three lineages] arising from Śiva and Śakti.
Because of the elision of that, because of being intent upon that, and also because of the sequence of its feet,
as well as through the union of the four quarters and the sequence of the eighteen [Tantras] of Śambhu.
By means of the sequential progression of that current and through the lineage of Śambhu’s feet,
one attains the status of a Guru of the ten Vidyās through the application of their respective coverings.
And [it is established] through the five divisions beginning with Śaiva, according to the sequence of synonyms;
likewise by means of the scripture, time, place, and the lineage tradition.
The multiplicity of divisions has been declared by means of the sense-bases of vision;
worship is proclaimed to be performed with the right hand, and libation with the left. (7.44)
(90) O Goddess, Pārvatī, the libation is performed with the right hand, and the drinking is done with that same [hand].
The deity is to be gratified with the left hand, while the libation to the Guru is performed with the right. (7.45)
One should perform the libation with the left hand alone;
the Keralas perform the libation with the right hand alone. (7.46)
O Goddess, according to the Brahmakaula doctrine, one should satisfy the Guru with the right hand and the deity with the left; this is proclaimed as the ritual libation (tarpaṇa).
Water, milk, milk that has turned sour, as well as consciousness-mixed [preparations], the pill of the essence of consciousness, and likewise eggplant and suraṇa root. (7.48)
The essence of milk, the liquor of the consciousness of milk, and the maiden—
O Supreme Goddess, this is the worship within the scope of the Kādikerala [script].
The Kāśmīra [tradition] is conjoined with the Urdhvāmnāya and others, and is endowed with the descent of power (śaktipāta);
it consists of the Ṛg-Kāśmīra, the Yajus-Kāśmīra, and the Sāma-Kāśmīra.
Now, O Pārvatī, hear from me the divisions of the Atharvaṇa and Kāśmīra [traditions], according to the sequence of the Divine, Siddha, and Human lineages, and the Mahākāla-krama.
And by means of the sequence of Kālavīra known as Atikālakarāla,
there are Kālī, the nine lords (Navanātha), and the eighty-four siddhis.
In the third [stage], due to the sequence of Kālikā, there is the elision of those two by means of Śiva and Śakti;
then, in due order, there is Kāmakalā-Kālī and Haṃsa-Kālī.

Through the fivefold division beginning with Śaiva and by way of the seven successive stages, there is merely a multiplicity of divisions; however, according to the Vāma tradition, this is known as *tarpaṇa* (satiating).
Worship has been fully described by Dakṣa, and the secondary rites (anukalpas) have likewise been proclaimed.
Now, I shall explain the Gauḍa [tradition] according to the sequence of its application.
Endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), Gauḍa is joined with five times five [categories]:
namely, Ṛggauḍa, Yajurgauḍa, and likewise Sāmagauḍa. (7.56) p. 91)
Now, O Goddess, listen as the Atharvagauda is described exactly as it is:
the Divine, the Siddha, and the Human lineages, along with Mahakala and Karalaka. (7.57)
Likewise, O Goddess, Vīranātha [arises] through the sequence of the nine lords (navanātha),
along with the eighty-four Siddhas and others, in the triad [of centers] from Śiva and Śakti.
From the elision of that [kalā], there arises the elision of the supreme *kāmakalā*.
O Supreme Goddess, in the same manner, the divisions within the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) have been proclaimed.
O Goddess, the equality [of these] in terms of the fivefold group beginning with Śaiva is proclaimed in the seven synonyms; their abundance has already been explained previously. (7.60)
O Goddess, it is taught that satisfaction is performed with the left hand and worship with the right;
likewise, the giving and drinking are done visibly according to the sequence of the Mahāvidyās.
O Goddess, [it is taught] according to the sequence of the Siddhas and the sequence of the Vidyās,
in accordance with the respective Yugas, through the distinctions of the Siddhas, the Vidyās, and so forth.

Through the sequence of the power of that form, through the sequence of its practice, through the various traditions of the contemplation of the wheel, and through the various divisions of conduct; || 7.63 ||
O Goddess, within the cosmic egg born of the union of Śakti, all essences are clearly manifest;
likewise, there is the recitation of names (nāmapārāyaṇa) and the recitation of mantras (mantrapārāyaṇa).
O Goddess, the *nāḍīpārāyaṇa* consists of the series beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*, as well as that beginning with *ka* and ending with *ha*.
When this [series] begins with *ka* and ends with *śambhu*, it is known as the sovereign called *Medhā*. (7.65)
And the divine imperial sacrifice (divyasāmrājyamedha) is proclaimed to end after a day, a weekday, a fortnight, a month, or thirty-six days.
Having performed the expiation according to the sequence of the five daily rites and the sequence of the periodic obligatory rites, either one's own guru or oneself [should perform it]. (7.67)

Having attained the previously mentioned sequence and by means of the progression through the apertures of the *kalās*, one should enter the initiation pavilion as the string for the arrows of desire. (7.68)
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) as before, O Maheśvarī, all the rites should be completed;
one should indeed bestow the name of the Command and practice the yoga-band (yogapaṭṭa).
O Supreme Goddess, the mantras of the limb-protections and the fifty lotus-mantras must indeed be heard, reflected upon, and beheld.
Everything else shall be as before; this has been stated in brief.
Thus it has been explained concisely; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of Initiation Beginning with 'Ka'," in the first section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 7 ||
The Eighth Chapter. The Goddess said: O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear that which is the most secret of secrets.
Śrī Śiva said:
The etymological derivation and the classification of substances are now being told; listen. 8.1.
The divisions of Vīra, Ādi, and Kaula have already been revealed;
O Supreme Goddess, those of Viṣṇu, Pāśupata, and others are now being described. (8.2)
Those who have undertaken the five-night vow are proclaimed as Pāñcarātras;
for up to five days, they must not even look upon Śaivas. (8-3)
Those who, having made a widow wear a sacred thread (*mudrā*), worship her, are asked, "Whose grace is this? and he who should reply, "It is Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s," [is a fool]. (8.4)
Those who consume the food offering intended for the deity as if it were their own, and those Vaiṣṇavas who are devoted to censuring Śiva, [fall into hell]. (8.5)
They even revile the Vaiṣṇavas; they are considered Pāñcarātras.
Having adopted the vow known as that of the heretics (pāṣaṇḍa), they are proclaimed to be heretics (pāṣaṇḍas). || 8.6 ||
One who wears the ashes of the cremation ground and accumulates the application of ashes,
O Goddess, may perform ritual bathing, the twilight prayers, and so forth, merely for worldly purposes.
A man who, being intent on hatred toward Viṣṇu, performs all [such acts], is called a heretic (pāṣaṇḍa); listen now, O Śivā, concerning the Kāpālika.
Feeding from a skull-bowl as his vessel, devoted to liquor and meat, constantly pointing out women, and always wearing a garland of severed heads. (8–9)
He who subsists on the fire of the cremation ground is known as a Kāpālika;
he is said to be of twelve kinds, with the Mahākāpālika being the highest. (8–10)
Devoid of bathing, giving, and other such rites, and free from both purity and impurity,
for him there is no recitation of mantras, no austerity, and no observance whatsoever.
Such would be the Cīna, both with parts and without parts, in two ways.
Listen now to the Jaina, O Great Goddess; he always carries a water-pot. (8-12)
The living soul alone is the supreme enjoyer; it is indeed that which acts and withdraws.
O Goddess, whatever happiness there is, that happiness has the nature of one's own self.
O Goddess, he is called a Jaina; in this same way, the Buddhists and others are considered [to be included].
O Goddess, O Beloved, there are likewise those who pluck out their hair and those who wear white garments.
Likewise, O Goddess, there are those who wear red garments, as well as those who wear blue robes and so forth;
they are known as the Bṛhadgurus, and others too, O Supreme Goddess. (8.15)
The non-violent ones and other such divisions are considered to be, in brief, O Goddess; now listen as those entitled to the mudrās are described. (8.16)
A Brahmin should not act in such a manner, for his Brahminhood would perish;
by wearing a [non-Brahminical] seal, a Brahmin shall go to the Raurava hell. (8.17)
For he who is devoid of the Vedas may indeed be a bearer of the mudrās;
but how can he who is accompanied by mudrās alone be a Brāhmaṇa? (8.18)
O Goddess, there are four kinds of mudrās; listen to these fourfold divisions, O beloved.
A Brāhmaṇa should contemplate them within his own body for the awakening of the state of Viṣṇu. (8.19)
A Kṣatriya should draw lines on his body, while a Vaiśya should apply the mudrās;
for Śūdras and those of lower castes, the heated metal seal (taptamudrā) is prescribed.
Even one endowed with extreme devotion should contemplate [the deity] but must not draw [it];
a Brahmin may draw it somewhere, but he must never fashion a physical image.
"Having become a god, one should worship the God; one who is not a god should not worship the God.
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, the nature of Viṣṇu must be realized within oneself. (8.22)
Then one should perform the recitation (japa), and the accomplishment of that mantra will come to pass.
In this very same way, O Maheśānī, shall be the sequence for the Śaiva mantras and others.
Upon seeing [an image] marked with the conch and the discus, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on;
O Goddess, a Brāhmaṇa should always meditate upon the trident and the hand-drum.
The wearing of the Śiva-liṅga and the wearing of the Śiva-mudrās and so forth—O Goddess, a twice-born man should avoid these; this has been declared here in brief. (8.25)
He who is a worshiper of Śakti is proclaimed as a Śākta;
and he who is endowed with the initiations of the Vaikhānasa and other traditions is indeed a Vaiṣṇava.
One who is endowed with the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan), the Śāmbhava state, and so forth, is proclaimed as a Śaiva;
however, one who is possessed solely by Śiva while reviling other deities [is not]. (8.27)
Thus has Vīraśaiva been described; now hear of the Vaiṣṇava known as Vīra.
He is solely devoted to Viṣṇu and a reviler of all other gods.
O Maheśvarī, both those men who partake in sin are called Vīravaiṣṇavas; however, he who is devoted to the recitation of the Candra-mantra is known as a Cāndra.
He whose mind is attached to the Sun is proclaimed as a Saura;
he who is a worshiper of Brahmā is considered Svāyambhuva.
That which is joined with Durgā, Caṇḍī, and others is proclaimed as the Daurga [rite].
All rituals have the Vedas as their root; the supreme Smṛti has the Vedas as its root. (8.31)
A twice-born man should never perform that which is devoid of the Veda;
one who is constantly devoted to the path of the Veda certainly becomes a true Brāhmaṇa. (8.32)
O Maheśvarī, he who is devoid of the Veda is proclaimed to be a Cāṇḍāla; yet, having placed one's own specific duty (svadharma) foremost, every task should be performed.
One who is constantly devoted to his own duty certainly attains happiness;
a Brahmin devoid of his own duty, who seizes the wealth of his son, is the lowest of the twice-born. (8.34)
O Maheśānī, having seen him, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
in his absence, O Maheśānī, one should enter the water with one's clothes on.
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should always avoid hatred toward mudrās and the like;
however, I have taught the mudrā to you for the sake of favoring those of inferior status.
"Truth, truth, O Great Goddess! What else do you wish to hear? The Śrī Devī said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear about the divisions of Viṣṇu and of Śiva."
Śrī Śiva said:
O Maheśānī, first there shall be Vaikhānasa, and likewise Śrī Rādhāvallabha; then Gokuleśa, and then Vṛndāvanī shall appear. (8.38)
The Pāñcarātra is the fifth, and the Śrīvīravaiṣṇava is the sixth;
O Maheśvarī, [the others are] Rāmānandī, Harivyāsī, and Nimbārka. (8.39)
Then, O Goddess, the ten divisions of the Bhāgavatas are proclaimed:
the Śikhī, the Muṇḍī, the Jaṭī, and likewise those with two or three staffs (daṇḍins) in succession.
O Maheśānī, the Ekadaṇḍī and likewise the Vīraśaiva are mentioned;
there are seven Pāśupatas declared, and the Vaiṣṇavas are considered to be tenfold.
O Goddess, O Śāmbhavī, listen with care to their latent impressions (vāsanā):
he who remains pervading and encompassing all is indeed Vaiṣṇava. (8.42)
O Goddess Śāmbhavī, listen with care: the Smārta-Vaiṣṇava is adorned by the initiation (dīkṣā) of the Vaikhānasa and other traditions, and he worships the venerable Rādhāvallabha. (8.43)
Devoted to the conduct of a Vaiṣṇava, having reached the further shore of the single system of Viṣṇu, with a mind focused on no other, tranquil in soul, and dedicated to the emblems of Viṣṇu. (8.44)
O Goddess, O beloved, listen to [the description of] Gokuleśa, the Lord of Śrī Rādhāvallabha;
he is endowed with various ornaments and adorned with various fragrances. (8.45)
He who delights the herd of cows, assuming the form of Kṛṣṇa at the end of the Kali age,
and who offers his body, wealth, and vital breaths as an oblation to Him— (verse 8.46).
O Goddess, he who is devoted to the inner power externally assumes the form of a Vaiṣṇava;
he is intent on the conduct of a Gandharva and is absorbed in the practice of being entwined by creepers.
The tradition of Gokuleśa bestows all perfections upon the earth;
O Queen of the Gods, now listen with diligence to that which is called Vṛndāvana. (8.48)
Free from desire, serene in soul, and devoted solely to the worship of Viṣṇu,
he was no longer fickle with attachment to women, yet he took delight in sporting in the forest.
O Śivā, he whose body is adorned with fragrances, who is solely devoted to the meditation on women, and who knows the reality of attaining the same form as Viṣṇu, is called a Vṛndāvanī. (8.50)
O Maheśānī, the Pāñcarātra and likewise the Vīravaiṣṇava have already been described previously, O Parameśvarī.
The letter *rā* is renowned as Śakti, and the letter *ma* is proclaimed to be Śiva;
at that time, he is blissful, tranquil in mind, serene in soul, and possessed of discernment. (8.52)
O Maheśānī, listen duly to Harivyāsa, who is proclaimed to be equal in form everywhere and a source of bliss to Rāma. 8-53.
Capable of destroying evil, a devotee of Viṣṇu with conquered senses,
endowed with the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), and dedicated to the abandonment of worldly conduct.
O Maheśānī, Harivyāsī, who assumes the nature of Śiva and Śakti, is intent on the welfare of others and accepts only those fruits that are purposeful. (8.55)
Now listen with diligence to the tradition known as Nimbārka;
it is devoted to the sequence of daily worship and is solely dedicated to its own independent system. (8.56)

Devoted to external worship and other rites, possessing exclusive devotion, with a serene mind, endowed with the qualities of the noble ones, pure, and intent upon conduct according to his own will; || 8.57 ||
The Lord Hari Nimbārka is independent and a hater of the Smṛti;
now, O Goddess, the Bhāgavata is being described—listen to it now. (8.58)

Śrī Śiva said:
Now listen as I speak of that which is most secret among secrets.
O Pārvatī, Meru is said to be of three kinds in its general form.

the Meru-prastāra-vinyāsa and that known as Kailāsa.

Now listen attentively to the characteristics of the Vahni-meru [mandala];
O beloved, one should cause forty-eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be constructed.

Within a single year, O Goddess of gods, that family perishes;
just as one who stands outside the Vedas, O Goddess, so too is a man who stands outside the twice-born.

From that, the Āṇavī [initiation] is to be known; from that, the Ṣaḍdarśanī [initiation] occurs;

thus, joined with the culmination of wisdom, he is Śiva himself—of this there is no doubt.

Just as the meditation on the *kāmakalā* is the sowing of the seed, so too is the purification of the seat and other elements; likewise is the worship of the site (*vāstu*).

(113) The restraint of the senses arises from attending upon the fire.
O Goddess, by attending upon the fire, the burning away of poverty occurs. (9-97)
One shall attain dispassion, eloquence of speech, and long life;
whatever desire one may wish for, that one certainly attains. (9.98)
Causing various wonders and honored in all the worlds, that which is offered as an oblation into the fire and that which is given bestows its fruit immediately. (9.99)
The sacred fire must always be tended by those who have performed the preparatory rites (*puraścaryā*) ten thousand times;
for one devoid of *puraścaryā*, this means of accomplishment is not prescribed.
In the nyāsa, Meru is of the nature of sattva; in the yantra, it becomes rājasa;
but Mahāmeru, through the service of fire, becomes tāmasa.
O Pārvatī, through a sāttvika delay, the fruit comes to fruition;
but in the case of a rājasa [delay], O Māyā, the fruit arises after some time.
O Goddess, for one who is *tāmasa*, the fruit shall always be merely immediate;
likewise, O Śivā, [for such a one] there is no qualification (*adhikāra*) and so forth, nor initiation (*dīkṣā*), nor even a name (*saṃjñā*) and so forth.
The fruits and so forth have been thus declared; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Accomplishment of Meru" in the first section of the latter part of the *Śrī-Śaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā.
The Ninth Chapter. || 9 ||
The Tenth Chapter.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the secret matter previously mentioned."
Śrī Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the determination of the Meru-prastāra.
O Parameśānī, O Pārvatī, it is explained starting from the root; O Maheśvarī, beginning with Ekāgni and ending with Śrīmedhā.
O Goddess, the *prastāra* is now being described according to the lineage of oral tradition;
first is the practice of the Single Fire (*ekāgni-sādhana*), which is designated by the name "Sun" (*sūrya*).
Then, O Goddess, one who performs the five-fire rite (pañcāgni) should cause four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be made;
the fifth is known as the solar fire (sūrya). Now listen attentively to the fire of Nanda.
There are eight sacrificial pits in the eight directions, and the ninth is named Sūrya;
then, O Goddess, there are twelve fires, making eleven pits in sequence.
O Pārvatī, hear now that sequence of the twelve fires known as Sūrya:
there are four Vedic fire-pits (kuṇḍas) to the south, arranged in pairs facing west and east.
In the north, there is a single pit; likewise, in the east and west, they are reversed.
O Goddess of the Gods, the Meru-pits follow the sequence of the two divisions.
Forty-eight [squares] are said to be their arrangement;
having first made a hexagon, one should then proceed with an octagon. (10.8)
The ten-spoked and the twelve-spoked [wheels] according to the sequence of the worlds;
the two sets of eight spokes, the hexagon, the ten-spoked, and the two sets of eight.
(115) Vasumehru has been described; now hear, O Pārvatī, about the middle [mandala].
First is the *bindu*, O Maheśānī, and then two crossroads (catvara). (10.10)
O Goddess, one should cause four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be made on the third courtyard;
O Goddess, one should cause eight sacrificial pits to be made on the fourth courtyard.
O Goddess, one should cause the ritual pits (kuṇḍas) for the arts to be constructed in the courtyard named Bāṇa;
then, in the sixth courtyard, there should be twenty pits.
O Goddess, one should cause twenty-four [deities] to be made on the seventh courtyard;
O Goddess, one should cause twenty-eight [deities] to be made on the eighth courtyard. || 10-13 ||
O Goddess of the gods, there are seven sacrificial pits; the Sun is considered to be the eleventh.
O Goddess, listen now to the Mahākāla doctrine according to this sequence of increasing by one.
Having first placed a single dot (bindu), one should place two circles (kuṇḍa) in the second [space],
four in number in the third, and six in number in the fourth.
In the fifth [section] there are eight [lines], while in the sixth there are twelve;
one should draw the boundary lines (vedaka) from east to west on the right and left sides.
O Goddess, having established [the central point], one should cause eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be made on the right and left;
O Supreme Goddess, one should likewise cause them to be made facing east and west.
On the seventh quadrangle, one should prepare twenty sacrificial pits;
on the eighth quadrangle, O Goddess, one should prepare twenty-two sacrificial pits.

In the east there are as many [mountains] as the number of mountains [previously mentioned], and facing them there are indeed seven; in the south there are as many as the number of Vedas, and facing them there are likewise as many as the south.
O Goddess of gods, one should cause [the lines] numbering seven (the count of the mountains) to be drawn on the right and left;
then, one should cause those numbering four (the count of the Vedas) to be drawn in the east and west. || 10-20 ||
O Goddess of the gods, having thus combined them, there are twenty-eight *kuṇḍas* [deducting four from the directions];
O Goddess, one should arrange twenty-six [of these] in the ninth courtyard. (10.21)
In the east there are eight [pīṭhas], and in the west likewise eight;
in the south there are five, and in the north they should be like those of Dakṣa.
Or else, O Goddess, one should have eight [pots] prepared on the south-east, or eight on the right and eight on the left. (10.23)
In the east, however, there are as many [pools] as the number of arrows, facing that [direction] as before;
thus combined, O Pārvatī, know there to be one hundred kuṇḍas.
Indeed, this Sun known as Ekottara has been described by me according to the sequence called Kailāsa; what else do you wish to hear? 10.25.
In this [rite], one should fashion the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) according to the sequence known as the "Chain" (śṛṅkhalā):
the pure pit, the power-pit, and likewise the pit consisting of both Śiva and Śakti.
O Goddess, one should fashion the sacrificial pits according to the procedure for nine pits; for one initiated into Nirvāṇa, there should be one hundred and eight.
O Goddess, O beloved, one should cause the venerable bindu to fall in the first square;
O Goddess, in the second square, one should perform the three fire-pits (kuṇḍas).

O Goddess, one should cause eight sacrificial pits (vedakuṇḍas) to be made on the third courtyard; O Goddess, one should cause eight sacrificial pits (vasukuṇḍas) to be made on the fourth courtyard. || 10-29 ||
O Goddess, in the quadrangle called Bāṇa, one should cause twenty-one [kuṇḍas] to be made;
O Goddess, in the quadrangle called Ṛtu, one should perform twenty [kuṇḍas].
O Goddess, at the quadrangle called after the sages (Ṛṣi), one should cause [the sacrificial pits] to be made in a number equal to the principles (tattva);
O Goddess, at the quadrangle called after the Vasus, there is a collection of thirty-two pits.
There are one hundred and seven pits, and the eighth is said to be the Sun;
O Goddess, now listen with care to the opinion of Akṣobhya.
The location of the *bindu* should be at the beginning; one should proceed to the second square.
O Goddess, in the third square, one should have the four sacrificial pits (*vedakuṇḍa*) constructed. (10.33)
O Goddess, one should cause eight [pits] to be made in the fourth courtyard;
O Goddess, one should cause the kalā-pits to be made in the courtyard called Ratna.
Then, at the sixth courtyard, one should prepare twenty sacrificial pits;
at the seventh courtyard, O Goddess, one should cause the number of vital points (*marmans*) to be made.
Now, in the eighth courtyard, there is the collection of thirty-two sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Furthermore, O Goddess, according to the division of nine courtyards in the Nīlamata, [it is as follows]. (10.36)
There, O Goddess, in the first square, the place of the Bindu is proclaimed;
in the second square, O Goddess, one should fashion [the squares] numbering as the moon (sixteen).
O Goddess, on the third courtyard, one should cause [the squares] numbering nine to be made;
O Goddess, on the fourth courtyard, one should cause those numbering four to be made. || 10-38 ||

O Goddess, one should cause [the shrines] numbering eight to be made at the quadrangle called Bhūta; O Goddess, one should cause those numbering sixteen to be made at the quadrangle called Rasa. || 10-39 ||
O Goddess, at the quadrangle called Ṛṣya, there should be twenty sacrificial pits;
O Goddess, at the eighth quadrangle, one should cause as many to be made as the number of the principles (tattvas).
O Goddess, at the ninth courtyard there is the withdrawal of the thirty-two sacrificial pits.
O Śivā, I shall now describe the third Meru according to the sequence of the nine [courtyards].
O Goddess, in the first square, the location of the Bindu is proclaimed;
in the second square, O Goddess, it is the number of eyes (two), as before. (10.42)
O Goddess, on the third courtyard one should cause [the squares] numbering four (the Vedas) to be made;
O Goddess, on the fourth courtyard one should cause [the squares] numbering six (the Rasas) to be made. || 10.43 ||
O Goddess, one should cause eight [units] to be made at the fifth crossroads;
O Goddess, those called the digits (kalās) [should be made] at the sixth, and ten at the seventh.

In the eighth [chapter], the number of principles (tattvas) is given; the number of vital points (marmas), however, is nine, according to the sequence of the nine apertures. O Śivā, there are three Merus. (10.45)
In the Kali age, however, there is eligibility for all three [classes], provided they possess the requisite qualification;
this practice is not said to be for one who is devoid of such qualification.
Thus has the doctrine known as Karāla been briefly declared;
now hear, O Pārvatī, about the one called Meru, which consists of one hundred and eight [verses]. 10.47.
First, having fashioned the *bindu*, one should then construct three *kuṇḍas*;
O Goddess, on the third square, one should cause [the others] to be made in a number equal to the *kalās*.
O Goddess, at the fourth courtyard one should cause eight [chambers] to be made;
O Goddess, at the courtyard called Bāṇa, one should cause eight [chambers] to be made.
O Goddess, one should cause twenty-four squares to be made in the area known as Ṛtu;
however, in the area known as Giri, one should cause twenty squares to be made.
O Goddess, at the crossroads known as Randhra, one should arrange twenty-six [sites];
O Beloved, one should have twenty-four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) constructed as before.
O Śivā, one should fashion a pair of fire-pits (kuṇḍas) to the south and north; O Maheśvarī, the pair of fire-pits may also be made facing east and west.
The eighth is named Sūrya; thus there are one hundred and eight.
Now hear, O Maheśvarī, about Meru according to the Ratnagarbha sequence.
Having first placed the *bindu*, one should place a pair of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) in the second [section];
one may arrange the pair of pits behind, in front, or to the sides.
O Śivā, one should arrange three sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) like a womb in the third courtyard;
O Goddess, in the fourth courtyard, one should have [pits] made numbering the seasons (six).
O Goddess, one should cause the Vasu-pits to be made in the courtyard named Bāṇa; O Goddess, one should cause the Kalā-pits to be made in the courtyard named Rasa. || 10.56 ||
In a courtyard of eleven cubits, one should prepare twenty sacrificial pits;
in a courtyard of eight cubits, one should likewise have twenty pits constructed. (10.57)
O Goddess, at the crossroads called Raṃdhra, one should cause the vital points (marmas) to be established;
thus, O Supreme Goddess, seven hundred sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) were produced.
The eighth is called Sūrya; thus, there are one hundred and eight [names] for the crossroads, the banners, and likewise for the six Śāmbhavas.
Now listen as the characteristics of the archways (toraṇas) are described;
they are progressively higher according to the divisions of two-by-two steps. (10.60)
It should rise in increments of three, according to the divisions of a *vitasti*;
its height should be one cubit (*hasta*), for it is indeed threefold, O Dear One. (10.61)
O Supreme Goddess, the length is endowed with twenty-four spans;
O Great Goddess, the bamboo pole is thus described, along with the gradual expansion of the pavilion.
O Dear One, there should be sixty-four banners, equal in number to the principles (tattvas),
made of jackfruit, *aśvattha*, mango, *karavīra*, and *kaitaka* flowers.
One should construct archways (toraṇas) adorned with various wonderful and diverse ornaments, such as rose-apples, pomegranates, wood-apples, and the like, as well as citron fruits and cloths.
O Goddess of the gods, the decoration of the crossroads is performed with substances consisting of nine colors, following the sequence of the left-hand path and the sequence of the right-hand path.
Having joined it with the emission of the *bindu*, either through the process of emanation and reabsorption,
or by means of the sequence of the eight groups (*aṣṭavarga*) and the sequence of the one hundred and eight *kalās*.
There, O Goddess of Gods, one should perform worship accompanied by the recitation of auspicious benedictions (svastivācana),
as well as the Mahāvidyā-maṇḍala and the Viyā-maṇḍala.
Having worshipped the four gates in the sequence of the four continents and the sequence of the four Vedas, one should contemplate the outer enclosure wall.
(120) Having visualized the great cremation ground, one should contemplate the Goddess there.
O Goddess, he who acts in this manner treats the oblation materials as if they were the deity itself. (10-69)
O Pārvatī, whatever flowers, fruits, grains, or anything else that exists within the world is obtained through the divisions of the seasons and the divisions of time. (10.70)
O Goddess, one should perform the fire-oblation there; one shall become a lord of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
One should diligently please the *ācārya* and worship the Guru with effort. (10.71)
Thereafter, one should honor the Brahmins with gold, jewels, garments, and other gifts;
by performing eight sets of eight [offerings] there, one shall become a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
One should cause twelve kettledrums to be sounded at the gate and in the corner,
along with the sounds of various musical instruments, making twenty-four in total.
Or, having assumed the blue attire of a Gandharva, one becomes a lord of accomplishments;
by attaining the six pārāyaṇas, one becomes a lord of all accomplishments.
O Goddess, whatever siddhis exist whatsoever upon the surface of the earth within the sphere of the universe, they all shall come under the feet of that person. (10.75)
This is a secret, even a most profound secret, to be guarded like one's own private parts;
or else, by means of wearing it around the neck, it may be worn with a banner and the beating of drums. (10.76)
"He shall even become a creator of Śakra, a giver of wealth, and a servant in the household.
Thus has it been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (10.77)

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of Meru," in the first section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 10 ||
The Eleventh Chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear that which is the most secret of secrets."
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess, a secret is being told; listen and be attentive. (11.1)
O Dear One, one should have all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) made in the shape of a crescent moon;
or alternatively, O Pārvatī, they may be made like the Śrīcakra—listen now to that procedure.
Four squares should indeed be made; in the first, there is the union with a dot (bindu).
There, a triangle should be drawn, and immediately after that, an eight-spoked wheel.
Then, O Goddess of gods, one should draw a ten-spoked [wheel], and a second ten-spoked [wheel];
then the mantra-weapon should be made, and then the serpent-petal, O Śivā.
O Goddess, one should then draw the petal known as the sixteenfold, followed by three circles;
this is the Śrīcakra, which has the form of Meru and is enriched with four doors and secondary ornaments.
Having made it gradually higher step by step, the wise one should construct it;
then, O Maheśānī, he should fashion a pavilion (maṇḍapa) upon that.
O Śivā, nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) arise there in succession;
having ignited the fire therein while preceded by meditation upon Sundarī. || 11-7 ||
O Goddess, one should fashion this great Meru, rich with weapons and ornaments and facing all directions, in the form of a petal. (11.8)
O Supreme Goddess, it is proclaimed that [the seat] has seven petals and is shaped like a lotus;
O Goddess, he who performs this becomes a lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
One should indeed practice the thirty-seven squares sequentially;
by way of emanation and withdrawal, the Kālacakra becomes twofold. (11.10)
Through the path of emanation and withdrawal, by means of the primary Śāmbhava yoga, the fourfold [yoga] has been described; one should practice the Kālacakra.
Therein, O Maheśānī, is the supreme Śrīvidyācakra;
beyond that, O Goddess, is the Parācakra, and after that, the one named Ṣaṭśāmbhava.
Listen to that which is described as fourfold in the lineage of Saṃvarteśa:
O Śivā, it is a quadrangle in human form, with its arms measured by the digits (kalās).
Is there an increasing height for each subsequent one, or is it the gathering of the Puruṣas?
There would be fifty-six [units] at the beginning, according to the sequence of the nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
In the second [chapter], however, there are fifty-two; in the third, sixty-two;
and in the fourth, O Supreme Goddess, there are fifty-four.
In the fifth [cycle] there are seventy-two, and in the sixth sequence sixty-four; O Maheśānī, one should worship Saṃvarteśa with the head-bindu. 11–16.
Or else, O beloved Pārvatī, listen to another sequence in a different manner:
having carefully constructed squares numbering twelve (the sun), O Pārvatī. (11–17)
There, O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, one should construct the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in sequence:
first, O Maheśānī, is the Bindu-pit, and in the second is the Vahni-pit.
O Goddess, one should cause [the squares] to be made numbering six on the third square;
those numbering eight on the fourth; and those numbering sixteen on the fifth.
In the sixth [chapter], O Śivā, there are twenty-two; in the seventh, thirty fire-pits (kuṇḍas);
and in the one called the eighth, O Goddess of the Gods, there are thirty-four.
In the sequence of the directions, there are thirty-eight, equal in number to the apertures (randhra), and forty-two;
likewise, in that which is designated by the number of Rudras, there are forty-eight.
In the twelfth [chapter], listen to the fifty-five-fold enumeration of the *kāma*s;
one should perform them according to the appropriate application, numbering fifty-eight. (11-22)
The great Mount Meru, known as Śāmbhava, bestows the status of a universal emperor;
by the mere knowledge of it, one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds. (11.23)
Thus has been briefly declared this most secret of secrets;
it must be hidden, hidden, hidden, like one's own private parts.
He is a man of knowledge and a man of realized wisdom, knowing the secrets of all the gods; he knows the fourfold Ṣoḍhā of Tāriṇī and the fivefold Ṣoḍhikā of Kālī.
The fivefold and sixfold [mantras] of Sundarī should be carefully deposited;
there shall be one [method] in the deposition of Śakti, while there is diversity in the depositions of the Cakras.
O Maheśānī, in the Tantra known as Śaktisaṃkhya, everything is one;
O Śivā, [this extends] from the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka) up to divine sovereignty.
O Goddess, this yoga has been declared, which brings about the most profound of secrets;
oh, that man who knows the divine empire is the most blessed among the blessed! (11.28)
One who is endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) should not perform prostrations;
he should always be perfected in meditation and ever devoted to that [practice]. (11.29)
By becoming intent on the contemplation of reality, a person becomes like a god;
[these qualities are] faith, steadiness of mind, generosity, and compassion. (11.30)
One should be devoted to the guru, devoted to the deity, and supremely devoted to fellow devotees;
one should avoid censuring others, harboring malice toward them, and slandering others. (11.31)
One should entirely avoid censuring women and striking them;
one should altogether renounce the property of others, the wives of others, and the food of others. (11.32)
One should avoid the power of others and shun the hands of others;
one should always dwell in solitude, especially on a mountain. (11.33)
One should contemplate this entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, as having the form of a woman;
remaining ever devoted to bliss, one should be intent upon the bliss of the Goddess. (11.34)
Having a pure vermilion tilaka, acting according to his own will, and having conquered his senses,
he should avoid anger, greed, pride, hypocrisy, envy, and fickleness;
he should also avoid idle chatter and especially excessive talk.
O Goddess, [I have taught] the mastery of posture, as well as the mastery of sleep, O Śivā. (11.36)
O Goddess, the wise man should by all means effect the conquest of the senses;
O Goddess, he should conquer his diet and practice the Khecarī Mudrā.
One should dwell constantly wherever one may be; wherever one may remember Śivā, one should worship Her—whether in a terrible forest or within a circle of beautiful women, O Auspicious One.
Having entered the circle of courtesans, he should always meditate upon Śivā;
moderate in speech, moderate in food, and moderate in his portions, he is most excellent.
Having contemplated this entire world of moving and non-moving beings as being of the nature of light,
and having meditated upon it, one should constantly recite the mantra and diligently abandon illusion (māyā).
Who am I? To whom do I belong? What is my true nature? What is my form? How do I abide? Where was I born? How was I produced? Of what form am I? And what indeed is mine? (11.41)
Thinking, "What has been commanded?", one should abandon everything like a blade of grass:
"Today I become Tārā; I myself am she in the form of Tārā. (11.42)
Whatever has been done by him, caused to be done, indicated, or reminded;
whatever has been impelled, shown, given, or is being given—[all that belongs to him]. (11.43)
By her all that is performed; there is no other agent on the surface of the earth.
In whatever place he who is endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) shines forth, [in that place she acts]. (11.44)
That region attains auspiciousness for a hundred thousand leagues in every direction;
however, initiation is not fruit-bearing for those who are devoid of the full consecration.
Having made pleasure and pain equal, gain and loss, victory and defeat; having established equanimity toward cold and heat, one should always have the mind fixed upon that [the Self].
By effecting absorption into the deity, a person becomes one who possesses the form of a god;
for those devoid of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), initiation and worship are fruitless.
O Maheśānī, one who has received the full initiation (pūrṇadīkṣā) may accept blessings;
however, he must never accept prostration from such a person, but rather act to please him.
By the mere act of pleasing him, all the deities are satisfied;
indeed, the authority over all mantras is established in his hand.
For he alone is proclaimed to be the very nature of the Great Vidyā;
Nīlā shall dwell in his mouth, and Kālī shall be held in his hand.
Sundarī resides in his home, Kamalā is within the range of his vision, Bagalā is present during his anger, and Bālāmbā dwells in his heart.
In this way, O Pārvatī, all other great vidyās and perfected vidyās come into the hands of such a person, O Goddess; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (11.52)
O Śivā, one should not provoke the anger of one who is endowed with the full consecration;
for by his anger, O Mistress of the Gods, this entire world perishes. (11.53)
By the mere act of pleasing him, the three worlds shall be protected.
A boy five years of age, endowed with the complete initiation, [attains this]. (11.54)
O Maheśānī, the most senior is not one who is superior by age;
rather, even one born of the Caṇḍāla caste is senior if he is endowed with the complete initiation.
O Maheśvarī, even compared to a Brāhmaṇa, he is superior in the rite known as the path of initiation; it is not a matter of age, nor of caste, nor of learning. (11.56)
O Goddess of the gods, O Pārvatī, whether he is a scholar or even a king, one must never, under any circumstances, show him contempt, O Goddess of the gods. (11.57)
O Maheśvarī, he who acts out of negligence, ignorance, delusion, hypocrisy, or even pride shall suffer a downfall.
"One should always worship him with diligence; otherwise, the word of Tāriṇī will not be fulfilled.
I, as Tārā, together with Bhairava, shall bring about his destruction. (11.59)
For one who has received the full consecration, the installation should be performed like that of a deity;
for, O Pārvatī, just as a deity always dwells in a temple, [so does the deity dwell in the installed image].
Likewise, O Goddess, this Vidyā always resides within the ten-thousand-fold full [mantra];
it must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret, like one's own womb.
Thus has it been briefly declared; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus, in the illustrious *Śaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, in the latter part, in the first section, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā, concerning the ritual of the Meru of the Six Śāmbhavas.
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Secret of the Accomplished Mother. || 11 ||
The Twelfth Chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear that which is the most secret of secrets."
O Śaṅkara, tell me that which was previously indicated by me.
The illustrious Śiva said: O Goddess of the lords of gods, I shall now speak of the secret, the most profound secret, and the secret of the Tārā-yoga; listen and be attentive. (12–2)
The union with Tārā is indeed the true yoga; likewise, the recitation of Tārā is the true recitation.
The mantra of Tārā is the most excellent among all great mantras. || 12-3 ||
He is the blessed one, he is the wise one, he is the observer of vows, and he is the initiated one;
he is the Self, he is Mahādeva, the Lord who transcends all gods. (12.4)
He alone is the Supreme Self here, saluted by all the gods;
he is the Seer, he is the Knower, and he is devoted to the bliss of Brahman. (12.5)
Fortunate indeed is his mother, and his father is like a god;
he is a reciter of the Tārā-mantra, endowed with the complete initiation, and Tāriṇī herself [is his protector].
The Lord of all, omnipresent, devoted to all mantras,
a knower of the meaning of all tantras, and dedicated to all tantras.
Devoted to the five Pārāyaṇas and the expounder of the five jewels,
if he is endowed with initiation, he may recite any mantra whatsoever upon beholding it.
From that one should know success; there is no need for deliberation here.
Mantras written in a book do not grant success in recitation after recitation. || 12-9 ||

O Goddess of the Gods, by the mere sight of him, the agitation caused by mantras is destroyed; this applies even to one who is mute or dull-witted, provided he is endowed with the complete initiation (pūrṇadīkṣā). (12.10)
O Supreme Goddess, he who touches water or clothing while keeping the mantra of Tārā foremost shall indeed become a preeminent great poet.
O Goddess of the Gods, when one places the hand upon the jar, then the Sarasvatī of the jar speaks everything for exactly two praharas.
This fruit of yoga has been declared to you out of affection, O Maheśvarī.
What more is to be said, O Goddess? What else do you wish to hear? (12-13)
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear that secret which was previously mentioned.
Śrī Śiva said:
This secret, even more secret than the secret, is being told out of affection for you.
When a great calamity has arrived, when a most terrible crisis of life has been reached, when the loss of a kingdom, the destruction of wealth, or the death of a son has occurred; || 12-15 ||
O Maheśvarī, when the fear of a great pestilence has arisen and the kingdom is in ruin,
[I shall teach] the yoga for protecting one's own kingdom and the destruction of the enemy's kingdom.
O Great Goddess, that supreme yoga which produces great joy and accomplishes the six rites is now being described; listen and be attentive. (12–17)
First, one should recite the five-syllabled Tārā together with the *kullukā*; then the presiding goddess Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, who is known by the name of the *kūrca* seed-syllable, which is supreme. (12.18)
The power of Kālī is that very same [power] in Śiva; it is indeed the seed-syllable (bīja) of Tārā.
Tārā is celebrated by the name Praṇava, and that very thing is proclaimed as such.
And that which is severed is proclaimed as the single-syllable mantra (ekākṣarīmantra).
O Goddess, within that triad, there is then what is called Mahākrodha. (12.20)
O Śivā, she who bears the form of the fourfold Vidyā and is called by the seed-syllable *kūrca* shall be renowned as Caṇḍaghaṇṭā; she is indeed named after the *kūrca* seed-syllable.
Merely by the recitation of which one partakes in the recitation of the three powers;
the *kūrca* seed-syllable is the supreme power, and the final one is called the *kīlaka*. (12.22)
Just as the deity Triśakti is considered, O Great Goddess, to consist of bliss, so too do Kālībīja, Tārā, Chinnā, and the Ekākṣarī likewise [consist of it]. (12.23)
The three-syllabled supreme vidyā is named Trailokyavijayā;
it is Tārā, Kālī, and likewise Chinnā; Tārā, Chinnā, and Kālikā. (12.24)
Kālī Chinnā, Tārā Chinnā, Kālī Tāriṇī, Chinnā Tārā, and Kālikā—these six divisions are the victorious Kalā. (12.25)
Satisfied by hearing the mantra, she is the deity Tāriṇī who bestows sovereignty over the three worlds; she is the primordial goddess, while Ghaṇṭikā is her counterpart.
But Vijayā, the supreme three-syllabled digit, is the presiding deity; O Mistress of the Gods, that very seed-syllable which is at the beginning is also present in her weapons and ornaments. (12.27)
The middle seed-syllable is the essential form (svarūpa), and the final seed-syllable is the vehicle;
O Maheśvarī, this is the supreme nine-syllabled vidyā, or it may consist of four syllables.
The thirty-syllable Mahātārā is declared to be the mouth of Triśakti;
she is the Trailokyavijayā Vidyā, who bestows boons upon mere remembrance.
That which is known as the weapon for conquering the three worlds has been thus proclaimed; O Goddess of the gods, that very seed-syllable at the beginning is declared to be the yantra itself.
Alternatively, O Śivā, worship should be performed at whichever seat (pīṭha) one has devotion for;
O Queen of the Gods, this application is proclaimed as "Chinnabāṇa" (the severed arrow).
O Maheśānī, the weapon of withdrawal is proclaimed to be the tip of the arrow;
that very same [arrow] is the Ārdrapaṭī Vidyā when it has a wet cloth, but it is the Jīvahā when it has a dry cloth. (12.32)
The one who proclaims what is auspicious and inauspicious becomes the narrator of glorious news;
the art of Mahāpadmāvatī is the narrator of the news of the three worlds.
The nineteen-syllable vidyā is the sphere of knowledge of the three worlds;
having muttered the root vidyā a few times, O Śivā, one should then mutter the other.
But for all of them, O Maheśānī, one should diligently offer recitation, worship, and the like, as well as the bali offering, ointment, and fragrance, O Pārvatī. (12.35)
Through the practice of three months, one should recite [the mantra] from sunrise until sunset;
whatever has arisen by means of a steady and stable posture, that one should offer.
By means of application to this practice, what is there that does not come into one's hand?
Through the employment of the imperial seal, what on earth is not accomplished? (12.37)
Kālī is said to consist of Tārā and to have the form of Vaṭuka;
likewise, there is the Praṇava and Māyā, joined with the pair of "dānas. (12.38)
The pair of *kuru*, the pair of seed-syllables, and *svāhyatā*—these constitute the twenty-one [syllables].
The goddess Dhāriṇī is the presiding deity of this [mantra], residing in the place of the banner.
One should draw the yantra upon a banner, with Baṭuka in the central square;
Baṭuka is depicted in the attire of a youth, wearing a sacred thread made of a serpent.
Richly adorned with the ornaments of a skull and a trident, surrounded by his own hosts and encircled by dogs of nine colors, he is the very embodiment of Brahman.
The Lord, who bestows manifest fruit in the Kali age, is seated upon a corpse-throne; the all-pervading one who grants victory over the three worlds is established upon a twelve-spoked wheel.
By holding this banner, one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds;
having won the station of great sovereignty, one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds. (12.43)
Especially according to the procedure for the preliminary rite known as the five-limbed (pañcāṅga),
one should avoid the black antelope and the deer, setting aside their mere species.
For the sake of pleasing the mind of Tāriṇī, one should offer as a sacrifice an elephant, a horse, or a human;
whatever is cooked for Śivā, that indeed should be offered.
The *kuṣmāṇḍa* fruit is known as a buffalo, the *karkaṭī* as a goat, the *bījapūra* as a human, and the *rambhā* flower as a horse. (12.46)
One should prepare the root dish according to the appropriate variety of fish—whether sattvic, rājasic, or, O Goddess, the third, which is tāmasa. (12.47)
"O Supreme Goddess, the threefold offering of oblations (balidāna) has been proclaimed.
The Śrī Devī said: What is the distinction regarding Baṭuka? What is his power, and what form does he assume? (12.48)
Whether he is of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, or of the nature of Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
whether he is the husband, the son, or the brother—tell me, O Lord, what ritual act should be performed? (12.49)
"In this regard, a doubt has arisen within me; dispel this doubt for me.
Śrī Śiva said: "It is a secret, a most profound secret, and a secret even more profound than the most profound. (12.50)
"How is that to be told, O Goddess? Take an oath, Pārvatī!
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"I swear by your two feet, and I swear by the peak of the Himālaya mountain."
"He alone shall become averse; what is the use of further prolixity?
(p. 132) Śrī Śiva said: "I am delighted by your oath; listen as that story is told. (12.52)
Vetālas, Pretas, Kuṣmāṇḍas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras;
as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and other planetary deities, O Maheśvarī. (12.53)
O Supreme Goddess, they have come into being; by them the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is swallowed up.
Some serve Viriñci, while others serve Śiva or Viṣṇu. (12.54)
Others worship the Mahāvidyā, but they are certainly not partakers of success;
O Great Goddess, Vetālas and others are merely stealers of their recitation, worship, and other rites. (12.55)
O Maheśānī, for the sake of destroying them and for the purpose of bestowing grace upon her devotees,
this Baṭuka has been manifested by Tārākālī.
O Maheśvarī, there are indeed fifty great mantras of the Mahāpadma class,
and the yoginīs are numbered in the tens of millions, by the crores.
O Śivā, there are tens of millions upon tens of millions of Bhairavas and numerous Great Vidyās; Tārā is numbered in the hundreds of billions (trikharva), while Kālī is ten billion (daśārbuda).
Sundarī, however, consists of the divisions of tens of millions of digits; she is joined with him, while Bālā is divided from the sixteen kharvas into a number of three crores.
O Goddess, Pārvatī consists of thirty-six hundred thousand Brahmā-missiles, sixteen crores of Māyās, and twelve crores of worlds as her constituent parts.
O Śivā, through the principle known as Siddhavidyā, there are one hundred thousand varieties of Dhūmrakalā,
and through the Mātaṅgī-mantra, there are eighty-four hundred thousand.
This entire splendor, which assumes the form of the entire universe, has arisen from all splendors; it is the eternal one in the form of a young brahmin.
O Maheśānī, that Supreme One assumes three forms through Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, who are endowed with the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as their respective powers.
(133) Even there, O Maheśvarī, the eternal form of the youth, divided tenfold, was given the sacred thread by Mahogratārā. (12.64)
The skull was given by Chinnā, and Kālī announced the time;
the trident was given by Kāla, at the base of which are the three Śaktis.
Kālī, Tārā, and likewise Chinnā exist in the form of the trident;
as do other deities, siddhis, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras. || 12-66 ||
Having assumed the form of a dog, they enjoy [it] continuously;
in this way, O Supreme Goddess, the form of a young ascetic (baṭuka) has arisen.
O Goddess of the Gods, from the moment Śiva assumed the form known as Baṭuka, since then the Vetālas and other such beings have no longer caused suffering.
Eager to behold their respective deities, they each attained their own spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
Thus, having worshipped the Baṭuka, or for the sake of worshipping the Vāstu deity, [one should proceed].
O Goddess of gods, those men who worship [her] are of the nature of Śiva;
O Goddess, they become accomplished practitioners (sādhakas) who are masters of all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 12-70 ||
The servitude of Vetālas and others, the host of Yakṣiṇīs and magical sandals, the play of the sword and collyrium, and the entry into another's body—[these are attained]. (12.71)
From that time on, O Great Goddess, everything beginning with the Śābara rites remains within the hand of the practitioner; indeed, by its mere recollection, it becomes as if held in the hand.
Thus the auspicious *baṭuka* is born, the bestower of all accomplishments;
having attained the form of yoga, the ten *vidyās* dwell within him. (12.73)
The pure tenth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, endowed with the ten yogas,
is declared to be the lunar day of Baṭuka, which brings about the manifestation of Baṭuka.
O Supreme Goddess, having attained the status of being the son of the Goddess, the young ascetic (baṭuka) arises in age after age, abandoning both you and me. (12.75)
O Goddess of the gods, their accomplishment is not achieved even in tens of millions or billions of aeons.
Regarding Kālī and Tārā, the one bearing a sword and a trident was previously described. (12.76)
O Supreme Goddess, the Baṭuka [form] is enriched with two, four, or eight hands;
it is the secret, the most secret, and the secret beyond the most secret.
O Goddess, this yoga bestows all accomplishments, grants universal sovereignty, rescues one from all calamities, and is the supreme protector of one's own army. (12.78)
O Maheśānī, he is the supreme destroyer and disperser of enemy armies and kingdoms; he causes various calamities within the realm of the foe.
O Goddess of the gods, O Śivā, by means of the practice of *vīrasādhana* for a single day and night,
Baṭuka, Tārā, and likewise Kālī shall become propitious.
O Goddess of the Gods, other methods may or may not succeed at times;
they must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret like one's own private parts.
Thus it has been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (12.81)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Application of Accomplishment," within the *Tārāsūkta*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā, in the first section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*. 12.
The thirteenth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the determination regarding Vīrarātri and other such observances."
Śrī Śiva said:
Vīrarātri, Mahārātri, and likewise Kālarātri. (13.1)
The night of delusion, the terrible night, and likewise the night of anger;
likewise the night of weakness, and the night of the stars. (13.2)
O Supreme Goddess, Śivarātri is described as the Divine Night and the Terrible Night respectively; listen and be attentive. (13.3)
The fourteenth lunar day, a solar transit (saṃkrānti), a family asterism, and a family day—
when these coincide at midnight, it is proclaimed as Vīrarātri.
The eighth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is indeed the Navarātra;
it is the Mahārātri, O Maheśānī. Listen, my beloved, to [the description of] Kālarātri.
On the fourteenth day, there is the Festival of Lamps (Dīpotsava), as well as the conjunction with the new moon (Amāyā-yoga);
O Maheśānī, this is Kālarātri, the beloved of Tārākālī. (13.6)
O Great Goddess, Janmāṣṭamī is proclaimed as the Night of Delusion;
until the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, the curse of Tārā is said to have prevailed. (13.7)
When the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa had taken place, the supreme Tāriṇī was liberated;
at the birth of Vindhyavāsinī, she arrived in the form of lightning.
The venerable Mahātāriṇī Vidyā is devoted to the great forest;
she is perfectly accomplished through mere remembrance and is the supreme bestower of memory and nourishment.
O Great Goddess, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, when Mars is present, Krodharātri will appear in the form of a star. (13.10)
O Maheśvarī, when the month of Mārgaśīrṣa has arrived, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
Ghorarātri is proclaimed to be of the nature of Mahākāla.
When the eleventh day of the dark fortnight occurs in the month of Phālguna,
if it is joined by Venus or Mars, it is declared to be Abalārātri.
If the tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha is pure, joined with a Friday, and endowed with the ten yogas, and if the eleventh day occurs during the night; || 13-13 ||
O Supreme Goddess, that lunar day is proclaimed as the Divine Night (Divyarātri),
specifically when the pure tenth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha is endowed with the ten yogas.

The lunar day (tithi) for Baṭuka has been declared as that which causes his manifestation; it is joined with the new moon (Amāvāsyā), combined with a Tuesday, and accompanied by a solar transit (saṃkrānti).
If an eclipse should occur when the moon is conjoined with the Kula-bear (Ursa Major),
it is declared to be a "Nights of the Stars" (tārārātri), which is obtained only through great fortune.
In the dark fortnight of Phālguna, at midnight on a Friday during the auspicious [nakṣatra],
Śivarātri occurred, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
If the new moon (Amāvāsyā) is conjoined with Venus and occurs during a solar eclipse,
and this conjunction takes place in the afternoon, that lunar day is known as Mṛtasaṃjīvanī.

Bathing, giving gifts, and other rites up to the fire-oblation performed on that eighth day of the month of Caitra which is conjoined with a solar transit (saṃkrānti) shall yield infinite fruit. (13–19)
The third lunar day in the month of Mādhava, when it is pure and conjoined with a Kula-day and a Kula-asterism, is known as Siddhirātri; it is filled with the energy of Tārākālī. (13–20)
O Goddess, the supreme Sarvasiddhīśvarī has been described as Dāruṇā.
Everything has been told in due order; now hear that which is called Parvarāja. (13–21)
The third lunar day of the month of Pauṣa, conjoined with a Saturday,
is also [auspicious] if it occurs while the sun is in Capricorn and is joined with one’s own birth asterism.
If it should coincide with the fourth lunar day, or in some cases with the Revatī asterism,
this festival known as Parvarāja is the most excellent among all festivals.

O Great Goddess, if the third lunar day of the month of Caitra is conjoined with the asterism Revatī, it is known as the Ṛddhi-yoga, which is highly commended for the performance of fire-offerings (homa).
Every month, the full moon day conjoined with the lunar mansion of that month and joined with the weekday of one's family lineage— that lunar day becomes most auspicious.
O Pārvatī, the eighth day of the dark fortnight of every month—whether it is conjoined with Tuesday, or conjoined with [the appropriate] lunar mansion, or even by itself—is [auspicious]. (13.26)
The goddess known as Rātri, who bestows all spiritual accomplishments,
occurs when the fourth lunar day of the month of Māgha is conjoined with Capricorn.
That night is known as the night of Gaṇapa, according to Auḍava;
it is the ninth day of the dark fortnight, conjoined with the Kula constellation. (13.28)
Or else, O Goddess, the night of success is proclaimed to be the fourth lunar day of the dark fortnight, when it is joined with a Kulavāra and a Kularkṣa.
If it is merely the night of Bāla joined with Mars during a saṃkrānti, or if the new moon is conjoined with Mars and associated with a Kula asterism; || 13-30 ||
Known as Kṛṣṇarātri, it brings joy to Akṣobhya;
it occurs when the new moon falls on a Sunday in conjunction with the Śravaṇa nakṣatra during the months of Pauṣa or Māgha.
That is to be known as Ardhodaya; Mahodaya is slightly less than that.
O Maheśānī, this is celebrated by the divine sages as Dharmarātri.
O Goddess, when there is a conjunction with Mars on the new moon day, or with Mercury, or with Venus, Jupiter, or the Sun, it is endowed with the Kula asterism. (13.33)
The Yoga of the Divine Mandala is superior to a hundred solar eclipses;
it is proclaimed as that which occurs on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha.

That lunar day should be known as belonging to the Sun; one should perform recitation, fire-oblations, and other rites when it is joined with the Sun, with the Kula constellations, and even with the [specific] day. (13.35)
Known as Mahāsaurī, she is the cause of the origin of the three worlds;
when the seventh lunar day of the month occurs conjoined with the sun. (13.36)
O Maheśānī, the eighth lunar day of the month falling on a Wednesday should be known as Haṃsī Tithi, which is devoted to the dharma of liberation. (13.37)
It is especially renowned as Viṣṇurātri in the month of Bhādrapada;
[it occurs] on the fifth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, on a Friday.
The fifth day of the spring season is declared to be the lunar day that revives desire;
it is characterized by the waving of lights, recitation, fire-offerings, chanting, and the dancing of Kāma.
O Supreme Goddess, on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, under that same asterism,
the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) should be performed, and one should carry out the tenfold protection.
The full moon day of the month of Caitra; on that day, there is the worship of Madana.
O Goddess, in every rite of learning, worship is performed during the proclaimed conjunction. (13–41)
"Indeed, by worshipping this yoga, they attain perfection; how much more so [for others]?
Thus it has been briefly explained. What else do you wish to hear? (13.42)

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Hero’s Night and Other Observances," in the *Siddhitantra*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā, in the first section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*. 13.
The Fourteenth Chapter.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Great God, increaser of the happiness of all!
By what means does Tārā, the savior of the three worlds, swiftly bestow accomplishment?
O Mahādeva, if I am dear to you, tell me this: what accomplishment does the illustrious Mahādakṣiṇā Kālī bestow upon us? (14.2)
Śrī Śiva said:
"How can this most secret of secrets be revealed to you?
O Goddess of gods, take an oath, and then I shall tell you the truth."
The illustrious Goddess said:
"I swear by your two feet that she alone shall be turned away from me.
The illustrious Śiva said:
I am delighted by this oath; listen now as it is being told.
By your command, the Siddhi named Madhumatī has appeared;
from your presence, Kālī, Tārā, and Śivā have become [manifest] as your own abode.
O Śivā, the face was given by Śrīvidyā, the pair of hands by Kālī,
the fingers by Tārā, and the heart-lotus by Bhuvaneśī.
The pair of feet was given by Chinnā, the two eyes by Mātaṅgī,
the forehead by Lakṣmī, and likewise by Siddhavidyā.
O Maheśānī, the hair was given by me; O Maheśvarī, the two ankles were given by the Brahmāstra-vidyā; the smile was given by Bālā; and the horse was given by me. (14.8)
O Goddess, Rucaka is [established] by Śrī, while Nigraha is by Dhūmāvatī;
the other deities are at the hairline, and the Brahmāṇḍa is in the lotus of the heart.
Thus, born in its entirety from the emergence of the mass of splendor,
this supreme accomplishment, Mahāmadhumatī, is the attractor of the three worlds.
Pārvatī, Arundhatī, Durgā, Mṛtasañjīvanī, and Parā—these shall quickly attract everything for the purpose of attracting the three worlds. (14.11)
Kālī became Śivā, whose nature is Tārā, and who manifested as a radiant abode; she was fully satisfied by the milk-rice and devoted to that milk-rice offering.
The supreme Vidyā Mahāmadhumatī is the attractor of the three worlds;
likewise, there is the Vidyā that attracts Bhairava and the one that attracts Vetālas. (14.13)
The goddess who attracts the Kinnaras and brings about the attraction of the gods—I shall proclaim her mantra, which is supreme for attracting the three worlds. (14.14)
The fifth [syllable] is joined with the letter *pa*, adorned with the *nāda* and the *bindu*;
conjoined with the *mahākāmakalā*, it is declared to be the single-syllabled *kalā*.
Having extracted "madhumatīm," which is endowed with desire and has no end;
and having extracted "sthāvarā" and "jaṅgamākarṣaṇī."

The syllables ending with the pair (Ṭha), followed by the fire-born consort (Svāhā) and the letters of Citkalā, are proclaimed as the eighteen-syllable Vidyā, the supreme attractor of the three worlds. (14–17)
The sage is declared to be Kāmadeva, and from that, Nivṛt-gāyatrī is the meter; O Maheśānī, she herself is proclaimed as the deity. (14–18)
O Maheśvarī, the seed-syllable *mrīṃ* and likewise *svāhā* are declared to be the Śakti;
its application is proclaimed for the attraction of both the stationary and the moving. (14-19)
One should perform the six limbs in sequence using the seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels;
thereafter, O Maheśvarī, one should perform the meditation that is about to be described.
Fair-limbed, with a face as beautiful as the autumnal moon, clad in yellow garments, full-figured, with a shimmering golden necklace upon her high,
swelling breasts; seated upon a white, lofty horse, three-eyed, and adorned with yellow unguents and garlands— [I salute her].
One should meditate upon her who is eager for milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and holds honey in her two arms, as well as a goad (*sṛṇi*).
One should perform the rites such as the binding of the directions and the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) just as for Kālī.
In the case of Śivā, there is no enclosure of the yantra; one should worship her alone. (14–22)
Everything has been declared as being like the three powers; listen now as the specific details are told.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the vidyā which effects the attraction of all things. (14.23)
O Goddess, for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*, seventy thousand repetitions have been prescribed by me to you as the practice for a perfected mantra (*siddhamantra*). (14–24)
O Maheśvarī, having reached a grove of plantain trees, one should recite the mantra at all times for the duration of a year, subsisting solely on milk-rice.
O Goddess, one should then recite it one hundred thousand times, just as in the *vīrasādhana*;
thereafter, O Maheśvarī, one should recite it seventy thousand times for the sake of direct perception.
Having eaten milk-rice with ghee and sugar on a plantain leaf in a forest of plantains devoid of people, one should remain vigilant.
Assuming the guise of a Gandharva and free from fear, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) with portions;
having first divided it into two parts, listen now to that procedure, O Pārvatī. (14–28)
One part, two parts, and one full part;
he should slowly consume the previous portion himself, along with a portion of the subsequent one. (14.29)
On a single plantain leaf, one should write the syllable *mrī* as the general rule;
during the first week, one should proceed in silence, however it may be. (14.30)
In the second week, O Goddess, he becomes like a golden image;
in the third week, O Goddess, he eats milk-rice directly before his eyes.
She grants the practitioner his desired boon by her very power;
she remains day and night together with the practitioner according to his wish. (14.32)
He draws [them] from the ocean, from Mount Sumeru, from the ends of the quarters,
from the netherworld (pātāla), from the world of Indra, and from the golden Śrīśaila mountain and its trees.
Furthermore, from afar and even from the surface of the earth, it instantly draws forth other objects—a river, a city, and jewels. (14.34)
He should also recount the news of those residing in the city and of kings;
he should quickly enter into the true secrets of his enemies as well. (14.35)
"This knowledge that attracts the three worlds must not be given to just anyone.
O Baṭuka, you take this; may it grant me success at all times.
Thus has been briefly stated the classification of the mantra and its method of accomplishment. (14-36)

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Limbs of the Tārā Ritual Manual," in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā, within the first section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*. 14.
The Fifteenth Chapter.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear other mantras and their methods of accomplishment."
Śrī Śiva said: The single-syllable mantra, having the primordial seed-syllable and two *ṭha*s, becomes three syllables. (15.1)
