The three-syllable mantra, joined with *svāhā* and *ṭha*, is honored by those who desire [its fruits].
When combined with the seed-syllable and the vocative address, it is proclaimed as the five-syllable mantra. (15.2)
Accompanied by the seed-syllable and the invocation, ending with two *ṭha*s, she is beloved by the Sage;
accompanied by the seed-syllable and the invocation, ending with *svāhā*, she is honored by the Rishis. || 15-3 ||
The six-syllable mantra ending with the dual vocative case bestows all desired objects;
when joined with the perfective participle *sambuddhiḥ* and *svāhā*, it effects the summoning of all. (15.4)
The ten-syllable Vidyā, which encompasses the seed and the end of the ritual action, possesses universal form;
O Supreme Goddess, it begins with the syllable *ka* and ends with the two *ṭha*s, consisting of eleven syllables.
That which begins with *karma* and ends with *vahnijāyā* (svāhā) is proclaimed as *vidyā*; that which begins with *bīja* and ends with the pair *karmaṭha* is proclaimed as *mahāvidyā*.

Then follows the seed-syllable and the word *svāhā*; this is proclaimed as the perfected Vidyā. The phrase for awakening the seed-syllable, ending with the ritual action (*karman*), is the supreme Kalā.
The word for awakening the seed-syllable is joined with two [forms of] the object;
the supreme [mantra] consists of the word for awakening the seed-syllable followed by the object and svāhā. (15.8)
The supreme [vidyā] consists of the syllable for awakening the seed-syllable (bījasambodhanapada) followed by *ṭha* and *svāhā*.
Then, the other vidyā is proclaimed as the seed-syllable followed by *ṭha* and *svāhā*. (15.9)
The invocation ending with *ṭha* and *svāhā* is the supreme Vidyā that grants all aims;
the seed-syllable rite ending with *ṭha* and *svāhā* is the Vidyā beautiful in all her limbs. (15.10)
Then there is the vocative case, and then the object; the next [mantra] should end in two *ṭha* suffixes.
Then there is the vocative case, and then the object; the next is endowed with the *ṭhāyuk* suffix and *svāhā*.
Then follows the invocation, the object of the rite, and the word "svāhā"; thus Śivasundarī is declared to have twenty-four divisions as the supreme energy (kalā).
Bālā, Madhumatī, and likewise Bhinnā, as well as Sundarī and Manoharā; she becomes Bhinnā in the accomplishment of the treasure (nidhi), and thus she is proclaimed to have three divisions.
Thus, the supreme mantra that attracts the three worlds has been declared in thirty ways.
Having gone to a secluded grove of plantain trees at the onset of night, [one should practice]. (15.14)
On an auspicious day and at an auspicious moment, one should perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) accompanied by one's specific desire for this eighteen-syllable mantra known as Mahāmadhumatī.
Having said, "For the sake of attaining success in the mantra," one should recite [it] from this day forward;
having extracted it twenty-one times, one should continue to recite it until the end of the day.

Then, one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* in the form of loud recitation (*japa*), having first performed the pair of six-limbed rites (*ṣaḍaṅga*), meditated [upon the deity], and worshipped [her]. (15–17)
Having prepared milk-rice with cow’s milk and placed it upon a plantain leaf, one should extract the seed-mantra ending in the dative case, preceded by the word "madhumatī. (15–18)
Having given and offered milk-rice (pāyasa) there again and again,
and once she has finished eating it, [he should offer] water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
Having shown [the deity] the betel leaf and having prostrated again and again,
one should set aside half of the milk-rice (pāyasa) separately and consume the remaining half oneself. (15–20)

O Goddess, having adorned oneself with divine garments and ornaments, and having assumed the attire of a Gandharva with red garlands and other finery, one should perform this three thousand times every day.
O Supreme Goddess, if one recites [the mantra] three hundred and thirty-four times for twenty-one days, the deity will become a granter of boons. (15–22)
Through union with a *baṭuka*, one certainly attains success and not otherwise.
This applies to whoever is a worshipper of Śrītārā as well as whoever is a worshipper of Kālikā. (15.23)
Having accomplished this vidyā, one attains success; it is not otherwise.
Whatever desires one prays for, that supreme vidyā, which effects the attraction of all things, grants those very desires moment by moment.
From the temple of Śiva, which was a fortress fortified by an iron wall.
Dhanada, Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu, Pārvatī, and Arundhatī—
thus he draws forth these ten Mahāvidyās at that very moment.
Lanka, the oceans, and the islands, along with the Siddhas, Yakṣas, and Mahoragas—even objects never before heard of—he draws forth at that very moment. (15.27)
O Śivā, one may instantly summon Kinnaras, Yātudhānas and others, as well as treasures and supernatural powers, and even Mount Sumeru and Kailāsa in a moment.
O Goddess, O Mistress of the Gods, he who practices with focused attention shall speak everything—whatever exists in those various places, as well as knowledge of the three periods of time. (15.29)
This vidyā that attracts the three worlds must not be given to just anyone;
having first accomplished the vidyā, one should thereafter achieve success. (15.30)
"It must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret like one's own womb.
Thus it has been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (15.31)

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Attainment of Madhumatī," in the first section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 15.
The sixteenth chapter. The venerable Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the definitive teaching on the initiation of the Krama."
The illustrious Śiva said:
How can I tell you that which is a secret, even a most profound secret?
Nevertheless, out of your true devotion, I shall speak; listen now.
She is known as the sixfold [deity] of the Moon and Fire, the Supreme (Parā) who is intent upon Nirvāṇa.
Then, O Goddess, there is the sixfold Śāmbhava [state], through the piercing of the cakras, as well as the realization of one's own body-cakra and the entry into another's body. (16.3)
From the knowledge of this, wisdom arises; thus has initiation been described by me to you.
This has been declared regarding the letter *ha*; now listen, O Maheśvarī, to that which begins with *ka*.
O Śivā, [the goddesses] are Candrāgnirasarājñī and Mahārājñī;
then, O Śivā, there are Mahākāmakalā, Kālī, and Guhyakālī. (16–5)
Guhyakālī is said to be twofold, namely Sakalā and Niṣkalā in sequence;
the ten-faced one is called Sakalā, while the Vāśiṣṭhikā is the Kalā.
She is proclaimed to be threefold—fierce, gentle, and extremely cruel;
she is also celebrated as Niṣkalā, ending with the secret name, according to the division of Kālī.
This wisdom alone, consisting of fifteen syllables— namely the moon (1), fire (3), the Vedas (4), and five (5)— bestows sovereignty when practiced with devotion according to the sequence of Nīla.
Haṃsatārā is Mahānīlā; at its end is Cīnaśāmbhavī.
Medhā, however, is Kevalā alone; Siddhi and Ṛddhikriyā are twofold.
The third is proclaimed as the initiation for the sacrifice of divine sovereignty;
it is divine in form, of celestial appearance, the very form of mantra, and supreme among the great. (16.10)
Containing all forms and existing since all time, she is the great sovereign through her wisdom;
the multiplicity of divisions is proclaimed according to the sequence of accomplishment and supernatural power.
The initiation known as Vidyārājyā is prescribed in the ritual of Chinnamastā;
likewise, [the initiations] are Candravahnirasa, Rakta, Śyāmā, and Ṣoḍaśī. (16.12)
Beyond the sixfold [set] is the seventeenth; beyond that is the Supreme (parā).
Dīpinī, Mālinī, and Kullā are, in sequence, the sovereignty of the Vidyās and so forth. (16.13)
O Maheśānī, that which is called Bagalā possesses imperial sovereignty and the highest status;
she is the subtle Meru of the moon and the Vedas, devoid of mantra, and whose essence is Śiva. (16.14)
The Heart-mantra, the Śatārṇā, the five weapons, and likewise the Kullukā—
by means of the sequential application of the Gāyatrī, one attains sovereign imperial power and the supreme state.
Endowed with this group of five and possessing the consciousness of universal sovereignty,
the Śrī Divya Sarvasāmrājya initiation shall be the most supreme of all.
Even beyond that, O Mistress of the Gods, there is no initiation within the sphere of the universe;
nor are there the tenfold divisions of the Vidyās born from the divisions of the Mahāvidyās. (16–17)
The various divisions of Siddhividyā, as well as the Mahāmantras,
their ancillary mantras (tadaṅgamantra), O Goddess of Gods, the Śābara, and the Daśaśābara.
O Goddess, there is the Kālaśābaraka as well as the Siddhaśābara;
likewise, the mantras of the threefold Darśana arise from the sequence of the Āmnāya. (16–19)

O Śivā, in the Kali age, the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya) consists of the *kādi*, *hādi*, and *kaha* [groups of mantras], as do the temple-mantras (*āyatanamantra*) and whatever network of mantras exists. (16–20)
O Goddess of gods, one shall possess all authority in this rite of initiation.
One who is endowed with this initiation is Śrī Kālikā herself. (16–21)
By means of the sequence of eight watches (praharas), she assumes the form of the ten Vidyās;
the Vidyā named Kāmakalā, along with her divisions, is the presiding deity of their functions.
Likewise, O Maheśānī, his limb-mantras and other mantras always reside within his mouth; [this is] the sequential initiation (kramadīkṣā) according to the fivefold division of the Vidyās.
O Śivā, the limb-mantras, the Gāyatrī, and the five Kullukas are declared to be the most secret of secrets in the ritual procedure for other vidyās. (16–24)

O Goddess, that lowest of practitioners who recites [the mantra] without the sequential initiation (kramadīkṣā) becomes impoverished, a great sinner, and one who takes away the children [of others]. || 16-25 ||
O Supreme Goddess, O Goddess, that lowest of practitioners who recites the mantra of Śrīvidyā, Kālikā, or Tārā without having received the Krama initiation— 16–26.
He was poor, most terrible, devoid of fortune, and censured;
he was blind, one-eyed, emaciated, hunchbacked, lame, impotent, and afflicted with leprosy.
He shall be afflicted by all diseases and overwhelmed by excessive anxiety; he shall be a stealer of sons, a stealer of wives, and a destroyer of daughters and kingdoms. (16–28)
Alternatively, he may become insane, suffer the agitation of mantras, incur the curse of the deity, and poverty shall always abide in his home. (16–29)
O Goddess of the gods, by this distinction, one who steals women is always incapacitated;
yet, if he is endowed with the Krama initiation, he certainly becomes a king. (16-30)
Endowed with great majesty, possessed of all accomplishments, victorious, disciplined, virtuous, perfected, the bestower of perfection, and auspicious. || 16-31 ||
With a joyful soul, a knower of truth, knowing the three periods of time, a seer, happy, the lord of ten million siddhis, a hero, handsome, and a deluder of desire. || 16-32 ||
The self of bliss, the supreme self, transcending all qualities beyond the highest, he is the manifest Lord of the Kings of Kings, equal to the heart and time in the Kali age. (16.33)
For one who worships this vidyā, poverty or wretchedness may occasionally arise due to being deprived of a guru, abandoning the lineage, or separation from the tradition. (16.34)
First, poverty shall prevail; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
For wherever there is the abode of the wish-fulfilling gem, there is the secret temple. (16.35)
There is a house consisting of all sovereign powers, with stairs whose nature is the nine gems;
there is a forest of *kalpa* trees, as well as a forest of *pārijāta* trees.
But where indeed could there be poverty for one who possesses the wish-fulfilling gem?
Therefore, for one who lacks the proper sequence, there is poverty at every step.
Having approached a Guru who is endowed with the [proper] lineage, the wise one should request the lineage;
otherwise, through delusion regarding the Guru, he shall attain poverty. (16.38)
Or he may become short-lived, O Goddess; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Even if his sovereignty were written by the decree of fate, his life would come to an end. (16.39)
Thus has been briefly declared the fruit for one who lacks the proper sequence. It must be kept secret, kept secret! What else do you wish to hear? (16.40)

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Gradual Initiation," in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā, within the first section of the northern portion of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*.
The seventeenth chapter.
The venerable Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear that secret which was previously mentioned."
That which must be hidden, that indeed must be hidden; speak of that with certainty.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess, that which is the most secret of secrets and has not been proclaimed to anyone—that very thing is now being told; listen and be attentive. (17-2)
The Utsarjana, the Upākarma, and likewise the Pavitrāropaṇa should be performed according to the prescribed rules; thereafter, the tying of the protective thread (Rakṣābandha) should be done.
O Supreme Goddess, the practitioner should always perform these rites in due order;
on the full moon day of the month of Caitra, he should perform the planting of the Madana tree.
When the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, the practitioner who does not perform the rite of the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) finds all his ritual actions to be fruitless.
O Maheśānī, it destroys everything, including the recitation performed for a full year and the virtuous rites such as fire-offerings and worship; therefore, one should practice this.
O Maheśānī, one should first perform the daily rite, and thereafter the occasional rite;
the ritual known as Upākarma is proclaimed to be as obligatory as the daily one.
The occasional rite is called the purificatory (pavitra), while the optional rite is the protective procedure (rakṣāvidhi).
That which contains two occasional rites is said to be the final optional one.
Where there are two optional rites, that is the first [type], born of a specific cause;
where there are two obligatory rites, that is the last, joined with both the optional and the obligatory.
According to Āśvalāyana, the full moon of Śrāvaṇa is the time; according to Kātyāyana, it should be on the full moon day.
For the Sāmavedins, it is also on the fifth lunar day or when the moon is in the constellation Hasta. (17.10)
The Upākarma rite should be performed, followed by the obligatory worship at its conclusion;
thereafter, the worship of the Pavitra should take place, and then the ritual for protection (rakṣāvidhi) should be carried out. || 17-11 ||
O Goddess, during the two periods of birth-impurity (sūtaka), during an eclipse, or at another solar transit (saṃkrama),
a man should perform the Upākarma rites in the month of Bhādrapada, O Mistress of the Gods.

One should always perform the protection of the sacred thread (*pavitrarakṣaṇa*) and the rite for peace (*śānti*) in the month of Bhādrapada, specifically on the fifth, the tenth, and likewise the fourteenth lunar days. || 17-13 ||
Especially on the full moon day, and particularly during an auspicious conjunction of the lunar mansion,
if an eclipse should occur, one should perform the protective rite.
In that regard, O Goddess, the Upākarma rite should always be performed; therefore, during a lunar eclipse, one should avoid the solar conjunction. (17.15)
Having accepted [the invitation], one should perform worship on the fourteenth or the full moon day;
[using a rosary] with ten, twenty-one, or twenty-seven knots.
O Goddess of the gods, [one may perform] fifty-four, one hundred and eight,
twenty-five, three hundred, or even a thousand knots.
The number eighteen is proclaimed in reverse order;
according to the sequence beginning with the highest, the purifier (pavitra) shall be of three kinds.
O Goddess, for rites of pacification (śāntikarma), the thread should be made of silk, gold, kuśa grass, wool, jewels, silver, or copper. (17–19)
O Goddess, O beloved, one should fashion it with two and a half knots, or three and a half knots, or even a single knot, in due order.
O Goddess, a serpent-noose (nāgapāśa) is proclaimed to consist of two and a half knots; O Goddess, a Brahma-knot (brahmagranthi) is proclaimed to consist of three and a half knots. || 17–21 ||
O Maheśānī, the knots of the *candragranthi* are determined by the number of threads;
there is no fixed rule regarding the threads for silk, nor for gold or silver. (17–22)
A knot is prescribed on a strip made of gold thread or born of gold;
having tied the knot, O Maheśānī, one should worship the deity of the knot.

It is declared that [the rosary] for a Vaiṣṇava should be made of thread, for a Śaiva it should be produced from a silk cloth (paṭṭa), and for a Śākta mantra it should be made of gold; however, that which is mentioned for both [Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva] is suitable in all cases.
O Goddess, in the *Pañcasiddhividhi*, that which is born of jewels is proclaimed as follows:
a circle, a triangle, the form of the earth (a square), a hexagon, and a six-pointed star. (17–25)
The eight-petaled [lotus], the eight-spoked, the ten-spoked, the fourteen-spoked, the twelve-spoked, the sixteen-spoked, and the five-spoked [wheel] as the fourteenth. || 17–26 ||
One should have these mechanical devices made—either the ivory-lotus or the moon-phase-lotus—with the machine in the center and various jewels surrounding it. (17–27)
O Supreme Goddess, one should wear it according to the sequence for protecting the sacred thread;
knots in the form of chains [made] of gold and other materials are thus proclaimed. (17–28)
O Supreme Goddess, one should have [the image] fashioned according to the sequence beginning with the highest quality:
using ruby, gem, and likewise the kuruvinda stone.
In diamond, lapis lazuli, emerald, topaz, ruby, sapphire, and green emerald; || 17-30 ||
Having performed [the rites] for Kīṭa, Śivaratna, Viṣṇuja, Binduratna, Māyūra, Pāca, and the one known as Kukkuṭa. (17-31)
O Goddess, when placed upon Kṛṣṇaśilā, a moonstone, coral, pearl, or a garment, the fruit of the protective yantra becomes equal to a treasure-chest of jewels. (17.32)
One should inscribe these diagrams for the sake of accomplishing all tasks, in the rites of Śrīvidyā, Kālikā, Tārā, and Chinnamastā, O Śivā. (17.33)
O Great Goddess, one should perform [the ritual] upon the four-petaled [lotus] for Mātaṅgī, Bhuvaneśvarī, and Kamalā; the mantra consists of four syllables. (17-34)
O Supreme Goddess, one should fashion the syllables and measures as fourfold;
just as the petals and the squares [of the mandala], so too should the syllables of the Vidyā be arranged.
O Supreme Goddess, one should draw [the form] or write down merely the seed-syllable;
O Goddess, one should act exactly as has been described regarding youth and beauty. (17.36)
O beloved, when one binds you with a mantra, or with a purifying cord (pavitra), or likewise with the root-mantra (mūla) or the vidyā that delivers from calamity, in due order; || 17-37 ||
O Goddess, one should perform the protection; thus the protection becomes all-effecting.
And for the sake of protection and for the sake of knowledge, the Balimukha was established by Gautama and others. (17-38)

Listen indeed to how the various divisions in the Sūtra were established in their proper sequence and according to their application: by Kapila and others for the sake of liberation, and by Śaṅkara and others for the sake of power.
One should have [the image] made in white, red, yellow, blue, or even green, as well as in camphor or many variegated colors, according to the appropriate application.
One should perform the rites according to the specific desires as appropriate;
one shall become a master of all accomplishments—of this there is no doubt. (17.41)
O Goddess, in the procedure for each vidyā, there shall be the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa);
O Goddess, in the procedure for each vidyā, protection (rakṣā) shall be performed according to the sequence of the letters.
O Dear One, it may be made from the eight fragrances, or from the thread of the living-wheel,
or from the essence of the flower-king, or produced from the sky.
In the same way, O Maheśvarī, the thread originating from the essence of agallochum is declared;
it is the secret, the most secret, and the most secret of secrets. (17.44)
It must be guarded, guarded, guarded like one's own womb;
whatever [teachings] exist within the cosmic egg or upon the surface of the earth. (17.45)
O Goddess, O Maheśānī, all supernatural powers arise for the practitioner who maintains this protection; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (17.46)
O Goddess, the fulfillment of desires shall come to pass; there is no need for deliberation here.
Thus has it been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (17.47)

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Sūtras," in the first part of the northern section of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 17 ||
The eighteenth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear that which is greater than the most secret of secrets."
Śrī Śiva said:
This most secret of secrets is being told; listen to the means of accomplishment.
O Pārvatī, for those who are endowed with the full initiation, consecration, and so forth,
the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) and the protective rite (rakṣā) are declared to be exactly the same.
Having performed either the immediate consecration or the preliminary consecration, the *pavitra* should be prepared for the sake of all desired aims. (18.3)
And with all the jewels, as well as the Garuḍa-jewel, one should perform protection and binding for the sake of successfully accomplishing all forms of protection. (18.4)
Tārā, Śrī, Kāmā, Vāṅ, Māyā, Kālī, Chinnā, Tāriṇī, Bagalā, Vimalā, Dhūmrā, and Vasordhārā constitute the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 18-5 ||
The three stars and the five stars [are located] from the conjunction of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣi) with Ākarṣiṇī;
likewise, the supreme Māyā is in Parāprāsādaka.
These are the seed-syllables and the arrows, arising from the desire for the howling of the pretas,
through the sequential application of one, two, three, four, five, and six syllables.
One should apply the vidyā to the yantra for the sake of attaining all siddhis;
and on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should perform the tenfold protection rite.
Protection of cattle, protection of horses, and thirdly, protection of elephants;
protection of people, protection of the country, protection of the home, and that which is called protection of alchemy (rasa). (18.9)
The protection of wealth, the protection of children, the protection of fields is considered supreme;
and the tenth is the protection of all—this tenfold protection is thus regarded. (18.10)
On the eighth and ninth days, on the fifth and tenth days,
on the fourteenth and the full moon day— on both fortnights as well.
First there should be the Upākarma rite, then the wearing of the *pavitra*, and at the end of that, the binding of the protective thread; one should perform this triad in this sequence. (18.12)

Indeed, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) for Gaṇeśa is proclaimed for the fourth day; on the fifth day, the wearing [of the thread] should be performed, and the preliminary consecration for Mātaṅgī. On the tenth day, the wearing should be performed, and the preliminary consecration on the seventh day.
O Maheśvarī, on the eighth day, worship should be performed and [the image] should be worn during the solar transit.
O Śivā, the consecration (adhivāsa) is performed on the eighth day and the retention (dhāraṇa) on the ninth;
this has been declared regarding Śakti. O Goddess, now hear the procedure for the Pāñcarātra.
O Śivā, on the ninth day there is indeed the consecration (adhivāsa), and on the tenth day the wearing (dhāraṇa);
for the Vaiṣṇava rite, it is on the twelfth day, and the removal (vidhāraṇa) on the thirteenth.
O Goddess, it is declared in the Śaiva tradition that the *adhivāsa* rite is performed on the fourteenth day and the worship on the full moon; likewise, for Śrīvidyā, the full moon is prescribed.
On the full moon day of the month of Caitra as well, one should perform the wearing of the *pavitra*;
the *pavitra* for celibate students (*brahmacārin*) should always be made of *kuśa* or *kāśa* grass. (18–18)
Those dwelling in the forest should wear garments made of hemp or flax; ascetics should wear ochre-colored robes; and a householder may wear robes of any color.
It is proclaimed that for kings it arises from golden thread, for kṣatriyas it is born of silver,
and for the twice-born it originates from [cotton] thread, in that respective order.
In that very same way, O Goddess, protection is in every respect equal here;
regarding this matter, O Sovereign of the Gods, hear three ancient legends (itihāsas).

In ancient times, protection was provided by Pārvatī to Śrī Kārttikeya; likewise, for the sake of subduing Devendra and for victory in the destruction of Vṛtra, [protection was given] upon the bed. (18–22)
In former times, O Goddess, in the Kṛta Yuga, the young student (baṭuka) was previously protected by the Mahāvidyās and others; likewise, Nahuṣa was the lord of Kṣatriyas. (18–23)
Having performed the *upākarma* ceremony, he then remained engaged in the *pavitrāropaṇa*;
having diligently prepared the *pavitra*, he brought it from the abode of Devendra to his own home.
O Goddess of the gods, that base man who, while on that path, is without protection—his intellect has become perverted, O Lord of men, for he is devoid of protection. (18–25)
By the mere binding of the protective thread, there is protection for twelve months;
O Goddess of the lords of gods, if it is not performed, a man becomes deprived of his intellect. (18–26)
O Great Goddess, Pārvatī, protection lasting for a full year is achieved through the application of protective binding, as well as by means of diagrams marked on the body and seed-syllable markings.
Protection is achieved everywhere by means of the seed-syllables (*aṅgabīja*) and the banners (*patākā*) and other such items;
here, the *upākarma* is proclaimed as the very consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the Vedas. (18–28)

The *pavitraka* is the protection for one who has received the Vedic mantras; the binding of the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*) is said to be for the purpose of protecting the presiding deity. (18–29)

Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the binding of the protective thread; for without protection, O Maheśānī, even ritual acts performed for the duration of a year [bear no fruit]. (18–30)
O Goddess, everything becomes fruitless and the deity turns away;
O Queen of the Gods, one should perform the binding of the protective thread even with all one's possessions. (18-31)
Then, O Goddess, all protection is indeed secured; of this there is no doubt.
The threefold [practice] is declared in sequence as the constant, the occasional, and the optional. (18.32)
"Thus has it been briefly proclaimed; what else do you wish to hear?

Śrī Śiva said:
"O Queen of the Gods, what is that secret? Tell me that, O sweet-spoken one.
Śrī Devī said:
The rite of the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) and likewise the investiture of the Madana [thread]. || 18-34 ||
"O Lord of the gods, if I am dear to you, let it be told.
Śrī Śiva said:
"The month of Āṣāḍha is the best; Śrāvaṇa is remembered as middling. (18.35)
The month of Bhādrapada is inferior; it consists of two fortnights, the bright and the dark.
The bright fortnight is recommended, but in its absence, the other is prescribed. (18.36)
On the fifth, the eighth, the ninth, and the tenth lunar days, as well as on the twelfth, the fourteenth, or even on the full moon day. (18.37)
Having tripled a thread made of cotton that is distinguished by silk, one should wash it with pure water.
Then one should purify [the area] with the mantras spoken for the western face and those for the southern faces;
thereafter, one should have beautiful pavitras prepared with mantras.
One hundred and eight is the best; half of that is the middling;

O Dear One, having carefully prepared the purifier (pavitra) according to the previously mentioned distinctions of threads or substances, one should tie a knot according to the prescribed rule.
O Daughter of the Mountain, one should perform the ten knots with the mantras recited for the northern [direction], adorned with various wonders using saffron and other substances. (18.42)

O Supreme Goddess, on the day of offering the purifiers (pavitra), one should perform either the previously mentioned preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) or an immediate consecration (sadyo'dhivāsana).
At night, immediately following the daily worship together with the initiates (samayins),
the laying of the thread is performed to the left with mantras associated with the upper lion-thrones.
Having offered prayers with hymns and performed protection by means of veiling rites,
one should likewise take a tooth-stick, perfume, sacrificial sandalwood, and clay.
Siddhārtha, as well as the dhātrī fruit, śṛṅgāra, bhūṣaṇa, and nakula—these eight are to be known in successive order. 18-46.
For the sake of attaining success, one should sequentially place the purifying thread and the vessel for the thread into bowls made of *aśvattha* leaves in the directions starting from the east.
Hu, Kāra, Soma, Svāhā, Īśa, Brahmā, Nāga, Śikhidhvaja, Sūrya, and Sadāśiva—these are all the nine supreme deities. (18.48)
In the Sūtras, one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa; and on the triple-thread (trisūtraka), Kṛpā, Pauruṣī, Vāṇī, Gāyatrī, and Aparājitā.
Vijayā and Jayā, the goddess Muktidā and Sadāśivā, Manonmanī as the ninth, and Sarvatomukhī as the tenth. (18.50)
The deities residing in the knots should be worshipped with the ritual services (upacāras) consisting of the constituent parts (kalās).

O Goddess of gods, O beloved, one should remember the sixteen eternal ones and Śrīvidyā;
one should worship the eight Tārās and the eight Vāṇīs in the place of the Kalās.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the Kālyā and the daily Nityās at dawn;
this is declared to be the procedure for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), after which the formal propitiation (ārādhana) shall take place. (18.53)
Following the daily worship (nityārcanā), this occasional rite (naimittika) should take place:
having duly worshipped the sacred threads (pavitrāṇi), one should provide a meal for the maidens.
Thereafter, one should worship one's own guru with garments, ornaments, and cattle according to one's ability; having prostrated, one should contemplate him in the form of the Goddess.
One should install the sacred thread (pavitra), avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
there, one should worship the Guru, who brings about the fruits of those respective rites. (18.56)
If he is not honored there, that ritual is always fruitless.
In the absence of the Guru, [one should honor] his son; in the absence of a son, his wife. (18.57)

In his absence, one should worship his grandson; in his absence, his daughter's son; and if none of these exist, in the absence of all others, one should worship another who is born of the Guru's lineage.
Wherever one worships the initiated [preceptor], there these rites become fruitful;
O Supreme Goddess, if he is not worshipped, they become fruitless. (18.59)
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and subsequently burnt the purificatory grass (pavitraka) in the fire,
one should worship the discus in the presence of the perfected ones (siddhas), honor it, and offer it as a gift.
"For one who does not perform worship in the fire, his dharma is fruitless.
Thus has it been declared in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (18.61)

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Transmission Initiation and the Investiture of the Purifier," in the first section of the northern part of the *Śrī-Śaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 18 ||
The Nineteenth Chapter.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear an ancient history."
The illustrious Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is the most secret of secrets.
For you, who are devoted to faith, nothing remains untold by me;
nor should this be spoken by you to anyone else, even at the cost of your own life. (19.2)
This is the secret of the gods for one desiring all perfections;
it is not a yoga consisting of knowledge, nor a ritual procedure, nor a formal worship.
There is no other practice, no recitation, no fire-offering, and no worship that can equal even a thousandth part of the secret [teaching] which is about to be described. (19.4)
In former times, royal sages attained perfection through her grace:
Kairava, Vṛhadaśva, Somadatta, and Bṛhadratha. (19.5)
Ajamīḍha, Kārttavīrya, Bhadrasena, Purūravas, Pṛthugrīva, Rantideva, Māndhātṛ, Nahuṣa, and Raghu. (19.6)
Vidūratha, Bharata, Divodāsa, Pratardana, Kṛśāśva, Jamadagni, Jaigīṣavya, and Devala; || 19-7 ||
Paiṭhīnasi, Vītihavya, Kaśyapa, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Saṃvarta, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Vyāsa, and likewise Śātānīka. (19–8)
Uddālaka, Bharadvāja, Jābāla, and likewise Jaimini;
[they attained] sovereignty over the seven continents and the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin). (19.9)
Former kings attained even a full measure of long life;
likewise, others achieved perfection in yoga and penance that accomplishes all goals.
The great seers have obtained the power to both curse and grace, and by whose favor the sovereignty over the three worlds remains within their grasp. (19.11)
Tārākṣa, Kamalākṣa, and likewise Vidyunmālī—
these three were indeed the brothers who were Daityas in the Kṛta Yuga.
O beloved, they performed severe divine penance for ten thousand years;
thereupon Prajāpati granted them the boon they had requested.
O Daityas, there were four boons granted to them; they were proud with the intoxication of their beauty.
One among them was the state of being unslayable by all living beings. (19.14)
The second [city] is situated at a distance of three hundred thousand *yojanas*; these three cities on earth cannot be overcome even by the gods. (19.15)
Having granted that boon, the Creator said: "Listen, my sons;
in all ways and throughout the three worlds, there is no immunity from death for anyone. (19.16)
O Dānavas, by every means possible, even through a single approach, you must all accept your own destruction. (19.17)
Having deliberated, they all said: "He who shall burn the three cities of the Tripuras with a single arrow in an instant—he shall be our death. (19.18)
Having said, "So be it," the Creator went to the world of Brahmā, which was filled with gods;
they too all acted exactly as had been previously deliberated.
O beloved, the golden city of Tārākṣa stands above them all; it is ten thousand yojanas in width and of the same extent in length.
The silver [city] of Kamalākṣa is ten thousand yojanas in extent;
that of Vidyunmālin is made of iron and is ten thousand [yojanas] in extent. (19–21)
Beyond three hundred thousand [yojanas] from them, at the limit of the sky, is their city,
provided with ramparts and moats, and likewise adorned with watchtowers.
It was adorned with banners, gate-towers, ladders, flags, and mechanical devices, and guarded by those bearing swords, nooses, goads, *ariṣṭa* weapons, maces, and bows. (19–23)
[He was accompanied] by thirty *nikharvas*, six *vṛndas*, ninety *arbudas*, and [ninety-six] *koṭis* of [beings] adorned with nooses, tridents, *bhuśuṇḍīs*, goads, discs, and mallets. (19–24)
Seeing each city overrun by the Dānavas, who were intoxicated with the pride of battle,
all the gods, including Indra, beheld such a calamity.
Some fled, some went forth as if under a curse,
some fought with the gods, and others abandoned the celestial realm.
Some entered the ocean, and some went to mountain caves;
some gave up their lives out of fear, while others fled in the four directions.
Seeing the gods in such a state, the lord of the deities went for refuge to Rudra, placing Prajāpati at his head.
Having prostrated themselves like a staff, those gods, together with Pitāmaha,
spoke with palms joined in reverence to Pinākin, the Lord of Umā.
"O Maheśāna, having obtained a boon from the Creator through their ascetic penance, the Tripura Asuras are harassing us, even though we dwell in mountain caves. (19.30)
O God, there is no one other than you who can grant us refuge; therefore, O Lord, Master of the Pramathas, we make this petition to you. (19–31)
Having gathered the celestial maidens, they lead them toward their own city; the world has become devoid of sacrifice, and the Nandana grove is stripped of its wish-fulfilling trees. (19.32)
The entire earth became devoid of humans, and even Amarāvatī was bereft of gods;
the rivers became waterless, and the seven oceans were stripped of their jewels.
Having hidden ourselves within the hollows of trees and on the necks of mountains,
we all remain there, afflicted by fear of him.
For among them, there is no teacher whatsoever in the three worlds other than you;
having slain those Asuras, establish us once again in heaven. (19.35)
Thus addressed by all who were prostrate before him, the bull-bannered Lord smiled and replied to all the gods, "Let my chariot be prepared."
Then Brahmā, smiling there, said to Maheśvara: "O Lord, a chariot must be fashioned; who is capable of mounting it other than you? (19.37)
He possesses no capacity at all for constructing that chariot, nor for its appropriate horses, weapons, armor, or even a turban. (19.38)
"O Śaṅkara, you yourself must decide today; whose intellect is there that could [doubt this]?
Being thus addressed by Brahmā, Śambhu spoke, gladdening the gods.
The four Vedas are like four horses; they undergo austerity through the *upākarma* rite.
Yet, when oppressed by the demon Śaṅkha, the Vedas depart from those who perform ritual actions. (19.40)
O Brahmin, through that asceticism of Tārākṣa and by the power of the upākarma rite, his [sin] was exhausted; Kāmalākṣa became purified. (19.41)
A rite of pacification performed for even a single year is remembered by the sages as *pavitra*.
Through the *pavitra*, the austerity of Kamalākṣa becomes perfected. (19.42)
The investiture with the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) is considered to be named "the auspiciousness of all" (sarvasvastyayana).
The four Vedas are the horses, and the earth is the complete chariot.
The sun and the moon shall be the two wheels; Mount Gandhamādana the pole-shaft;
the Vindhya mountain the nave; and Kailāsa shall indeed be the axle. (19.44)
May Mount Meru be my flagpole, and the Lord Brahmā my charioteer;
may the syllable Om be the whip, and the Purāṇas the reins. (19.45)
May Mount Mandara become my bow, Vāsuki my bowstring;
may Viṣṇu become my arrow, and may the winds enter my two arms.
Let Yama, Mṛtyu, and Kāla enter into the middle of the hoods;
let Vāsava be upon the back of the arrow, and both Kubera and Varuṇa [in their respective places]. (19.47)
In the position of your feathers reside all the deities;
the two Aśvins are situated on the two quills, and all the sacrifices are at your feet. (19.48)
It has eight parts and the ten sciences; it has a hundred stations and a hundred spokes.
The bamboo staff is thirty-six finger-breadths long and is joined with the mantra-binding.
The arrows have the form of the sun with its twelve finger-breadths (manvaṅgula) and range over Maināka;
Kālī knows Sadāśiva as the target for the Pināka bow.
Śaṅkara, by his own will, fashioned another simple [weapon];
yet Śiva, having obtained the sixfold weapon and armor, was without protection.
Not having obtained a protection suitable for himself, Śambhu became anxious.
Closing his three eyes, the Lord of the World remained there for a long time.
Then, having entered into meditative absorption, he praised Viśvatāriṇī;
having offered praise, he prayed for the tenfold supreme protection.
Then she also bestowed upon him ten kinds of supreme protection;
this protection, consisting of the ten sciences, is named "Victory over the Three Worlds."
O Brahmin, because it illuminates the Vedas, it is proclaimed as the Illuminating Weapon (Dīpakāstra);
it is the sovereign queen of the eighty-four divisions [of Tantra], the knowledge higher than the highest. (19.55)
(166) Endowed with these nine traditional methods, she is the shatterer of the cosmic egg;
known as the weapon of paralyzing power in heaven, she is the conqueror of the three worlds on earth. (19.56)
The weapon of attraction in the netherworld (pātāla), the destroyer of the demon Tripura, known as Kālīmukhā, [is effective] against enemy people as well as against those who dispute. (19.57)
She is proclaimed as Tārāmukhā, yet she has the form of Chinnā in every respect;
she is the embodiment of the Triśakti-vidyā, known by the name Trailokyavijayā. (19.58)
For the sake of destroying the three [cities] and for the supreme protection of the triple power,
Śaṅkara, having arrived, departed toward Tripura well-satisfied.
And having aimed the Pāśupata weapon, the bull-bannered god pierced the three cities of the Daityas with a single arrow.
In an instant, having been reduced to ashes, the Daityas went to the abode of Yama;
from that time forth, O Śrī Devī, you became renowned as Rakṣā (the Protectress).
"The protection called 'Supramundane' shall arise through mindfulness of me.
Thus was this event related as it occurred in the past; therefore, it is proclaimed as "Protection" (Rakṣā).
The man who wears a thread consecrated with this mantra finds protection from all wicked and harmful beings. (19.63)
Great poisons, great spirits, pūtanas, rākṣasas, and others, as well as cruel daityas and dānavas, perish in a mere instant. (19.64)
This very protection was revealed in the past to Baṭuka;
having bound it with the ten Great Vidyās, [it was bestowed] upon Baṭukabhairava. (19.65)
O Goddess, one should in every way bind the yantra, the banner, and the thread, interwoven with the syllables of the mantra; thus, protection will be accomplished in all respects.
O Auspicious One, this event occurred long ago in the month of Śrāvaṇa;
it must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret like one's own private parts. (19.67)
Thus has it been briefly proclaimed; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends [the section] in the first part of the Uttarabhāga of the Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and the great and fierce Tārā.
The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Upākarma, the Pavitrāropaṇa, and the Protective Rite."
The Twentieth Chapter.
The Holy Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the ritual procedure for the installation of Madana."
Śrī Śiva said:
Just as the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) is performed, so too is the worship of Madana.
The three months beginning with Caitra consist of two fortnights each, the bright and the dark;
among these, each preceding period of time is superior to the one that follows. (20.2)
On the eighth, the fourteenth, or even on the full moon day,
one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) during the first part of the night, or immediately.
Having addressed Madana at the altar with the four Kalpalatās and others,
he was bathed with the water from the eyes of Rati, which had arisen from the eyes of Kāma.
O deluder of the ṛṣis, gandharvas, and siddhas, homage be to you!
O you who have arisen from the grace of Śiva, be present here. (20.5)
"Having completely severed all that is contrary to Śiva, you must be led away by the command of Śiva";
having thus addressed Rati and Kāma, the wise man should worship them there. (20.6)
Having personally uprooted Madana along with his roots and sprouts, or else having had him brought by another, she presented him to the Lord for a price.
O Goddess, one should place it on the left within the Sarvatobhadra lotus;
one should then place Madana in a vessel with eight spokes and worship it again.
“O Bhuvaneśānī, ‘Praṇavaṃ bhuvaneśāni rataye namaḥ’—this, O Maheśānī, is the mantra of Rati; now the mantra of Kāma is being told. (20.9)
One should worship Madana, situated in the pericarp, there with these two mantras: "Oṃ" (the Praṇava), "Kāmabīja," and "Kāmāya namaḥ. (10)
Then, one should place small boxes upon the petals of that lotus, starting from the east,
using eight mantras for each of the eight directions, containing the eight substances in their respective order.
Kāma, Bhasmaśarīra, Anaṅga, Manmatha, he whose face is like springtime, Smara, and the bearer of the sugarcane bow. || 20-12 ||
Puṣpabāṇa, Tārā, and the others are proclaimed to have prominent teeth;
then, O Dear One, [one should add] camphor, the two types of rocanā, and musk. (20.13)
O Pārvatī, one should prepare the eight substances consisting of agallochum, saffron, the fruit of the āmalakī, sandalwood, and fragrant flowers. (20.14)
Having properly worshipped Madana with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings,
one should, with a serene mind, recite the Anaṅga-gāyatrī as much as one is able.
Having said "to Kāmadeva," one should then say "vidmahe";
thus there is the Aṅgagāyatrī: "tanno 'naṅgaḥ pracodayāt. (20.16)
Homage be to the one whose arrows are flowers, who brings joy to the world, to Manmatha, and to him who is dear to Rati and Prīti, the eyes of the world. (20.17)
O Goddess, after this mantra, one should then offer salutations;
then, with Madana in hand, one should perform the supplication with divine [mantras]. (20.18)
O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, you have been summoned by me at this very moment;
however, according to my capacity, I shall perform each preceding rite in due order under your command. (20.19)
One should satisfy the Triple Power (triśakti) with the mantra known as *vijñāpanā*.
Then, O Goddess of Gods, one should worship her with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and other offerings. (20.20)
O Mother of the World consisting of sixteen syllables, O Bestower of the fruits of desired objects, O Goddess, Sovereign of Kāmeśvarī, fulfill my rites and my desires! (20–21)
O Goddess, O Sovereign, one should pray with this [mantra] and afterwards worship Madana;
then one should perform the veiling with the armor-mantra, protected by the weapon-mantra as well.
Then one should perform the vigil; however, if the vigil has not been performed immediately, then having risen in the morning, one should perform the daily worship.
Then one should perform the prognostication and the worship of Madana;
by that alone, the great worship is accomplished, and the middle [grade] flower is thus described.
Having prepared an excellent food offering (naivedya) that is pleasing to the mind according to the prescribed rules, one should offer betel leaf with camphor and then offer this prayer: || 20-25 ||
O Mistress of all the circles of the mandala, O Embodiment of all vidyās, O Mother of the gods, by your command, let this which I desire come to pass for me. (20–26)
Then, having worshipped his own guru with flowers, incense, garments, and other offerings,
and having given him the *madanaka* fruit, he should bow down to him and propitiate him.
Then one should joyfully engage in water-sports together with the initiates (samayins),
and, accompanied by friends, one should perform the distribution of food.
Thus, for the wise man who performs this procedure for the installation of Madana,
his annual worship shall become a source of delight for the Three Śaktis.
Thus has the history been told in detail in brief;
now I shall explain the general [method] by which one attains accomplishment.
O Goddess, when Madana was reduced to ashes for the purpose of destroying my asceticism during my birth as a mountain, Rati and Prīti were then deeply distressed. (20.31)
O Śivā, the creeper of passion was born from the tears of her eyes;
O beautiful-eyed one, its fragrance and its excellence were truly great.
Being pleased by that, O beloved, a boon was granted from my heart;
therefore, for the sake of Rati and Prīti, Madana was manifested.
And for that practitioner who worships Madana for half a year, his worship of Madana will be equivalent to a full year's worship. || 20-34 ||
"Thus, O goddess worshipped by the gods, this boon was granted to him by me alone;
otherwise, all that fruit of his actions would have resulted only in the fulfillment of his desires. (20.35)
Therefore, O one worshipped by heroes, the worship with *madana* and other rites should be performed;
having taken the *madana* plant together with its roots, one should place it in a lotus-shaped vessel. (20.36)
Having divided Madana into nine parts, one should worship them immediately thereafter with the seed-syllable of the sound of bliss (Ānandasvara) together with the Bindu in nine ways.
One should worship Madana in sequence with the nine kinds of jewels and other offerings;
thereafter, one should indeed consecrate him with the Aghora-vidyā.
Or, as previously described, one should perform protection with the Astra-mantra while [the deity] is seated upon the lion-throne in the southern direction, and concealment with the Kavaca-mantra.
One should brandish the bound trident-mudrā above the Madana tree;
on the fourteenth day of the month of Caitra, the consecration of the Madana tree shall take place.
One should worship with the weapon-mantra facing upward and with the heart-mantra;
indeed, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) at the base of the sandalwood tree.
On the first day, one should perform the unsurpassed preliminary consecration (adhivāsa),
or even an immediate consecration, for the sake of obtaining the fruit of a year’s worship.
At dawn on the fourteenth day, one should then perform the daily worship;
having fashioned a nine-cornered figure of great luster with vermilion (sindūra). (20.43)
The best of teachers, having consecrated nine vessels filled with gold, silver, and other materials, or a single beautiful pitcher, should establish it there.
Having fashioned a mandala to the right, adorned with saffron and other pigments,
one should draw an Aśoka tree and then delineate a triangular mandala.
In the center of that, O Dear One, one should worship Kāma, who has the luster of Varuṇa,
wearing red garments and adorned with red ornaments, on the left and right sides.
For the sake of attaining all perfections, one should worship Kāma, who is accompanied by Vasanta, who wields the bow of five arrows, and who is enriched by the splendor of Rati and Prīti.
O Bhuvaneśānī, having extracted the Vāgbhava, Śrī, and Kāma, along with "Kāmāya namaḥ," this nine-syllable mantra was revealed, O lady of excellent complexion. (20.48)
The three seed-syllables of desire have been proclaimed; one should first write the syllable *Ātma*.
"Obeisance to Rati" (*ratyai namaḥ*)—this eight-syllabled mantra of Rati, O fair-faced one, [should be written]. (20.49)
One should utter "prīti" (joy) in the place of rati; the mantra for joy consists of eight syllables.
Gaurī and Śyāmā are Rati and Prīti; they are used in the rites of wandering and adorning with garlands.
Having meditated on the interior of the heart of Kāma, which is the color of a lotus and betel and is resplendent with red garments, upon the left and right [sides]. (20.51)
Thereafter, one should worship Vasanta, who dwells in the midst of a Kadamba forest,
fair-complexioned and holding in his left hand a jar filled with nectar.
Having worshipped Kāma together with his limbs, while he holds a collection of various flowers in his right hand, one should then present incense, lamps, and other offerings. (20.53)
O Goddess of the gods, having worshipped correctly Him who embodies all the deities, one should properly worship the Krama and then feed a young maiden. (20.54)
Having worshipped the married women, one should worship the assembly of Yoginīs;
the Brāhmaṇas and people of various philosophical schools should be honored on all sides. (20.55)
Thereafter, one should perform the limb-offering (aṅgahavana) and honor the Guru with ornaments such as jewels,
thousands of bhāras of gold, and delightful divine garments.
O Goddess, after performing worship, the Madanāropaṇa rite is then prescribed;
O Daughter of the Mountain, the annual worship of that [deity] becomes fruitful.
Thus has it been briefly proclaimed; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the [chapter] titled "The Installation of Madana" in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā, within the first section of the Uttarabhāga of the glorious Śaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja.
The twentieth chapter. || 20 ||
The Twenty-first Chapter.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear another excellent secret."
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Goddess of gods, even though it is a secret, [I shall speak] by virtue of the application of the sequence of the *samaya*.
I shall now fully explain the rules regarding the transcription of the Tantra:
